title: Cell type versus reversible cell state
open: Which molecular differences distinguish a persistent neuronal or glial cell type from a reversible state — driven by activity, metabolism, development, or disease? Formally, the goal is a framework that predicts longitudinal cell identity and state transitions under controlled perturbations.
status: Whole-mouse-brain and adult-human-brain transcriptomic atlases — Yao et al. (2023), DOI `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`, and Siletti et al. (2023), DOI `10.1126/science.add7046` — greatly expanded cell-type classification in 2023, but static molecular clusters do not by themselves resolve the type-versus-state distinction.
solved_when: A framework exists that can predict longitudinal identity and state transitions under controlled perturbations, separating type-defining differences from reversible state-dependent ones.
why: It establishes what a cell census should actually count and which molecular classifications can support causal experiments rather than merely descriptive clustering.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Functional proteome beyond the transcriptome
open: Can we measure, in the very same identified cells, RNA levels, protein abundance, protein localization, and protein modification state alongside physiology — and does adding these molecular layers actually improve our ability to predict a cell's function beyond what the transcriptome alone tells us?
status: The 2023 brain atlases — Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain* (DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`) and Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain* (DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`) — establish transcriptomic and regulatory reference points; however, a transcript count is not a measurement of localized functional protein.
solved_when: Matched multi-layer measurements (RNA, protein abundance, localization, modification state, and physiology) exist in identified cells, with a demonstrated determination of which additional molecular layers materially improve functional prediction over transcriptomic classification alone.
why: It would resolve the growing discrepancy between molecular classification of cell types and the actual behavior of those cells.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Physiological functions of synaptic condensates
open: When, if ever, are phase-separated synaptic assemblies actually required for organizing synaptic vesicles or supporting plasticity in living brains? A definitive answer requires perturbing the phase behavior itself, independently of changes in protein concentration or binding affinity.
status: Synapsin–vesicle phase separation was demonstrated by Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`; however, that result does not by itself establish the full in-vivo causal role.
solved_when: An in-vivo experiment shows that selectively disrupting phase separation at synapses — while holding protein concentration and binding affinity fixed — alters vesicle organization or plasticity, or conversely demonstrates no such effect under equivalent perturbation.
why: It would distinguish a genuine mechanistic organizational principle from an in-vitro analogy, determining whether condensate physics is a useful framework for understanding synaptic function.
key_works: Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.

title: Molecular identity of synaptic tags
open: What molecular states mark particular synapses so that later-arriving plasticity-related products are captured there rather than elsewhere? A satisfying answer should specify these tags' lifetimes, their synapse specificity, and how they are reset.
status: Synaptic tagging was experimentally established by Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`; identifying a complete, context-general molecular implementation remains open.
solved_when: The molecular species (or states) constituting the synaptic tag are identified, together with quantitative characterization of their lifetimes, specificity, and reset mechanisms — valid as a complete, context-general implementation rather than a single-case account.
why: It explains how a neuron routes broadly produced resources to selected synapses, which is the core of input-specific long-term plasticity.
key_works: Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Synaptic memory despite molecular turnover
open: How can a memory stored as a synaptic modification persist when the molecules that embody it are continually replaced? A satisfactory answer would exhibit a maintenance mechanism that accounts for both the long-term persistence of a memory trace and its selective erasure.
status: Multiscale synaptic models provide favorable retention properties, but their biological state variables and renewal mechanisms remain to be established.
solved_when: A maintenance mechanism is demonstrated that predicts both persistence and selective erasure of a synaptic modification despite turnover of its constituent molecules.
why: It resolves the mismatch between short molecular lifetimes and long memory lifetimes, determining whether synapses can in principle serve as durable physical substrates for memory.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Dendritic computations actually used during behavior
open: Which nonlinear dendritic operations are actually necessary for specific natural behaviors, rather than merely possible under controlled stimulation?
status: Human cortical dendrites exhibit powerful nonlinear computations ex vivo; their deployment during ordinary human behavior is not established by those experiments. Key works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.
solved_when: Particular natural behaviors are shown to depend causally on specific nonlinear dendritic operations — that is, the operations are established as necessary, not just demonstrable, in vivo.
why: It settles whether neurons should be modeled as single computational units or as structured computational networks.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.

title: Myelin’s timing versus metabolic contributions
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Can we experimentally disentangle myelin's role in speeding electrical conduction from its role in metabolically supporting the axon, and measure how much each contributes to learning and long-term axonal survival?
status: Learning-related myelination is causally implicated (McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`), but disrupting myelin-related processes can affect several functions simultaneously, so the contributions remain unseparated. Relevant metabolic context comes from Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.
solved_when: A preparation or intervention is demonstrated that isolates myelin-dependent conduction-timing changes from myelin-dependent metabolic-support changes, with a quantitative accounting of each mechanism's respective contribution to learning and long-term axonal survival.
why: It determines which myelin functions a therapy must restore — timing, metabolic support, or both — rather than treating myelin as a single undifferentiated target.
key_works: McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Branch-specific axonal transmission reliability
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: During natural activity, does an action potential reliably invade every branch of an identified axon, and can branch-specific failures or timing changes be predicted? A successful answer would characterize, for each branch of a single identified axon, the conditions under which transmission succeeds or fails in vivo.
status: Dense connectomes establish the branching geometry of axons, but anatomical continuity does not establish reliable, state-independent transmission to every terminal.
solved_when: An experimental measurement of branch-specific action-potential invasion during natural activity is obtained for an identified axon, together with a predictive account of which branches fail and how timing changes across branches.
why: It tests whether an axon broadcasts one identical message to all of its targets, or whether branch-level transmission failures make individual targets receive distinct messages.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`.

title: Predictive developmental wiring code
open: Can we predict, from lineage, molecular recognition, geometry, and developmental activity, which individual neurons will connect to which — and does the prediction survive when one component of the developmental program is altered? Formally, this asks for a predictive wiring law validated by targeted perturbation of the developmental program, not merely a description of mature connectivity.
status: Modern cell atlases and connectomes — e.g., Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y` — provide endpoints, but they do not constitute a generative developmental wiring law.
solved_when: A predictive rule correctly identifies which individual neurons connect using lineage, molecular recognition, geometry, and developmental activity, and its predictions remain valid after altering one component of the developmental program.
why: It would connect developmental biology to mature circuit architecture, turning static connectomes into generative explanations of how circuits are built.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`.

title: Context-specific necessity of gliotransmission
open: Which astrocyte populations actually release transmitters under physiological conditions, and in which circuits or behaviors is that release necessary? Formally, the goal is a cell-type-specific, context-resolved map of gliotransmission and its causal necessity for circuit computation and behavior.
status: A specialized glutamatergic astrocyte population was reported in de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`; this does not establish universal glutamate release by astrocytes.
solved_when: Specific astrocyte populations are identified as releasing transmitters under physiological conditions, with causal evidence (cell-type-specific intervention) showing when that release is necessary for a defined circuit computation or behavior.
why: It resolves a major mechanistic dispute about gliotransmission without treating astrocytes as a uniform class.
key_works: de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Synapse-specific selection for elimination
open: What makes a single synapse a target for removal rather than its neighbor? Formally, identify the combination of activity, complement, surface signals, and microglial state that determines whether a particular synapse is removed or spared.
status: Complement-dependent elimination and activity-dependent microglial pruning were established in 2007–2012, notably by Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`, and Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`; a predictive synapse-by-synapse selection rule remains open.
solved_when: A predictive synapse-by-synapse selection rule is specified that accounts for the joint contributions of activity, complement, surface signals, and microglial state and correctly predicts removal versus sparing of individual synapses.
why: Such a rule would allow targeted preservation or removal of specific neural connections.
key_works: Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`; Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.

title: Reconciling sleep-dependent clearance measurements
open: Do sleep and anesthesia actually reduce brain waste clearance, or do the conflicting measurements reflect differences in tracers, compartments, behavioral states, and analysis rather than in the underlying physiology? A resolution requires experiments with matched methods and transport models that can separately quantify tracer entry, redistribution, and true elimination.
status: Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`, reported reduced clearance during sleep and anesthesia; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`, implicated sleep-related vasomotion in glymphatic clearance. The assays and mechanisms in these studies have not been directly reconciled.
solved_when: The apparent conflict between the reported findings is directly reconciled: matched-tracer, matched-compartment, matched-state measurements, analyzed with transport models that distinguish entry, redistribution, and elimination, yield a consistent account of both datasets.
why: It determines whether proposed clearance therapies target the correct physiological process — a therapy aimed at the wrong mechanism (e.g., reduced clearance vs. vasomotion-driven clearance) would fail or misdirect clinical effort.
key_works: Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Noninvasive human clearance quantification
open: Can we measure how the human brain clears solutes noninvasively — with a method that is validated, repeatable, and free of invasive tracer administration, while distinguishing the relevant compartments? In other words, is there a routine human assay of brain solute elimination that resolves the compartments through which clearance actually occurs?
status: Mechanistic animal studies and anatomical drainage discoveries provide the foundations, but their measurements are not automatically transferable to routine human monitoring. Key works include Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`; and Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`.
solved_when: A validated, repeatable method exists for quantifying brain solute elimination in humans that requires no invasive tracer administration and distinguishes the relevant compartments.
why: It would make clearance hypotheses testable in longitudinal human studies, which is currently impossible with invasive-tracer approaches.
key_works: Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`; Miao et al. (2024), *Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-024-01638-y`.

title: Learning without symmetric feedback weights
open: Can accurate multilayer learning be achieved with biologically realistic feedback that lacks the symmetric weight transport required by backpropagation, and conversely, in which settings is such asymmetric feedback provably insufficient?
status: Feedback alignment and inference-based learning supply partial computational solutions, but their biological implementation and general guarantees remain open. Key works: Lillicrap et al. (2016), *Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning*, DOI: `10.1038/ncomms13276`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.
solved_when: A characterization is given — sufficient conditions under which asymmetric feedback supports accurate multilayer learning, and impossibility results delimiting when it cannot — with general guarantees beyond partial computational solutions.
why: It determines whether the weight-transport obstacle to biologically plausible learning is a fundamental limitation or merely an artifact of the architecture, shaping which learning rules the brain could plausibly implement.
key_works: Lillicrap et al. (2016), *Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning*, DOI: `10.1038/ncomms13276`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.

title: Genuine neural criticality versus statistical lookalikes
open: How can we tell whether neural activity is genuinely critical when noncritical systems can generate deceptively similar avalanche statistics? The question is to find criteria or tests that distinguish true critical dynamics from statistical lookalikes produced by subsampling, filtering, or external drive.
status: Neuronal avalanches were reported by Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`; power-law-like observations alone do not settle the underlying dynamical regime.
solved_when: A method exists that reliably discriminates true critical dynamics from noncritical lookalikes (subsampled, filtered, or externally driven systems) across realistic measurement conditions.
why: It tests a major proposed organizing principle of neural activity, determining whether the critical brain hypothesis has genuine dynamical content or is an artifact of measurement.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.

title: Predictive coding versus alternative mismatch mechanisms
open: Can we design experiments that tell whether a neural mismatch response reflects genuine prediction-error computation, as opposed to adaptation, movement-related feedback, or some other mechanism that produces the same signal? In other words, what discriminating interventions separate explicit predictive coding from observationally similar alternatives in visual cortex?
status: Sensorimotor mismatch signals were reported in mouse visual cortex in 2012 (Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`), following the predictive-coding framework of Rao and Ballard (1999), *Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects*, DOI: `10.1038/4580`; however, the mismatch response alone does not uniquely identify a predictive-coding architecture.
solved_when: A set of experimental interventions is specified and carried out whose outcomes are consistent with explicit prediction-error computation but cannot be explained by adaptation, movement feedback, or other competing mismatch-generating mechanisms.
why: Predictive coding is a widely used explanatory framework for visual responses, and without discriminating tests it remains unfalsifiable in the face of mismatch signals it predicts.
key_works: Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`; Rao and Ballard (1999), *Predictive coding in the visual cortex: a functional interpretation of some extra-classical receptive-field effects*, DOI: `10.1038/4580`.

title: Causal selection of one speaker in a crowd
open: How does the brain causally select one speaker's representation in a multi-talker scene while retaining the ability to switch attention to another speaker? In formal terms, what are the causal contributions of auditory cortical and control circuits to this selective representation and target switching?
status: Selective cortical representation of an attended speaker was demonstrated in 2012 by Mesgarani and Chang, *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; however, a representation does not itself establish the selection mechanism.
solved_when: The selection mechanism is identified: the causal roles of auditory and control circuits in selecting one speaker's representation and enabling switching between speakers are established experimentally, going beyond demonstrating that a selective representation exists.
why: It explains a central limitation of real-world hearing — the inability to follow one voice among many — and connects to blind source separation in signal processing and attention under overlapping inputs in AI.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.

title: Reliable human cochlear-synaptopathy diagnosis
open: Is there a noninvasive measure that can quantify cochlear synapse loss in an individual person and predict that person's specific hearing difficulties, independently of other auditory damage?
status: Mouse work established lasting neural degeneration after apparently temporary noise-related threshold changes in 2009 (Kujawa and Liberman, *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after "temporary" noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`); individual human quantification remains a distinct challenge.
solved_when: A validated noninvasive marker exists that quantifies cochlear synapse loss at the individual level and predicts specific hearing difficulties independently of other auditory damage.
why: It makes otherwise hidden injury measurable before major threshold loss.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`.

title: Nonlinear perception of odor mixtures
open: When is a mixture of odorants perceived as its constituent components, as a new unified odor, or as a suppression of some components? The goal is a predictive account that determines the perceptual regime from component identity, concentration, and prior exposure.
status: Single-molecule perceptual models and receptor-interaction studies supply pieces of the problem, but mixture perception is not reducible to averaging component descriptors. Key works include Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`, and Fukutani et al. (2023), *Antagonistic interactions between odorants alter human odor perception` (verify bibliographic identifier).
solved_when: A model is given that predicts, from component identity, concentration, and prior exposure of a mixture, whether perception will be elemental, configural, or suppressive — verified against empirical mixture-perception data.
why: Most natural olfactory environments contain mixtures, so understanding how mixtures are perceived is essential for any general account of smell; moreover, since mixture perception is not reducible to averaging component descriptors, current single-odor models fail exactly where real-world olfaction lives.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Fukutani et al. (2023), *Antagonistic interactions between odorants alter human odor perception* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Motor cortical dynamics-to-muscle commands
open: Which dimensions of motor cortical population activity causally drive muscle activation, and which instead reflect movement preparation, sensory feedback, or correlated internal state? Formally, the goal is to identify the causal mapping from population dynamics to motor output, separating output-generating dimensions from other structured activity.
status: Rotational population dynamics were demonstrated during reaching in 2012 (Churchland et al., 2012, *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`), and subsequent work argued such dynamics are better explained by a dynamical system than representational tuning (Michaels, Dann, and Scherberger, 2016, *Neural Population Dynamics during Reaching Are Better Explained by a Dynamical System than Representational Tuning*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005175`). However, descriptive dynamics do not by themselves identify the output-generating mechanism.
solved_when: A framework or analysis exists that identifies, within recorded motor population activity, which dimensions causally generate muscle activation versus those reflecting preparation, feedback, or correlated internal state, and this separation is validated against physical movement output.
why: It connects population-level models of motor cortex to actual physical movement, turning descriptive dynamics into a mechanistic account of how cortical activity produces muscle commands.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Michaels, Dann, and Scherberger (2016), *Neural Population Dynamics during Reaching Are Better Explained by a Dynamical System than Representational Tuning*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005175`.

title: Cerebellar credit assignment for delayed outcomes
open: How does cerebellar plasticity manage to associate an outcome with the specific earlier neural activity that caused it, once the delay between them exceeds a simple coincidence window? In formal terms, what temporal eligibility mechanism links reward expectation signals in cerebellar circuits to particular synapses across extended delays?
status: Reward expectations are known to be represented in cerebellar circuits, as shown by Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; however, the temporal eligibility mechanism linking these representations to particular synapses remains a separate open question. Related theoretical work includes Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`, with connections to reinforcement learning (delayed credit) and chemical kinetics (eligibility-trace lifetimes).
solved_when: A mechanism is identified — experimentally characterized — that explains how cerebellar plasticity assigns credit to the relevant earlier synaptic activity for outcomes arriving after delays longer than a simple coincidence window.
why: It would explain how learning succeeds in temporally extended real-world actions, where causes and outcomes are separated in time.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`.

title: Joining local maps into global knowledge
open: Explain how separately learned spatial representations are aligned when an animal discovers a connection between environments, including inconsistent or ambiguous correspondences.
status: Place-code dynamics demonstrate representational flexibility, but do not specify a general map-merging algorithm.
why: Explains flexible route planning and discovery of shortcuts.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`; Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Physiological-state-dependent value
open: How do bodily states such as thirst, hunger, and fatigue transform the value an animal assigns to outcomes and its willingness to work for them? A satisfying theory would specify the computation that maps physiological state variables to subjective value and effort-based decisions.
status: Thirst circuits have been shown to anticipate the physiological consequences of eating and drinking (Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`), and dopamine signals dissociate aspects of motivation such as learning versus willingness to work (Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`); however, a unified state-to-value computation remains open.
solved_when: A unified, testable account exists of how internal physiological states are integrated into value signals and motivation to work, explaining the state-dependence of valuation across such states.
why: It would connect homeostatic regulation to flexible decision-making, showing how the brain maintains internal balance while still supporting adaptive choice.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Redundant mechanisms of social attachment
open: How does social attachment persist when a proposed signaling pathway, such as oxytocin receptor signaling, is absent — and which of developmental compensation, redundant circuitry, or context-dependent necessity explains it?
status: Oxytocin-receptor knockout prairie voles retained social attachment in a 2023 study (Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, Neuron; PMID: `36708707`), challenging simple claims of universal receptor necessity.
solved_when: An experimental account distinguishes among developmental compensation, redundant circuitry, and context-dependent necessity, explaining how attachment is retained when the pathway is missing.
why: It prevents overgeneralizing a single molecule into a complete social mechanism.
key_works: Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, Neuron; PMID: `36708707`.

title: Cellular variables that generate sleep need
open: Which cellular quantities, accumulated during wakefulness, causally generate the pressure to sleep — and do different cell populations track different components of that need?
status: Clearance and vascular studies — including Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`, and Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027` — establish processes linked to sleep, but none alone establishes the complete variable that makes sleep necessary.
solved_when: A specific cellular variable (or set of variables) accumulated during wakefulness is shown to causally generate sleep pressure, and it is determined whether distinct cell populations track distinct needs.
why: It separates the causes of sleep need from processes that merely occur during sleep, giving a mechanistic account of why sleep is necessary.
key_works: Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Human enteric functional diversity
open: Which molecularly defined human enteric populations actually carry out distinct sensory, motor, and secretory functions, and how do those functions vary along the gut?
status: The 2020 atlas by Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`, identifies candidate populations; direct human functional assignments remain a separate experimental program.
solved_when: Human enteric populations defined at single-cell resolution have direct experimental functional assignments for sensory, motor, and secretory roles, mapped along the gut axis.
why: It enables cell-selective treatment rather than broad modulation of gut activity.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Complete magnetoreception mechanism
open: Can we trace, in a single defined species, the full chain from a magnetic-field sensor to navigation behavior — identifying the in-vivo receptor, the physical transduction process, the neural pathway carrying the signal, and the behavioral readout it produces?
status: Cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird showed magnetic sensitivity in 2021 experiments, but this falls short of a complete receptor-to-navigation causal chain. Key work: Xu et al. (2021), *Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9`.
solved_when: A single species has an experimentally verified causal chain: an identified in-vivo magnetoreceptor, a characterized physical transduction mechanism, a mapped neural pathway to the relevant circuits, and a demonstrated behavioral readout of magnetic orientation.
why: It would connect a subtle quantum-level physical effect to a fully verified sensory system, establishing magnetoreception as a understood sense rather than a candidate mechanism.
key_works: Xu et al. (2021), *Magnetic sensitivity of cryptochrome 4 from a migratory songbird*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-03618-9`.

title: Toxic tau species and causal propagation
open: Which tau assemblies actually drive neuronal dysfunction, which are merely markers of disease, and which cellular processes are required for tau to spread between cells?
status: Human Alzheimer tau filament structures were resolved by cryo-EM in Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`; however, structural identification does not establish that every observed assembly has the same toxicity or propagation role.
solved_when: The tau species present in disease are catalogued with demonstrated causal roles — each identified as toxic driver, marker, or propagation-competent — and the cellular processes necessary for intercellular spread are experimentally established.
why: A solution lets anti-tau therapies be aimed at the assemblies and processes that matter, rather than at bystanders.
key_works: Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.

title: Durable benefit from dopaminergic cell replacement
open: Can implanted dopamine-producing neurons deliver lasting, controlled clinical benefit in patients with Parkinson’s disease? More formally: can replacement dopaminergic cells achieve stable integration, appropriate functional regulation, and protection from recurrent pathology over the long term?
status: A 2025 phase I trial of hES-derived dopaminergic cells is an important milestone; its early safety and feasibility results do not settle durable comparative efficacy. Key work: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.
solved_when: Long-term, controlled clinical evidence demonstrates durable benefit from replacement dopamine neurons, including stable integration, appropriate regulation, and protection from recurrent pathology.
why: A solution determines whether cell replacement can become a reproducible restorative treatment for Parkinson’s disease rather than an experimental procedure.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.

title: Broad functional restoration after spinal cord injury
open: Can a person with spinal cord injury regain coordinated mobility together with sensory and autonomic function — not just a single assisted motor task — across the diverse range of injuries seen clinically? In formal terms, the goal is broad functional restoration spanning motor, sensory, and autonomic domains over heterogeneous injury profiles.
status: The 2023 brain–spine interface restored walking in a proof-of-concept setting (Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`); general recovery across people and functions remains open.
solved_when: Functional restoration is demonstrated that spans coordinated mobility, sensory, and autonomic functions across diverse injuries, rather than a single assisted motor task in a proof-of-concept setting.
why: It targets the full burden of spinal cord injury, which single-task demonstrations leave unaddressed.
key_works: Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Adult-like maturation of human neural organoids
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Can human neural organoids be driven to a state of genuine adult-like maturation across molecular, electrophysiological, metabolic, and plasticity measures, rather than a state validated by a single marker?
status: Organoids currently model aspects of development, and transplantation improves maturation and integration; fully validated adult-like equivalence remains a separate target. Key works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.
solved_when: Organoids are produced and validated as adult-like across molecular, electrophysiological, metabolic, and plasticity properties, with maturation assessed multidimensionally rather than by any one marker alone.
why: It enables better models of adult disease and physiology, which immature organoids cannot faithfully represent.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Simultaneous whole-brain cellular recording in behaving mammals
open: Can we record the relevant fast activity of every relevant cell in a mammalian brain at once, while the animal behaves normally? That is, achieve simultaneous cellular-resolution recording across an entire behaving mammalian brain, with quantified coverage and without perturbing behavior.
status: The 2025 brain-wide mouse map of the International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`, aggregates extensive recordings across animals and sessions; it is not simultaneous cellular recording of one whole brain. High-density probes such as those of Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`, enable stable long-term recordings but at far from whole-brain scale.
solved_when: Fast activity is recorded simultaneously across an entire mammalian brain at cellular resolution in a behaving animal, with coverage explicitly quantified and normal behavior preserved.
why: It resolves patterns of coordination across brain areas that cannot be reconstructed reliably from recordings pieced together across separate sessions.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: R10.03. The approximately 150-CAG transition in Huntington’s neurons
open: Is the sharp change observed near roughly 150 somatic HTT CAG repeats a genuine causal biological threshold for neuronal failure, a collection of cell-type-specific thresholds, or an apparent boundary produced by sampling bias and selective loss of the most vulnerable cells? A satisfactory answer should predict the transition from repeat length, interruption structure, cell identity, and age.
status: A 2025 single-cell study (Handsaker et al. (2025), *Long somatic DNA-repeat expansion drives neurodegeneration in Huntington’s disease*, PMID: `39824182`) linked extensive somatic expansion to loss of striatal projection-neuron identity, with a marked transition around 150 repeats in the sampled cells. This result should not be read as establishing an invariant threshold for every neuronal population or patient.
solved_when: There exists a validated account of the approximately 150-repeat transition — causal threshold, distributed cell-specific thresholds, or sampling artifact — that predicts the transition as a function of repeat length, interruption structure, cell identity, and age, and that distinguishes these explanations across neuronal populations and patients.
why: It would convert repeat-length measurements into mechanistically grounded estimates of how close a given neuron is to failure, rather than treating an observed boundary as an invariant law.
key_works: Handsaker et al. (2025), *Long somatic DNA-repeat expansion drives neurodegeneration in Huntington’s disease*, PMID: `39824182`.

title: R10.04. Suppressing MSH3 without exchanging repeat expansion for other genomic damage
open: Can we find a window of tissue and time in which lowering MSH3 activity suppresses pathogenic repeat expansion without trading it for other kinds of genomic damage? Formally, the goal is to define a tissue-specific and time-dependent intervention window in which MSH3 reduction meaningfully stabilizes repeats while broader mutation burdens remain acceptable over extended periods.
status: In 2025, antisense-mediated MSH3 suppression reduced somatic CAG expansion in Huntington’s disease patient-derived striatal neurons (Bunting et al. (2025), *Antisense oligonucleotide–mediated MSH3 suppression reduces somatic CAG repeat expansion in Huntington’s disease iPSC–derived striatal neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.adn4600`). Long-term genomic safety and the necessary degree of suppression remain separate open questions beyond that culture result.
solved_when: A tissue-specific, time-dependent intervention window is defined in which MSH3 reduction measurably suppresses repeat expansion and long-term measurement shows no unacceptable accumulation of other DNA errors, with the required degree of suppression quantified.
why: It determines whether a promising repeat-expansion intervention has a usable long-term therapeutic margin rather than merely working in culture.
key_works: Bunting et al. (2025), *Antisense oligonucleotide–mediated MSH3 suppression reduces somatic CAG repeat expansion in Huntington’s disease iPSC–derived striatal neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.adn4600`.

title: R10.06. Replacing damaged neuronal nuclear pores without opening the barrier
open: How do aged neurons inspect, repair, and replace damaged components of exceptionally long-lived nuclear pore complexes while preserving nuclear selectivity? In particular, can defective pores be selectively renewed without transient leakage or wholesale disruption of nuclear transport?
status: Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins were identified in rat brain in 2012 by Savas et al. (2012), *Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins in the rat brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1217421`. However, component longevity does not establish that pores are immutable, and evidence of component exchange by itself does not explain how damaged assemblies could be safely replaced in old neurons.
solved_when: A mechanism is established by which damaged nuclear pore complex components in aged neurons can be selectively repaired or replaced while maintaining the nuclear permeability barrier — that is, without transient leakage or wholesale disruption of nuclear transport.
why: It provides a specific intervention target for the deterioration of nuclear compartmentalization, a concrete entry point rather than a general appeal to aging.
key_works: Savas et al. (2012), *Extremely long-lived nuclear pore proteins in the rat brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1217421`.

title: R10.07. What information the axon-to-cilium serotonin synapse conveys
open: Does serotonin delivered to a neuronal primary cilium carry instructions that are meaningfully different from serotonin acting elsewhere on the same cell? Formally, if the ciliary route is selectively disrupted while nonciliary serotonergic signaling is preserved, what changes arise in nuclear regulation and in behavior?
status: An axon–cilium serotonergic synapse and a cilium-to-nucleus signaling pathway were demonstrated in 2022 (Sheu et al. (2022), *A serotonergic axon-cilium synapse drives nuclear signaling to alter chromatin accessibility*, PMID: `36055200`). The anatomical connection and its chromatin effects are established; the behavior-specific informational role of this pathway remains the open target.
solved_when: A preparation is achieved that selectively blocks the axon-to-cilium serotonin synapse while leaving nonciliary serotonin signaling intact, and this manipulation is shown to alter nuclear regulation and behavior in predicted ways, establishing whether the ciliary route conveys distinguishable information.
why: A positive answer would reveal a dedicated channel through which particular inputs regulate long-term cellular programs, such as chromatin-state changes, independently of ordinary synaptic serotonin signaling.
key_works: Sheu et al. (2022), *A serotonergic axon-cilium synapse drives nuclear signaling to alter chromatin accessibility*, PMID: `36055200`.

title: R10.08. Reissner-fiber mechanics versus urotensin signaling in spine morphogenesis
open: How do Reissner-fiber tension, its motion, biochemical interactions, and cerebrospinal-fluid-contacting neuronal signaling each contribute to maintaining the shape of the body axis? A solution should predict which deformities follow selective mechanical disruption of the fiber versus selective interruption of the downstream signaling pathway.
status: Reissner-fiber-dependent urotensin signaling was linked to prevention of spinal curvature in 2020 [Lu et al. (2020), *Reissner fibre-induced urotensin signalling from cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons prevents scoliosis of vertebrate spine*, DOI: `10.1242/bio.052027`]. A September 2025 preprint reported that motile cilia rotate a tensioned, anchored fiber, adding a mechanical mechanism that must be integrated with the signaling results [Bearce et al. (2025), *Motile cilia spin the Reissner fiber, a tensioned and anchored extracellular thread essential for body morphogenesis*, preprint, DOI: `10.1101/2025.09.25.678623`].
solved_when: A quantitative account exists that separates the mechanical and signaling contributions and correctly predicts which spinal deformities result from selectively disrupting fiber mechanics versus selectively blocking urotensin signaling downstream.
why: It connects nervous-system fluid mechanics to a concrete developmental orthopedic phenotype, linking how the brain and spinal cord move fluid to how the vertebrate spine forms straight.
key_works: Lu et al. (2020), *Reissner fibre-induced urotensin signalling from cerebrospinal fluid-contacting neurons prevents scoliosis of vertebrate spine*, DOI: `10.1242/bio.052027`; Bearce et al. (2025), *Motile cilia spin the Reissner fiber, a tensioned and anchored extracellular thread essential for body morphogenesis*, preprint, DOI: `10.1101/2025.09.25.678623`.

title: R10.10. Physically consistent, independently validated chloride microdomains
open: Do neighboring compartments within a single neuron genuinely hold different free chloride activities, or are the apparent differences artifacts of distinct sensor environments, pH, or chloride-binding conditions? Determine the transport, buffering, and geometrical requirements under which the measured chloride gradients can persist.
status: A 2021 study reported chloride microdomains associated with heterogeneous GABA responses (Rahmati et al. (2021), *Unique Actions of GABA Arising from Cytoplasmic Chloride Microdomains*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3175-20.2021`). The remaining challenge is independent quantitative validation and a transport model that explains the gradients' stability under realistic diffusion and activity.
solved_when: A model is derived specifying the transport, buffering, and geometrical conditions needed for the measured subcellular chloride gradients to persist under realistic diffusion and activity, and this prediction is independently quantitatively validated.
why: It decides whether describing a neuron's intracellular chloride by a single value is an inadequate account of inhibitory signaling, or whether microdomain differences are measurement artifacts.
key_works: Rahmati et al. (2021), *Unique Actions of GABA Arising from Cytoplasmic Chloride Microdomains*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3175-20.2021`.

title: R10.12. Homeostatic compensation in axon-carrying-dendrite neurons
open: How do neurons whose axon originates from a dendrite maintain stable excitability when their axon initial segment lacks the homeostatic plasticity seen in comparison neurons? Formally, determine whether compensation shifts to dendritic conductances, inhibition, synaptic scaling, or some other compartment or mechanism.
status: A study published online in 2024 and in a 2025 journal issue found preserved initial-segment architecture and trafficking-barrier function in cultured axon-carrying-dendrite neurons, but absent initial-segment homeostatic plasticity under the tested conditions, fewer cisternal organelles, and fewer inhibitory inputs. The barrier's existence is therefore not the open question. Key works: Han et al. (2025), *Unveiling the cell biology of hippocampal neurons with dendritic axon origin*, DOI: `10.1083/jcb.202403141`; Thome et al. (2014), *Axon-Carrying Dendrites Convey Privileged Synaptic Input in Hippocampal Neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2014.08.013`.
solved_when: A mechanism is identified that accounts for excitability stabilization in axon-carrying-dendrite neurons despite absent initial-segment homeostatic plasticity, with experimental evidence localizing the compensation to dendritic conductances, inhibition, synaptic scaling, or another compartment.
why: It tests whether a distinct neuronal geometry requires a distinct stability mechanism, which would constrain how homeostatic control is distributed across neuronal compartments.
key_works: Han et al. (2025), *Unveiling the cell biology of hippocampal neurons with dendritic axon origin*, DOI: `10.1083/jcb.202403141`; Thome et al. (2014), *Axon-Carrying Dendrites Convey Privileged Synaptic Input in Hippocampal Neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2014.08.013`.

title: R10.13. Dynamic regulation of the periaxonal nanocircuit
open: How do the geometry and ionic composition of the nanoscale periaxonal space evolve during realistic spike trains, and do those changes actively regulate conduction, or do they instead produce activity-dependent failure and timing noise?
status: A 2020 study combined recordings, ultrastructure, and modeling to establish a conductive periaxonal pathway in saltatory conduction (Cohen et al. (2020), *Saltatory Conduction along Myelinated Axons Involves a Periaxonal Nanocircuit*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.11.039`). Its existence does not settle whether nanospace width and conductivity are dynamically controlled during behavior.
solved_when: Measurements show how nanospace width and conductivity change during realistic spike trains, and it is determined whether these dynamics act as active regulation of conduction versus a source of activity-dependent failure and timing noise.
why: It identifies a potential regulator of axonal timing that is distinct from changing myelin thickness or internode length.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2020), *Saltatory Conduction along Myelinated Axons Involves a Periaxonal Nanocircuit*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.11.039`.

title: R10.14. Replenishment and fate of the adult silent-filopodial synapse reserve
open: Are adult filopodial silent synapses continuously replenished, consumed by learning, recycled, or converted into long-lived spines? A satisfactory answer would quantify the reserve's turnover and test whether depleting it limits subsequent learning.
status: In 2022, filopodia were identified as a major substrate of silent synapses in sampled adult mouse visual-cortical neurons, and their functional recruitment was demonstrated (Vardalaki, Chung, and Harnett (2022), *Filopodia are a structural substrate for silent synapses in adult neocortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05483-6`). The unresolved issue is the reserve's long-term lifecycle, not whether adult silent synapses exist.
solved_when: The turnover dynamics of the adult filopodial silent-synapse reserve are quantified, and it is determined whether the reserve is replenished, consumed, recycled, or converted into long-lived spines, including whether its depletion limits subsequent learning.
why: A solution would reveal whether adult learning draws on a renewable structural resource, or whether unused synaptic capacity is a finite reserve that can be exhausted.
key_works: Vardalaki, Chung, and Harnett (2022), *Filopodia are a structural substrate for silent synapses in adult neocortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05483-6`.

title: R10.15. Regulation of opposing transmitters inside the same vesicle
open: Determine how the glutamate-to-GABA content of individual co-packaged vesicles is established and whether it changes with activity or physiological state. Predict when a release event produces net excitation, inhibition, or a timing-dependent combination at its target.
status: A 2022 study demonstrated co-packaging of glutamate and GABA in individual vesicles at a defined central synapse (Kim et al. (2022), *Co-packaging of opposing neurotransmitters in individual synaptic vesicles in the central nervous system*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.01.007`). Co-packaging itself is therefore not hypothetical; its stoichiometric regulation and functional flexibility are the finer-grained targets. Analytical approaches to the phenomenon have been reviewed in Kim and Sabatini (2023), *Analytical approaches to examine gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamate vesicular co-packaging*, DOI: `10.3389/fnsyn.2022.1076616`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account of vesicular transmitter stoichiometry is provided that specifies how the glutamate-to-GABA ratio in a single vesicle is set, how that ratio varies with activity or physiological state, and a predictive rule for whether a given release event yields net excitation, net inhibition, or a timing-dependent combination at its target.
why: Challenges models that assign a single fixed sign to a presynaptic release event, requiring instead that mixed-sign transmission from a shared carrier be treated as a regulated and potentially dynamic signaling code.
key_works: Kim et al. (2022), *Co-packaging of opposing neurotransmitters in individual synaptic vesicles in the central nervous system*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.01.007`; Kim and Sabatini (2023), *Analytical approaches to examine gamma-aminobutyric acid and glutamate vesicular co-packaging*, DOI: `10.3389/fnsyn.2022.1076616`.

title: R10.16. Arc capsid cargo selection and recipient specificity
open: Which endogenous RNAs does the Arc capsid preferentially package, which cells receive them, and what does the transferred cargo do once it arrives? More precisely, can we separate Arc's intercellular transfer functions from its intracellular roles through interventions that preserve one while disrupting the other?
status: In 2018, Arc was shown to form virus-like capsids and mediate intercellular RNA transfer (Pastuzyn et al. (2018), *The Neuronal Gene Arc Encodes a Repurposed Retrotransposon Gag Protein that Mediates Intercellular RNA Transfer*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.12.024`). These findings do not establish a complete endogenous cargo-selection code or prove which behavioral effects require transfer between cells.
solved_when: The endogenous cargo selected for packaging into Arc particles is identified, the recipient cells and their responses to transferred cargo are characterized, and interventions dissociating intercellular transfer from intracellular Arc function demonstrate which effects require transfer between cells.
why: A solution would establish a genetically encoded intercellular communication channel distinct from neurotransmission, with cargo and recipient specificity.
key_works: Pastuzyn et al. (2018), *The Neuronal Gene Arc Encodes a Repurposed Retrotransposon Gag Protein that Mediates Intercellular RNA Transfer*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.12.024`.

title: R10.17. Identities and receptors of neuronal membrane-proteasome peptides
open: Identify the physiologically released peptides produced by neuronal membrane proteasomes, and establish which receptors or uptake mechanisms mediate their effects. In particular, distinguish direct receptor binding by these peptides from indirect changes in glutamate signaling or extracellular protein processing.
status: Work published in 2024 linked membrane-proteasome-derived peptides to NMDAR-dependent signaling and gene-expression changes [Türker, Brennan, and Margolis (2024), *Neuronal membrane proteasome-derived peptides modulate NMDAR-dependent neuronal signaling to promote changes in gene expression*, DOI: `10.1091/mbc.E23-06-0218`], and another study implicated membrane proteasomes in peripheral nociceptor activity [Villalón Landeros et al. (2024), *The nociceptive activity of peripheral sensory neurons is modulated by the neuronal membrane proteasome*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114058`]. However, NMDAR dependence does not establish that the peptides directly bind NMDARs.
solved_when: The released peptide identities are determined and the receptors or uptake mechanisms mediating their physiological effects are established, with direct receptor binding distinguished from indirect effects on glutamate signaling or extracellular protein processing.
why: A solution could uncover a signaling system whose molecular messages remain inadequately identified.
key_works: Türker, Brennan, and Margolis (2024), *Neuronal membrane proteasome-derived peptides modulate NMDAR-dependent neuronal signaling to promote changes in gene expression*, DOI: `10.1091/mbc.E23-06-0218`; Villalón Landeros et al. (2024), *The nociceptive activity of peripheral sensory neurons is modulated by the neuronal membrane proteasome*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114058`.

title: R10.20. The last reversible state after SARM1 activation
open: Where exactly is the point of no return for an axon after SARM1 activation — the biochemical and electrophysiological boundary beyond which recovery becomes impossible? And how does that boundary shift with the type of injury, the neuronal subtype, and the duration of activation, judged by restoration of conduction and synaptic output rather than survival alone?
status: A 2025 human-neuron study, Loreto et al. (2025), *SARM1 activation induces reversible mitochondrial dysfunction and can be prevented in human neurons by antisense oligonucleotides* (DOI: `10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106986`), demonstrated reversible mitochondrial dysfunction after SARM1 activation and protection through antisense intervention. Reversibility is therefore already demonstrated in a defined setting; the open target is a predictive, transferable rescue window and proof of complete functional recovery.
solved_when: A predictive, transferable rescue window is defined: quantitative characterization of the biochemical and electrophysiological boundary beyond which recovery cannot occur, its dependence on injury type, neuronal subtype, and duration, together with proof of complete functional recovery (restored conduction and synaptic output) within that window.
why: It establishes when intervention can still rescue an existing axon rather than merely delay fragmentation.
key_works: Loreto et al. (2025), *SARM1 activation induces reversible mitochondrial dysfunction and can be prevented in human neurons by antisense oligonucleotides*, DOI: `10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106986`.

title: R10.23. The metastable visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise
open: What is the metastable visual-pigment state proposed to generate continuous dark noise, in molecular conformation and transition kinetics? A complete answer would also predict how mutations change this continuous noise independently of photon sensitivity and of discrete thermal activation events.
status: A 2024 study attributed an important continuous-noise component to visual pigment and proposed a metastable pigment state, but the state's detailed molecular identity remains a mechanistic target rather than a solved structural result. Key work: Chai et al. (2024), *Dark continuous noise from visual pigment as a major mechanism underlying rod–cone difference in light sensitivity*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2418031121`.
solved_when: The metastable pigment state's molecular conformation and transition kinetics are identified, and a quantitative account is given of how mutations alter the continuous dark noise independently of photon sensitivity and discrete thermal activation events.
why: It would explain a fundamental sensory-noise source at molecular resolution.
key_works: Chai et al. (2024), *Dark continuous noise from visual pigment as a major mechanism underlying rod–cone difference in light sensitivity*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2418031121`.

title: R10.25. The downstream use of suppressed-by-contrast retinal ganglion cells
open: Do suppressed-by-contrast retinal ganglion cells actually help the brain tell apart visual changes caused by our own actions from those caused by the external world? Formally: identify their downstream readers and predict the behavioral consequences of selectively altering their suppression signals, testing whether they are causally involved in perceptual stabilization.
status: In 2015, a genetically identified population of suppressed-by-contrast retinal ganglion cells was shown to reliably signal stimuli resembling saccades and blinks, with their specific excitatory and inhibitory mechanisms characterized. Reliable signaling of these self-generated stimuli is thus established; whether such signaling is necessary for perceptual stabilization remains the open target. Key work: Tien et al. (2015), *Genetically Identified Suppressed-by-Contrast Retinal Ganglion Cells Reliably Signal Self-Generated Visual Stimuli*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1521-15.2015`.
solved_when: A causal role is demonstrated — downstream readers of suppressed-by-contrast cells are identified, and selective manipulation of their suppression signals produces the predicted behavioral effects on distinguishing self-generated from external visual changes.
why: It would connect an unusual retinal response class to a concrete computation, rather than leaving it as a physiological curiosity.
key_works: Tien et al. (2015), *Genetically Identified Suppressed-by-Contrast Retinal Ganglion Cells Reliably Signal Self-Generated Visual Stimuli*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1521-15.2015`.

title: R10.27. Can artificial cone-subpopulation signals create an additional learned chromatic dimension?
open: Can selectively stimulating subpopulations within a single cone class give rise to a genuinely new learned chromatic dimension — a perceptual distinction that cannot be reduced to ordinary color coordinates or spatial texture? Formally, the question is whether such a signal supports generalizable discrimination across novel spatial arrangements, with brightness and pattern cues controlled for.
status: The 2025 Oz study demonstrated colors outside the ordinary natural gamut through selective cone stimulation (Fong et al. (2025), *Novel color via stimulation of individual photoreceptors at population scale*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`). However, an expanded gamut, including the reported “olo” percept, is not by itself evidence of an additional independent dimension of color vision.
solved_when: A demonstration that discrimination trained with cone-subpopulation stimulation generalizes across new spatial arrangements, with controls excluding brightness and pattern cues, establishes a distinction irreducible to ordinary color coordinates or spatial texture.
why: It tests whether adult visual processing can acquire a new sensory coordinate rather than merely experience unusually strong activation of existing coordinates.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), *Novel color via stimulation of individual photoreceptors at population scale*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.28. Tenfold scaling of individually addressed, spectrally typed cones
open: Can a retinal stimulation system be scaled from the roughly thousand individually addressed cones demonstrated today to ten thousand, with each cone still identified and spectrally typed? Formally, the goal is to reach ~10⁴ cones while keeping cross-activation, retinal exposure, tracking failures, and perceptual reproducibility within predefined acceptance limits — an engineering target, not a published performance claim.
status: The 2025 Oz prototype (Fong et al. (2025), DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`, identified in R10.27) operated at approximately the thousand-cone scale and demonstrated image and video stimuli; however, scaling spatial coverage without losing cone-level targeting is a distinct problem from demonstrating the initial percept. Related challenges include adaptive-optics high-resolution targeting under motion and real-time tracking with tightly bounded misdelivery.
solved_when: A controlled stimulation system addresses on the order of 10⁴ individually typed cones (up from ~10³), with cross-activation, retinal exposure, tracking failures, and perceptual reproducibility all held to predefined acceptance limits.
why: Scaling to this level would enable far richer tests of neural adaptation to artificial sensory channels than the current thousand-cone scale permits.
key_works: Fong et al. (2025), the Oz study identified in R10.27, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adu1052`.

title: R10.30. The competence boundary for PTBP1-based astrocyte reprogramming
open: Does any reproducibly defined mature-astrocyte state genuinely convert to neurons after PTBP1 loss, or is there a bounded negative result across those states? Formally, any positive claim must show irreversible lineage commitment, durable neuronal physiology, and exclusion of pre-existing neurons or labeling artifacts.
status: A 2025 study found that PTBP1 depletion in lineage-traced mature astrocytes altered splicing without broadly producing neuronal features (Zhang et al. (2025), *PTBP1 depletion in mature astrocytes reveals distinct splicing alterations without neuronal features*, eLife research report `107683`; preprint DOI: `10.1101/2025.05.30.657115`). The next problem is not to repeat an unqualified conversion claim, but to identify the actual competence boundary — or explain why PTBP1 removal is insufficient.
solved_when: Either a reproducibly defined mature-astrocyte state is shown to undergo genuine neuronal conversion after PTBP1 depletion — with irreversible lineage, durable neuronal physiology, and exclusion of pre-existing neurons or labeling artifacts — or a bounded negative result is established across those states.
why: It prevents a potentially misleading regeneration strategy from advancing on ambiguous cell-labeling evidence.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2025), *PTBP1 depletion in mature astrocytes reveals distinct splicing alterations without neuronal features*, eLife research report `107683`; preprint DOI: `10.1101/2025.05.30.657115`.

title: R10.33. Quantitative partition of central and peripheral tACS effects
open: When transcranial alternating-current stimulation produces a behavioral or physiological effect, how much of that effect comes from fields acting directly on the brain versus from stimulation of peripheral nerves? A satisfying answer would predict this quantitative partition across anatomies and tasks, replacing the default assumption that one mechanism always dominates.
status: In 2019, one study demonstrated that motor-system effects could arise through peripheral nerves (Asamoah, Khatoun, and McLaughlin (2019), *tACS motor system effects can be caused by transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves*, PMID: `30655523`), while another demonstrated entrainment of primate single-neuron activity (Krause et al. (2019), *Transcranial alternating current stimulation entrains single-neuron activity in the primate brain*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1815958116`). The useful unresolved question is context-dependent causal contribution, not a binary claim that direct or indirect effects never occur.
solved_when: A quantitative method exists that decomposes a tACS effect into its central (direct brain-field) and peripheral (peripheral-nerve) contributions, and whose predictions of that partition are validated across different anatomies and tasks rather than holding only in a single setting.
why: Without such a partition, tACS results are ambiguous about mechanism, so stimulation parameters cannot be rationally targeted; with it, stimulation outcomes become interpretable and targeting can be improved.
key_works: Asamoah, Khatoun, and McLaughlin (2019), *tACS motor system effects can be caused by transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves*, PMID: `30655523`; Krause et al. (2019), *Transcranial alternating current stimulation entrains single-neuron activity in the primate brain*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1815958116`.

title: R10.36. Causal leaders and replacement rules in the GnRH pulse generator
open: Do the kisspeptin neurons recruited earliest in a hormone pulse actually cause it, or are they just the first visible sign of a distributed transition? Formally, what happens to pulse generation when an apparent leader is removed — does pulsing cease, shift in timing, or reorganize with another cell taking over?
status: In-vivo imaging in 2022 revealed a temporal recruitment order within the pulse generator (Moore et al. (2022), *In vivo imaging of the GnRH pulse generator reveals a temporal order of neuronal activation and synchronization during each pulse*, PMID: `35110409`), and subsequent work examined synchronization mechanisms (Han et al. (2023), *Mechanism of kisspeptin neuron synchronization for pulsatile hormone secretion in male mice*, Cell Reports 42, article `111914`). However, the observed ordering does not by itself establish a fixed pacemaker hierarchy or its resilience to cell loss.
solved_when: There is an experimental determination of whether removing an early-recruited ("leader") kisspeptin neuron suppresses GnRH pulses, alters their timing, or triggers another cell to assume the initiating role — distinguishing causal initiation from mere early reporting of the distributed transition.
why: It distinguishes a replaceable distributed oscillator from a small set of indispensable pulse initiators, which determines how resilient the pulse generator is to loss of individual cells.
key_works: Moore et al. (2022), *In vivo imaging of the GnRH pulse generator reveals a temporal order of neuronal activation and synchronization during each pulse*, PMID: `35110409`; Han et al. (2023), *Mechanism of kisspeptin neuron synchronization for pulsatile hormone secretion in male mice*, Cell Reports 42, article `111914`.

title: R10.38. The molecular message from cerebrospinal fluid to skull marrow
open: Which cerebrospinal-fluid molecules instruct particular skull-marrow progenitors and immune-cell populations after a defined neural injury, and does the resulting response carry spatial information about the injury site or merely amount to a generalized inflammatory signal?
status: Direct cerebrospinal-fluid access to skull bone-marrow niches through dural channels, together with injury-associated marrow responses, was demonstrated in 2022 (Mazzitelli et al. (2022), *Cerebrospinal fluid regulates skull bone marrow niches via direct access through dural channels*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-022-01029-1`). The route exists; the unresolved target is the specific message, the recipient program, and how these differ from circulating signals.
solved_when: The specific CSF molecules and their skull-marrow recipient populations are identified after a defined neural injury, and it is determined whether the response preserves spatial information about the injury or is a generalized inflammatory signal.
why: A solution would make local neuroimmune recruitment selectively controllable without suppressing systemic immunity.
key_works: Mazzitelli et al. (2022), *Cerebrospinal fluid regulates skull bone marrow niches via direct access through dural channels*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-022-01029-1`.

title: R10.39. Biological learning versus decoder adaptation in cultured-neuron computing
open: How much of the observed task improvement in cultured-neuron systems comes from plasticity inside the living neural tissue itself, rather than from adaptation of the electronic decoder, fixed reservoir dynamics, or changes in stimulation statistics? A convincing answer requires fixed-readout and matched-control conditions together with selective disruption of the proposed biological plasticity mechanism.
status: DishBrain (Kagan et al. (2022), *In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.09.001`) and Brainoware (Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`) reported task-relevant behavior or computation using living neural preparations. These demonstrations motivate—but do not replace—a causal accounting of which component learned and what was retained. Claims about "sentience" are not required to formulate or solve this technical problem.
solved_when: There is a causal accounting, under fixed-readout and matched-control conditions plus selective disruption of the proposed biological plasticity mechanism, of which component learned, what was retained, and how much task improvement is attributable to changes inside the living tissue versus decoder adaptation, fixed reservoir dynamics, or stimulation-statistics changes.
why: It establishes whether living tissue provides adaptive computation beyond what a fixed nonlinear substrate with a trained readout would already deliver.
key_works: Kagan et al. (2022), *In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2022.09.001`; Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: R10.40. End-to-end efficiency advantage for living neural computing
open: Can a living neural computing system beat electronics by a factor of ten in energy or total operating cost per successfully completed task once everything is counted? The comparison must include incubation, fluid handling, amplifiers, stimulation, training, failed cultures, and replacement, and must match task accuracy, throughput, and availability rather than comparing isolated neuronal energy consumption.
status: Brainoware demonstrated organoid-based reservoir computation in 2023 (Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`), but this is not an end-to-end demonstration of a tenfold efficiency advantage after all supporting equipment and biological maintenance are included.
solved_when: A proposed demonstration shows a tenfold improvement in energy or total operating cost per successfully completed task against a specified electronic baseline, with the accounting covering incubation, fluid handling, amplifiers, stimulation, training, failed cultures, and replacement, at matched task accuracy, throughput, and availability.
why: It determines whether biological computing has a practical advantage rather than an attractive comparison drawn at only one system boundary.
key_works: Cai et al. (2023), *Brain organoid reservoir computing for artificial intelligence*, DOI: `10.1038/s41928-023-01069-w`.

title: Tenfold cheaper verified connectomics
open: Can an entire verified connectome be produced for a tenth of today's total cost — covering acquisition, reconstruction, proofreading, storage, and access — while keeping measured synapse and connectivity error rates intact? Formally, the goal is a tenfold reduction in end-to-end cost relative to a preregistered baseline, with error rates maintained at measured levels.
status: A proposed moonshot with no solution yet; MICrONS supplies a substantial real pipeline against which component and end-to-end improvements can be measured. Key work: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.
