solved_when: A pipeline achieves at least a tenfold reduction in total acquisition, reconstruction, proofreading, storage, and access cost against a preregistered baseline, while maintaining measured synapse and connectivity error rates.
why: A tenfold cost reduction would make replication across animals, conditions, and laboratories feasible, turning connectomics from single-hero efforts into a repeatable comparative science.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Cross-species cell-type homology
open: Can we build a correspondence between cell types across species that tells true evolutionary homology apart from convergent molecular similarity? The correspondence should be validated not only by transcriptomic similarity but by developmental lineage, connectivity, physiology, and perturbation responses.
status: Comparative cellular censuses currently provide candidate alignments, but matching transcriptomic clusters is only a partial result, not a complete evolutionary correspondence. Key works include Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; and Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.
solved_when: Cross-species cell-type correspondences are established that discriminate homology from convergent similarity, with validation across developmental lineage, connectivity, physiology, and perturbation responses.
why: It determines which findings from animal studies can legitimately be transferred to humans.
key_works: Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Predicting physiology from molecular identity
open: Can we predict how a neuron behaves — its intrinsic dynamics, how it integrates synaptic input, and how it responds to neuromodulators — purely from measurements of its molecular identity? A complete answer would be a general molecular-to-electrophysiological predictive law that also quantifies its uncertainty and flags when it fails out of distribution.
status: Transcriptomic atlases and detailed human-neuron physiology supply complementary measurements, but neither establishes a general molecular-to-electrophysiological predictive law. Key works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`.
solved_when: A predictive law exists that maps molecular measurements to intrinsic dynamics, synaptic integration, and neuromodulator responses, with calibrated uncertainty estimates and explicit detection of out-of-distribution failures.
why: It would turn descriptive cell-type labels into executable biological models, making transcriptomic atlases directly usable for predicting neuronal function.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`.

title: Rare-cell and rare-region completeness
open: Which human neural cell populations are still being systematically missed by current sampling, and can we collect enough spatially resolved examples of them to tell genuinely rare cell types apart from technical artifacts or unusual cellular states?
status: Large human and mouse atlases substantially reduce the gap, but their sampling designs do not certify discovery of every rare population across individuals and life stages, as in Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, and Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`.
solved_when: A documented estimate identifies the undersampled human neural cell populations, and for each, sufficient spatially resolved examples have been obtained to distinguish rare types from artifacts and unusual states.
why: Rare populations can be disproportionately important for disease or specialized functions, so missing them leaves blind spots precisely where the stakes are highest.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`.

title: Noncoding variant-to-circuit causality
open: For a disease-associated noncoding variant, can we trace and experimentally establish the full causal chain from variant to circuit? That is, identify its causal regulatory element, target gene, relevant cell state, physiological consequence, and circuit-level effect, and validate the chain with allele-specific perturbation and rescue.
status: Human chromatin-accessibility atlases nominate regulatory mechanisms, but association and accessibility alone do not establish the causal chain. Key work: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.
solved_when: The complete chain — regulatory element, target gene, cell state, physiological consequence, and circuit-level effect — is identified for a disease-associated noncoding variant and validated by allele-specific perturbation and rescue.
why: It converts genetic association into actionable mechanisms, turning risk loci into understood biology that can be targeted.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Polygenic effects as physiological mechanisms
open: How do many small-effect genetic variants combine to alter specific physiological computations, rather than merely predicting a diagnostic label? Formally, this asks for a mechanistic composition rule — additive, epistatic, or cell-state-dependent — that maps polygenic variation to changes in neural function, and it should be tested prospectively rather than fit retrospectively.
status: Large schizophrenia association studies, notably Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`, identify many loci, but locus discovery does not yet supply a mechanistic composition rule.
solved_when: A prospective test discriminates among additive, epistatic, and cell-state-dependent composition models, yielding a rule that links small-effect variants to specific computations rather than only to a diagnostic label.
why: A composition rule would make polygenic risk biologically interpretable, enabling stratification of patients and rational selection of interventions rather than label prediction alone.
key_works: Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`.

title: Somatic mutations that change neural function
open: Which mutations acquired during a neuron's or glial cell's lifetime actually change its physiology, an organism's cognition, or the course of neurodegeneration — and how large must a clone of such mutant cells grow before its effects become measurable?
status: Single-neuron sequencing demonstrated informative somatic variation in 2015 (Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`), but detecting mutations remains distinct from establishing their functional importance.
solved_when: Specific somatic mutations are causally linked to altered neural function, cognition, or degeneration, and the minimum clone size required for a measurable effect is determined.
why: This distinguishes whether brain mosaicism is mostly a passive lineage record, a genuine disease mechanism, or both.
key_works: Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`.

title: Developmental lineage-to-connectivity mapping
open: Can we reconstruct, in the same tissue, both the developmental lineage of neurons and their full synaptic connectivity, and then ask which wiring properties are explained by shared ancestry once location and cell type are controlled for?
status: Somatic lineage information (e.g., Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`) and dense connectomics (e.g., MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`) exist separately; their combination remains a demanding multimodal target.
solved_when: A single tissue sample yields both a somatic-mutation-based lineage reconstruction and a dense connectome, with an analysis identifying wiring properties that common ancestry predicts independently of spatial position and cell type.
why: It reveals how developmental history constrains circuit architecture, telling us whether connectivity is shaped by lineage beyond what geography and cell identity already explain.
key_works: Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Durable information in neuronal chromatin
open: Do activity-induced chromatin changes in neurons actually store information that guides behavior, or do they only permit plasticity — or are they merely downstream consequences of it? A resolution requires intervention: selectively erasing a given chromatin change, and selectively restoring it, to see which role it plays.
status: Cell-specific chromatin maps reveal regulatory structure, but static accessibility does not establish an enduring memory-storage mechanism. Key works: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.
solved_when: A causal test distinguishes storage, permissive, and consequential roles — selective erasure and restoration of specific activity-induced chromatin changes, with behavioral and plasticity readouts showing whether information is stored, merely enabled, or unaffected.
why: It could establish a durable physical substrate for long-term adaptation, and equally reveal how pathological states persist.
key_works: Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Rules for synaptic nanocolumn alignment
open: What rules govern how presynaptic release machinery and postsynaptic receptors acquire, maintain, and modify their nanoscale alignment at a synapse? A complete answer would predict the effect of moving specific molecular components on this alignment without changing their abundance.
status: Trans-synaptic nanocolumns were demonstrated in 2016 by Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`; the general assembly and plasticity rules remain incompletely specified.
solved_when: The assembly and plasticity rules governing trans-synaptic nanocolumns are specified completely enough to predict how repositioning specific synaptic components (holding abundance constant) alters nanoscale alignment.
why: It links molecular geometry to synaptic efficacy, connecting where molecules sit to how well a synapse works.
key_works: Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`.

title: Release probability from molecular configuration
open: Can the active zone's physical structure — its molecular arrangement and vesicle organization — be used to predict when a given synapse will release vesicles and how that likelihood changes with use? In formal terms, is there a generally validated probabilistic input-output model that maps measured active-zone architecture and molecular state to release probability, multivesicular release, and short-term plasticity at individual synapses?
status: Nanoscale alignment and vesicle-organization studies provide structural constraints on the problem, but no generally validated probabilistic input-output model has been achieved. Key works include Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`, and Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.
solved_when: A predictive model exists that takes measured active-zone architecture and molecular state as inputs and outputs release probability, multivesicular release, and short-term plasticity at individual synapses, and this model is generally validated rather than applicable only to specific preparations.
why: It supplies the missing parameterization needed for mechanistic circuit simulation, grounding network-level models in the actual molecular anatomy of individual synapses rather than fitted abstractions.
key_works: Tang et al. (2016), *A trans-synaptic nanocolumn aligns neurotransmitter release to receptors*, DOI: `10.1038/nature19058`; Milovanovic et al. (2018), *A liquid phase of synapsin and lipid vesicles*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5671`.

title: Branch-specific inhibitory routing
open: Can inhibition act as a router inside a single neuron, steering distinct information streams through particular dendritic branches? More formally, is there a branch-level rule by which spatially targeted inhibition selects which streams propagate, and does it predict the behavioral consequences of targeted inhibitory perturbations?
status: Nonlinear dendritic physiology supplies a plausible substrate for such routing, but existing single-cell demonstrations do not supply a general branch-level routing rule. Key works include Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`, and Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.
solved_when: A branch-level routing rule is established that determines whether and how inhibition routes distinct information streams through individual dendritic branches, and that predicts behavior-specific consequences of spatially targeted inhibitory perturbations.
why: It would explain how a neuron achieves flexible, routing-based computation without any change in anatomical connectivity.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Poirazi, Brannon, and Mel (2003), *Pyramidal neuron as two-layer neural network*, DOI: `10.1016/S0896-6273(03)00149-1`.

title: Predicting spikes from complete synaptic input
open: Can we measure a neuron's complete synaptic input — excitatory, inhibitory, and modulatory — well enough to predict its spikes in a behaving animal, with calibrated uncertainty on those predictions?
status: High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation has been characterized in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons (Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`), but recording every relevant input to an intact behaving neuron remains a separate, unsolved measurement challenge.
solved_when: A single neuron's full input across behavioral states is measured and used to predict its spiking with stated, calibrated uncertainty.
why: Complete input measurement makes spike prediction a stringent, prospective test of cellular models, rather than a retrospective fit to their outputs.
key_works: Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`.

title: Human-specific dendritic computational advantages
open: Which differences between human and nonhuman dendrites actually change what a neuron can compute, once confounds like morphology, age, tissue condition, and recording protocol are controlled for?
status: Human dendritic nonlinearities and sodium-spike properties have been reported, including Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`, and Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`; however, a species-general comparative account of their functional advantages remains incomplete.
solved_when: A comparative framework exists that isolates species-specific dendritic properties and demonstrates — under matched morphology, age, tissue condition, and recording protocol — which of them alter computational capability relative to nonhuman neurons.
why: It tests whether proposed cellular-level mechanisms genuinely contribute to human cognition, rather than being artifacts of experimental or anatomical confounds.
key_works: Gidon et al. (2020), *Dendritic action potentials and computation in human layer 2/3 cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aax6239`; Gooch et al. (2022), *High-fidelity dendritic sodium spike generation in human layer 2/3 neocortical pyramidal neurons*, DOI: `10.1016/j.celrep.2022.111500`.

title: Dendrites as biological credit-assignment machinery
open: Do the electrical and biochemical signals within individual dendritic compartments actually carry instructive errors or targets for learning, rather than merely modulating excitability? If so, what learning rules do these compartment-specific signals implement, such that the predicted dendritic and synaptic changes match what is measured experimentally?
status: Biologically motivated learning algorithms, including Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`, and Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`, demonstrate computational possibilities for dendrite-based credit assignment; however, they do not establish that a specific dendritic implementation operates in vivo.
solved_when: A mechanistic account exists showing that compartment-specific dendritic signals function as instructive error/target signals, together with derived learning rules whose predicted dendritic and synaptic plasticity matches experimental measurements.
why: It would bridge the gap between cellular physiology and efficient learning, explaining how biological circuits solve credit assignment at the level of single neurons.
key_works: Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`; Song et al. (2024), *Inferring neural activity before plasticity as a foundation for learning beyond backpropagation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01514-1`.

title: Activity-dependent myelin timing rules
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: How does neural activity shape the geometry of myelin — the placement, length, and thickness of individual internodes — so that conduction delays are tuned rather than merely reduced? A satisfactory account would predict which temporal relationships among spiking neurons are the targets of this optimization during learning.
status: Mouse experiments show that motor learning requires new myelination — McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960` — and that myelination reduces asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity during motor learning — Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`. Timing-related consequences of activity-dependent myelination have been demonstrated, but the adaptation rule itself remains unresolved.
solved_when: A rule is specified that maps activity patterns to internode placement, length, and thickness, and this rule predicts which temporal relationships are optimized during learning; predictions should be testable against the demonstrated timing-related consequences of new myelination.
why: It would add adaptive transmission delays as a mechanism to models of learning, extending them beyond synaptic plasticity alone.
key_works: McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`; Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`.

title: Functionally precise remyelination
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Can damaged CNS myelin be restored so that conduction delays and metabolic support match what the original circuit required, rather than merely producing new myelin? In other words, can remyelination be made functionally precise, not just structurally detectable?
status: Evidence linking myelination to coordinated activity — including Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`, and McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960` — makes timing fidelity a distinct repair target beyond histological remyelination.
solved_when: A repair strategy is shown to rebuild myelin that reproduces the original circuit's conduction timing and provides appropriate metabolic support, not merely histological evidence of myelin formation.
why: It would tell us whether structural repair actually restores coordinated behavior, rather than leaving timing fidelity of the repaired circuit unaddressed.
key_works: Kato et al. (2020), *Motor learning requires myelination to reduce asynchrony and spontaneity in neural activity*, DOI: `10.1002/glia.23713`; McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`.

title: Behavioral necessity of ephaptic coupling
subfield: Axons, myelin, and nonsynaptic electrical interactions
open: Do endogenous extracellular electric fields, acting ephaptically, causally shape neural computation in the living brain — independent of chemical synapses and gap junctions? The task is to determine, circuit by circuit, when such fields are necessary for a behavior or computation, and to measure their effect sizes under physiological conditions using perturbations that selectively disrupt ephaptic coupling.
status: Ephaptic effects in cortex were demonstrated in 2011; their existence is not in question, but their circuit-specific computational necessity remains unresolved. Key work: Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`.
solved_when: A preparation is identified in which selectively perturbing ephaptic coupling (without altering chemical synapses or gap junctions) produces a measurable, physiologically relevant change in a circuit's computation or behavior, with the effect size quantified under physiological conditions.
why: It tests whether the standard description of neural circuits as synaptic networks omits a consequential class of interactions, which would change how circuit models are built and interpreted.
key_works: Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`.

title: Individual cortical folding from growth mechanisms
open: Can we predict how an individual brain's cortex will fold, starting from measured tissue growth, mechanical properties, and regional developmental programs? A complete theory should track the folding trajectory of a specific brain — including malformations — and quantify its uncertainty.
status: Physical growth models reproduced important folding features in 2016 (Tallinen et al. (2016), *On the growth and form of cortical convolutions*, DOI: `10.1038/nphys3632`), but they are not a complete patient-specific developmental predictor.
solved_when: A patient-specific predictor exists that takes measured growth, mechanics, and regional developmental programs as inputs and reproduces the individual's folding trajectory, including malformations, with quantified uncertainty.
why: It would connect cellular-scale growth abnormalities to brain-scale anatomy, giving a mechanistic account of how malformations arise in individual patients.
key_works: Tallinen et al. (2016), *On the growth and form of cortical convolutions*, DOI: `10.1038/nphys3632`.

title: Selective reopening of critical periods
open: Can a specific critical period of plasticity be selectively reopened in the adult brain — achieving targeted, durable functional improvement — without destabilizing established skills or inducing unwanted learning? Formally, the goal is a method that restores a defined plasticity window with control over its scope and duration.
status: Psychedelics reopened a social-reward learning critical period in mice in 2023 (Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`); generalization to other systems and safe, selective reopening in humans remains open.
solved_when: A specified plasticity window is reopened in adults, producing targeted and durable functional improvement while leaving established skills intact and avoiding unwanted learning.
why: It would enable rehabilitation after injury or developmental deficits while avoiding the indiscriminate plasticity that erases existing function.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Instructive content of spontaneous developmental activity
open: Which features of spontaneous activity during development actually instruct neural wiring, and which merely permit maturation to proceed? Replace native activity patterns with controlled alternatives and test whether the predicted changes in wiring follow.
status: Activity-dependent synapse elimination offers a causal foothold on the problem, but does not specify what information developmental activity patterns carry. Key work: Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.
solved_when: A controlled-substitution experiment identifies specific features of spontaneous activity whose alteration reproducibly changes wiring in the predicted direction, distinguishing instructive from permissive features.
why: It separates genuinely self-generated training signals from generic trophic activity, telling us whether the developing brain is teaching itself or simply maturing.
key_works: Schafer et al. (2012), *Microglia sculpt postnatal neural circuits in an activity and complement-dependent manner*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.026`.

title: Timing-specific developmental vulnerability
open: Why does the same genetic or environmental perturbation produce different outcomes depending on when during development it strikes? More formally, can we predict — for defined cell populations and functions — which developmental windows are vulnerable to a given perturbation?
status: Autism genetics implicates both developmental and functional processes; identifying genes does not resolve when their perturbation becomes consequential. Key work: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.
solved_when: A framework exists that predicts, for specified perturbations, the vulnerable developmental windows for defined cell populations and functions, with those predictions validated experimentally.
why: It would make the timing of prevention and intervention mechanistically grounded rather than empirical.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Astrocytic microdomain integration
open: How do local signals within the fine processes of a single astrocyte combine — do they summate, stay independent, or occasionally trigger a larger, cell-wide response? A formal answer should predict the spatial and temporal influence of such microdomain events on nearby synapses.
status: The identification of functionally specialized astrocytes sharpens the question, but population identity does not specify computation within an individual astrocyte. de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.
solved_when: A theory is provided that specifies the conditions under which local signals in fine astrocytic processes remain independent versus integrate into larger responses, and that quantitatively predicts their spatial and temporal influence on nearby synapses.
why: It establishes the appropriate computational units for astrocyte models, determining whether modeling should proceed at the level of microdomains or the whole cell.
key_works: de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Lactate as fuel versus signal
open: Does astrocyte-derived lactate support long-term memory primarily by serving as metabolic fuel, or by acting as a signal — and can these roles be cleanly separated in vivo? A satisfying answer would quantify the relevant lactate fluxes and perform rescue experiments that discriminate between energy-substrate and signaling mechanisms.
status: Astrocyte–neuron lactate transport was causally implicated in long-term memory formation by Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`; however, that result does not settle all transport directions or signaling functions of lactate.
solved_when: The energetic and signaling contributions of astrocyte-derived lactate during memory formation are experimentally disentangled, with quantified fluxes and rescue results that distinguish fuel use from signaling action.
why: It determines what metabolic interventions intended to support or rescue memory must actually replace — substrate, signal, or both.
key_works: Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`.

title: Astrocyte state-to-function mapping
open: Which observable molecular states of an astrocyte determine what that cell actually does — to synapses, brain metabolism, vascular regulation, and repair — and how do those states change within a single cell over time? Formally, the goal is a state-to-function map linking transcriptomic/spatial astrocyte states to measurable functional outputs, including transitions between states within the same cells.
status: Cell atlases and specialized-gliotransmission findings — including Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`, and de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w` — provide candidate astrocyte subdivisions, but no comprehensive functional state-transition map yet exists.
solved_when: A comprehensive functional state-transition map exists that connects the molecular state classifications from cell atlases to experimentally testable effects on synapses, metabolism, vascular regulation, and repair, including within-cell state transitions.
why: It replaces the broad, largely uninterpretable "reactive astrocyte" label with specific, testable functions, enabling mechanistic prediction of what a given astrocyte state does in health and disease.
key_works: Yao et al. (2023), *A high-resolution transcriptomic and spatial atlas of cell types in the whole mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06812-z`; de Ceglia et al. (2023), *Specialized astrocytes mediate glutamatergic gliotransmission in the CNS*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06502-w`.

title: Astrocyte-mediated resource allocation
open: By what rule do astrocytes distribute metabolic support among the synapses that depend on them — is it driven by local activity, by anticipated demand, or by competition between synapses? And do these allocation rules determine which synapses are capable of learning?
status: Lactate-transport experiments connect astrocytic metabolism to memory — notably Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`, within the energy framework of Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001` — but no resource-allocation algorithm across competing synapses has been established.
solved_when: A resource-allocation algorithm governing astrocyte metabolic support across competing synapses is established, together with a demonstration of how that rule influences which synapses can learn.
why: It would tie the brain's metabolic constraints directly to learning selectivity, explaining why some synapses learn and others do not on the basis of energy availability rather than plasticity rules alone.
key_works: Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Protective versus destructive microglial programs
open: Can we selectively disarm the harmful actions of microglia while leaving their protective functions — pathogen control, debris clearance, and repair — intact? More precisely, what interventions separate these programs, and does that separation hold across distinct stages of disease?
status: Microglia can be protective during infection, while complement-associated synapse elimination provides a different functional pathway; "turning microglia off" is not a mechanism-specific solution. Key works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`.
solved_when: Interventions are identified that suppress harmful microglial actions while preserving pathogen control, debris removal, and repair, and the separation is validated across disease stages.
why: It prevents therapies that, by broadly shutting microglia down, also remove the beneficial immune functions the brain depends on.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Stevens et al. (2007), *The classical complement cascade mediates CNS synapse elimination*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2007.10.036`.

title: Long-lived immune memory in the brain
open: Which long-lasting changes in microglia or border-associated immune cells store a record of earlier infection, stress, or injury in the brain, and would erasing that record alter the brain's vulnerability to later neurological insults? Formally, the goal is to identify the persistent molecular or cellular states that encode immune memory in the CNS and test their causal role in subsequent disease susceptibility.
status: Infection studies establish important microglial responses — Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229` — but acute protection does not explain the persistence or causal consequences of later immune states; related single-cell chromatin work includes Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.
solved_when: The persistent microglial or border-immune changes encoding prior infection, stress, or injury are identified, and it is shown experimentally whether resetting them changes later neurological vulnerability.
why: A solution would explain how earlier inflammatory events exert delayed effects on the brain, connecting past immune history to later neurological outcomes.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Li et al. (2023), *A comparative atlas of single-cell chromatin accessibility in the human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adf7044`.

title: Meningeal immune-to-circuit signaling
open: How do immune and lymphatic processes in the meninges actually change the activity of specific neural circuits? A satisfying answer would map the routes and conditions of this signaling while cleanly separating drainage effects from cytokine, vascular, and neural mechanisms.
status: Meningeal lymphatic vessels were characterized in 2015 (Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`); their existence does not establish a complete causal map to cognition or behavior.
solved_when: A causal map exists linking meningeal immune and lymphatic processes to defined neural circuits, with drainage effects distinguished from cytokine, vascular, and neural signaling routes.
why: It would connect peripheral immunity to brain function through defined mechanisms, replacing correlation with mechanism.
key_works: Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`.

title: Epstein–Barr virus-to-multiple-sclerosis mechanism
open: Which events following Epstein–Barr virus infection lead to multiple sclerosis in susceptible people, and which intervention can interrupt that causal pathway?
status: A major longitudinal study strengthened the association between Epstein–Barr virus and multiple sclerosis in 2022 (Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`); the remaining problem is not whether an association exists, but the intervening mechanism and preventive leverage.
solved_when: A mechanistic pathway from Epstein–Barr virus infection to multiple sclerosis is identified experimentally, together with a demonstrated intervention that interrupts it.
why: A solution would enable mechanism-based prevention of multiple sclerosis rather than treatment after substantial neurological injury has already occurred.
key_works: Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`.

title: Convection versus diffusion in brain solute transport
open: How much of molecular transport through living brain tissue is carried by simple diffusion versus bulk flow, dispersion, and exchange between compartments — and how do those shares depend on molecule size? More formally, this asks for a quantified decomposition of the transport mechanisms underlying solute movement in brain tissue, identifiable from experimental measurements.
status: Sleep-clearance and vasomotion experiments constrain transport — notably Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`, and Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027` — but a single tracer measurement cannot identify all underlying transport mechanisms.
solved_when: The relative contributions of diffusion, bulk flow, dispersion, and compartment exchange to solute transport are quantified for molecules of different sizes in living brain tissue, with the mechanisms identifiable from available measurements rather than a single underdetermined tracer experiment.
why: It establishes which physical interventions could materially change clearance, distinguishing levers that genuinely alter solute transport from those that do not.
key_works: Xie et al. (2013), *Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1241224`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: State-dependent neurovascular transfer functions
open: Can we predict the vascular response to identified neural and glial activity when the brain's state changes — across sleep, attention, aging, and disease — rather than assuming one fixed neural-to-hemodynamic relationship?
status: Sleep-related vascular dynamics show the relevant state dependence — Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027` — but mapping such findings to quantitative interpretation of human imaging remains a separate open problem; the energetic framing traces to Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.
solved_when: A predictive account exists of how neural and glial activity map to vascular responses across the states named (sleep, attention, aging, and disease), replacing the assumption of a single fixed neural-to-hemodynamic transfer function.
why: It would sharpen the interpretation of functional imaging signals and clarify how vascular mechanisms contribute to disease.
key_works: Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`; Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`.

title: Cell-selective barrier repair
open: Can a damaged brain barrier be repaired so that its transport and immune selectivity are restored, without indiscriminately blocking beneficial exchange or driving pathological closure? Formally, the goal is a cell-selective engineering strategy that re-establishes controlled barrier function in a disease-specific manner.
status: Molecular atlases, such as Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, improve the cellular starting point, but identifying barrier-associated cells is not equivalent to controlling barrier function in a disease-specific manner; related structural and functional understanding of CNS lymphatic vessels comes from Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`.
solved_when: A method exists that restores a damaged brain barrier's selective transport and immune gating while preserving beneficial exchange and avoiding pathological closure, demonstrated in a disease-specific setting.
why: It would enable safer treatment of barrier leakage, inflammation, and drug-delivery failures across neurological disease.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Louveau et al. (2015), *Structural and functional features of central nervous system lymphatic vessels*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14432`.

title: Synapse-resolved energy budgets in vivo
open: Can we measure, at the level of individually identified synapses in a living animal, how much ATP is produced and consumed during behavior? A complete account would partition these costs among signaling, plasticity, maintenance, and failed transmission.
status: Quantitative energy budgets and experiments linking local ATP synthesis to synaptic function provide the foundations: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`, and Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`. A behaviorally resolved accounting remains incomplete.
solved_when: ATP production and consumption are quantified at identified synapses in vivo during behavior, with the accounting broken down into the costs of signaling, plasticity, maintenance, and failed transmission.
why: It reveals which neural computations are limited by local energy availability, rather than by connectivity or coding strategy.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`.

title: Mitochondrial placement as a computational constraint
open: Does the placement and trafficking of mitochondria determine which neuronal branches and synapses can sustain high activity and support learning? More precisely, can causal mitochondrial relocation — tested independently of overall mitochondrial health — predict and enable sustained activity at particular sites?
status: Local ATP synthesis is known to be functionally important for synaptic function, as shown by Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`, but this does not specify an optimal placement or trafficking rule for extended neurons.
solved_when: A demonstration that manipulating mitochondrial trafficking or local reserve capacity (causally, and independent of overall mitochondrial health) alters which branches or synapses can sustain high activity and learning, yielding a predictive rule for mitochondrial placement in extended neurons.
why: It would connect organelle logistics directly to information processing, explaining how local metabolic supply constrains computation in neurons.
key_works: Rangaraju, Calloway, and Ryan (2014), *Activity-driven local ATP synthesis is required for synaptic function*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2013.12.042`.

title: Causal functions of regional brain lipid composition
open: Do the lipid compositions of different brain regions causally shape neural excitability, synaptic organization, and region-specific vulnerability, or are they downstream markers of cell composition? Put differently, can manipulating regional lipid patterns be shown to alter these functional properties?
status: A spatial mouse-brain lipid atlas was published in September 2026 by Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`. Mapping lipid distributions is a milestone, not a complete functional explanation.
solved_when: Regional lipid patterns are experimentally shown to causally influence excitability, synaptic organization, or vulnerability — through targeted manipulation of lipid composition producing predicted functional changes — rather than merely correlating with cell composition.
why: It would open intervention targets for neural function and disease vulnerability that transcriptomics alone cannot reveal.
key_works: Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`.

title: Dynamic intercellular lipid-flux atlas
open: Can we measure the synthesis, transfer, remodeling, and degradation of defined lipids as they move between neurons and glia during learning, aging, and injury? That is, can the field move from static lipid abundance maps to a dynamic, cell-type-resolved atlas of intercellular lipid flux?
status: The 2026 lipid atlas (Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`) establishes spatial organization of brain lipids, but a static abundance map is not a measurement of intercellular flux; no dynamic flux atlas yet exists.
solved_when: A measurement framework exists that quantifies synthesis, transfer, remodeling, and degradation of defined lipids between neurons and glia across learning, aging, and injury — not merely their spatial abundance.
why: It would let researchers distinguish failures of lipid supply from altered use or impaired clearance, separating cause from consequence in neurodegenerative and injury contexts.
key_works: Fusar Bassini et al. (2026), *The lipidomic architecture of the mouse brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-026-11050-0`.

title: Energy–accuracy–latency bounds for neural computation
open: Are there fundamental limits that tie together how much energy a neural circuit spends, how accurately it computes, and how fast it responds? More formally, derive biologically constrained bounds linking energy use, inference accuracy, response time, and reliability, and determine how close identifiable circuits operate to those bounds.
status: Classical neural energy budgets, such as Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`, quantify important costs; however, they do not establish general optimality limits for natural computations. Related work on information-limiting correlations includes Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.
solved_when: A set of biologically constrained bounds relating energy use, inference accuracy, response time, and reliability is derived, together with an assessment of how close identifiable circuits operate to those bounds.
why: Such bounds would separate avoidable inefficiency in neural circuits from costs imposed by physical limits, telling us which observed energy expenditures are actually necessary.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Complete mammalian synapse-resolved connectome
open: Can we reconstruct the complete wiring diagram of a mammalian nervous system at synaptic resolution? The target is a full circuit map, complete with explicit error estimates, biological metadata, and reproducible access.
status: An adult fly brain was mapped in 2024 (Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`), and MICrONS delivered approximately cubic-millimeter-scale mouse cortical functional connectomics in 2025 (MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`). Neither constitutes a complete mammalian connectome.
solved_when: A complete mammalian synapse-resolved connectome is delivered, with quantified error estimates on the reconstruction, attached biological metadata, and openly reproducible access to the data.
why: It enables genuinely brain-wide tests of anatomical network hypotheses, replacing extrapolation from partial maps with direct measurement.
key_works: Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Predicting activity from a connectome
open: Can we predict how a neural circuit's activity — and the behavioral consequences of perturbing it — follows from its measured wiring diagram together with explicitly specified additional biological variables? Formally, given a connectome plus stated auxiliary variables, predict neural responses to unseen stimuli and the effects of interventions not used in fitting.
status: The MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`, aligns structure and activity, and Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`, supplies perturbational measurements; however, anatomical mapping alone does not solve functional prediction.
solved_when: A method taking a measured connectome plus explicitly specified additional biological variables predicts neural responses and behavioral effects of interventions that were not observed, with predictive accuracy demonstrated on unseen perturbations rather than on data used for model construction.
why: It tests what explanatory information a connectome actually contains — whether structure alone (plus specified variables) determines function — and anatomical mapping without such prediction does not answer this.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Extrasynaptic and modulatory connectomes
open: Can we map the nonsynaptic channels of neural communication — neuromodulators, volume transmission, ephaptic and other extrasynaptic routes — as systematically as synaptic connectomes are mapped? A complete answer would specify, for each such route, the receptor states involved and the spatial reach over which it operates.
status: The worm propagation atlas (Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`) demonstrates the value of measuring effective communication rather than inferring all influence from synaptic edges; ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons has been characterized (Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`).
solved_when: A functional connectome of extrasynaptic and modulatory communication exists, characterizing each nonsynaptic route's effective communication, receptor state, and spatial reach — with measurements of effective communication rather than inference from synaptic edges alone.
why: Without it, even anatomically complete connectomes remain functionally incomplete, missing whole classes of influence between neurons.
key_works: Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`; Anastassiou et al. (2011), *Ephaptic coupling of cortical neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.2727`.

title: Longitudinal synapse-resolved connectomics
open: Can we repeatedly observe the same substantial neural circuit at synapse resolution, watching synapses form, disappear, and remodel over time while keeping functional measurements and cell identities intact?
status: Dense electron-microscopy connectomes, such as Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`, provide exceptional structural detail but are endpoint measurements; chronic activity studies, such as Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`, do not recover the same complete synaptic graph.
solved_when: A longitudinal dataset exists in which the same circuit's complete synaptic graph is recovered at multiple time points, with cell identities preserved across time and concurrent functional measurements maintained.
why: It would make structural learning and degeneration directly observable, turning connectomics from endpoint snapshots into a record of change.
key_works: Dorkenwald et al. (2024), *Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-024-07558-y`; Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Information-limiting correlations in natural behavior
open: Which correlations in large neural populations actually limit behaviorally available information, rather than merely appearing as artifacts of finite recordings?
status: Theoretical information-limiting correlations were characterized in 2014 by Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`; identifying and estimating their real biological contribution remains difficult.
solved_when: The real biological contribution of information-limiting correlations in large populations is identified and estimated, distinguishing genuinely information-limiting structure from finite-sample correlations.
why: It determines whether adding neurons improves information or mainly adds redundancy.
key_works: Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Neural code timescale selection
open: When do downstream circuits actually read out a neural code in terms of precise spike timing, spike counts, or whole population trajectories — and when do they switch between these? A satisfactory theory would predict, for a given task, which timescale of code is used and under what conditions the readout switches.
status: Population dynamics and information-theoretic results — e.g., Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`, and Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807` — establish useful descriptions of neural codes, but no single universally relevant temporal code has been identified.
solved_when: A framework exists that correctly predicts which temporal coding scheme (timing, counting, population trajectories, or mixtures) is used by downstream circuits for a given task, including the conditions under which task-dependent switches occur.
why: It determines what recording resolution and what decoder assumptions are biologically justified when analyzing or modeling neural data.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Representation of uncertainty
open: Can we determine which format the brain uses to represent uncertainty — a probabilistic population code, a sampling-based representation, or a deterministic alternative? The question is whether single-trial neural dynamics and causal perturbations can yield predictions that discriminate among these candidate representations.
status: Brain-wide studies have identified representations of prior information, but observing prior-related activity does not settle the neural format of uncertainty. Key works: Ma et al. (2006), *Bayesian inference with probabilistic population codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1790`; Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.
solved_when: A distinguishing test based on single-trial dynamics and causal perturbations is specified and applied, cleanly separating probabilistic population codes, sampling-based representations, and deterministic alternatives in experimental data.
why: It would explain the neural basis of confidence, inference, exploration, and decision variability.
key_works: Ma et al. (2006), *Bayesian inference with probabilistic population codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1790`; Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.

title: True dimensionality of neural representations
open: What is the true dimensionality and spectral structure of neural population representations once noise, finite trial counts, stimulus sampling, and behavioral confounds are properly corrected for? More formally, can we derive estimators of representational dimensionality whose bias and variance are controlled under realistic experimental conditions?
status: A 2019 visual-cortex study reported high-dimensional geometry: Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`. A 2025 reanalysis sharpened concerns about estimating those properties reliably: Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.
solved_when: A method exists that reliably estimates representational dimensionality and spectral structure while correcting for noise, finite trials, stimulus sampling, and behavioral confounds, with demonstrated reliability on real population data.
why: It determines whether claims about coding efficiency, generalization, and neural manifold structure survive statistical scrutiny, or are artifacts of uncorrected estimation biases.
key_works: Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`; Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.

title: Binding distributed features into individual objects
open: What mechanism assigns each distributed feature to the correct object or event when several similar objects are present at once? Formally, how does a neural population code achieve feature-to-object assignment rather than merely representing features in a distributed geometry?
status: Large-scale population descriptions have revealed distributed representations, but representational geometry alone does not specify how features are assigned to objects. Key works include Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`, and Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.
solved_when: A mechanism is identified that explains how distributed features are bound to the correct individual objects, including in the demanding case of multiple similar objects presented simultaneously.
why: It would explain compositional perception — how the brain perceives complex scenes without conflating features that belong to different sources.
key_works: Stringer et al. (2019), *High-dimensional geometry of population responses in visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1346-5`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: General biological credit assignment
open: Can a single learning rule, computable from purely local information, assign credit in the brain's actual architecture — across recurrent circuits, delayed outcomes, and multiple interacting regions — and can it be validated as the mechanism the brain itself uses? In other words, derive such a local learning mechanism and identify it experimentally in biological circuits.
status: E-prop provides a computationally effective eligibility-trace approach; it is not a general experimental identification of the brain's learning rule (Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`).
solved_when: A local learning mechanism is both derived (handling recurrence, delayed outcomes, and multi-region interaction) and experimentally validated as operating in biological circuits.
why: It would connect synaptic change to successful learning of complex behavior, explaining how the brain's plasticity implements credit assignment rather than merely describing it.
key_works: Bellec et al. (2020), *A solution to the learning dilemma for recurrent networks of spiking neurons*, DOI: `10.1038/s41467-020-17236-y`.

title: Capacity–lifetime tradeoffs in biological memory
open: What are the fundamental limits on how much a biological memory system can store and how long it can retain it, when synapses are subject to realistic noise, turnover, bounded molecular resources, and continual learning? Can sharp capacity–lifetime tradeoff bounds be derived for synapses under these conditions?
status: Multiscale consolidation models achieve strong theoretical retention properties, but matching their assumptions and limits to biology remains unresolved; see Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on storage capacity and retention lifetime are derived for a synaptic memory model incorporating realistic noise, turnover, bounded molecular resources, and continual learning.
why: Such bounds would separate inherent architectural limitations of biological memory from biological failures that could in principle be remedied.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Homeostasis without erasing learned structure
open: How can a neuron or circuit stabilize its activity levels through homeostatic mechanisms without erasing the relative synaptic changes that encode what it has learned? Formally, what plasticity rule jointly maintains activity homeostasis and preserves learned synaptic structure, while predicting responses to prolonged perturbation and continued learning?
status: Circuit degeneracy and consolidation models show that stable outputs and persistent memories can arise in different ways, but a unified biological rule remains open. Key works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.
solved_when: A mechanism or rule is identified that stabilizes activity while preserving useful relative synaptic changes, and this rule demonstrably predicts responses both to prolonged perturbation and to continued learning.
why: It would explain how brains remain stable without becoming unable to learn, resolving the stability–plasticity dilemma at the level of a biological plasticity rule.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Molecular implementation of behavioral-timescale plasticity
open: What molecular mechanism carries an eligibility trace lasting seconds, so that a synapse can link an input to an event that arrives long after it? Formally, identify the eligibility traces and instructive signals that associate inputs with events separated by seconds, and determine where the same rule applies outside hippocampal place learning.
status: Behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity was demonstrated in CA1 in 2017 (Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`); its complete molecular implementation and scope remain open.
solved_when: The eligibility traces and instructive signals underlying behavioral-timescale plasticity are identified and characterized, and the scope of the rule is determined beyond hippocampal place learning.
why: A solution explains rapid learning from temporally extended experience, closing the gap between behavioral timescales and known synaptic mechanisms.
key_works: Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`.

title: Causal computational benefits of criticality
open: Can we causally demonstrate that operating at criticality benefits computation in a neural circuit? The goal is to manipulate an identified circuit toward and away from a measured critical regime while controlling confounds, and then test the predicted changes in learning, sensitivity, and robustness.
status: Avalanche observations motivate the criticality hypothesis, but demonstrating a distributional signature is distinct from proving a behavioral advantage; no causal test currently closes this gap. Key work: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.
solved_when: A circuit can be experimentally driven to both sides of its measured critical regime with confounds controlled, and the predicted changes in learning, sensitivity, and robustness are confirmed or refuted across those manipulations.
why: It determines whether criticality is functional, incidental, or task-dependent — settling whether the widely observed avalanche signatures have any causal behavioral meaning.
key_works: Beggs and Plenz (2003), *Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003`.

title: Circuit identifiability under degeneracy
open: Which combinations of anatomical, electrophysiological, and perturbational measurements suffice to uniquely identify the parameters of a neural circuit — and which leave unavoidable equivalence classes of indistinguishable parameter sets?
status: Distinct parameter sets producing similar network activity were demonstrated by Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; no general identifiability theory for realistic circuits yet exists.
solved_when: A general identifiability theory for realistic circuits is established, characterizing exactly which measurement combinations uniquely determine circuit parameters and which admit degenerate equivalence classes.
why: Without it, a successfully fitted model can be overinterpreted as the unique mechanism underlying observed activity.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`.

title: Stable behavior with drifting neural representations
open: How can downstream brain areas read out stable information from population codes whose tuning keeps changing over time? Formally, determine the mechanisms — coordinated drift, redundant coding, or continuous decoder adaptation — that allow stable behavior to persist despite ongoing representational drift.
status: Longitudinal hippocampal recordings documented changing place codes in 2013; recording drift does not explain successful downstream readout. Key works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.
solved_when: A theoretical account identifies which of coordinated drift, redundant coding, or continuous decoder adaptation suffices to preserve stable downstream readout under drifting upstream population codes, and distinguishes these mechanisms empirically or analytically.
why: It explains how the brain maintains lifelong behavioral reliability despite ongoing biological change in its representations.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Effective communication across distributed brain activity
open: When does activity in one brain region actually change the computation another region performs, rather than both merely covarying with a shared behavioral variable? Formally, can we distinguish directed causal communication from correlation induced by hidden common causes in distributed neural activity?
status: The 2025 brain-wide mouse activity map from International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`, greatly expands coverage across regions and laboratories, but broad representation is not equivalent to directed causal communication.
solved_when: A method or analysis demonstrates, on brain-wide recordings, whether activity in one region effectively alters another region's computation, separating directed causal influence from shared-variable covariation.
why: It separates information availability from information use, telling us which regions genuinely communicate rather than which merely reflect the same behavior.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Recurrent computation in difficult object recognition
open: Which recurrent interactions in visual cortex are actually necessary for recognizing objects that are occluded, ambiguous, or unfamiliar? More formally, can we identify the recurrent circuit elements whose perturbation predicts specific failures in difficult object recognition?
status: Performance-optimized models explain important visual responses — Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111` — but predictive fit does not establish the causal recurrent algorithm. The MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`, provides connectomic data relevant to testing such mechanisms.
solved_when: A characterization of the recurrent interactions required for difficult object recognition is given, together with predictions of recognition failures from targeted circuit perturbations that are confirmed by those perturbations.
why: It would connect visual robustness to specific circuit mechanisms, moving from correlational models to causal understanding of recurrent computation.
key_works: Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`; MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`.

title: Visual models that generalize beyond benchmark images
open: Can a visual model predict neural responses and behavior on genuinely novel inputs — new scene statistics, active viewing conditions, unusual viewpoints, and visual illusions — without any task-specific refitting? In other words, does a single model generalize across the full space of visual experience rather than the statistics of a particular benchmark?
status: Hierarchical models achieve substantial predictive success, while population-geometry work exposes the importance of stimulus and noise sampling. Key works: Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`; Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.
solved_when: A model quantitatively predicts neural responses and behavior for novel scene statistics, active viewing, unusual viewpoints, and visual illusions, with no task-specific refitting for any of these conditions.
why: It tests whether models explain vision itself rather than a particular dataset, separating genuine mechanistic understanding from benchmark overfitting.
key_works: Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`; Pospisil and Pillow (2025), *Revisiting the high-dimensional geometry of population responses in the visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2506535122`.

title: Wiring rules that create visual invariance
open: Which connectivity motifs, as actually measured in visual cortex circuits, suffice to produce tolerance to translation, scale, pose, and illumination — and which of these invariances cannot arise from wiring alone and instead require learning or feedback?
status: Functional connectomics now permits direct structure–response comparisons, but motif identification is not yet a complete generative account of invariance. Key works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`.
solved_when: A principled account identifies the measured connectivity motifs that generate each of translation, scale, pose, and illumination tolerance, and specifies which of these invariances require learning or feedback rather than wiring alone.
why: It links visual computations to physical circuit design, explaining invariance in terms of anatomy rather than learned weights alone.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Yamins et al. (2014), *Performance-optimized hierarchical models predict neural responses in higher visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.1403112111`.

title: Active vision’s sampling policy
open: How does the nervous system choose eye, head, and body movements to gather the visual information a task requires? In particular, what is the policy by which neural uncertainty about the current scene shapes the next movement?
status: Sensorimotor mismatch experiments establish an interaction between movement and visual input, but do not identify a general information-acquisition policy (Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener, 2012, *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`).
solved_when: A general information-acquisition policy is identified that explains how movements are selected in the service of task-relevant visual information, including the role of neural uncertainty in that selection.
why: It would replace passive-image descriptions of vision with an account of natural, active seeing grounded in how animals actually sample the world.
key_works: Keller, Bonhoeffer, and Hübener (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`.

title: Functionally precise auditory synapse regeneration
open: Can damaged connections between hair cells and the auditory nerve be regenerated so that they carry the right tuning, timing, and central integration — and can this be shown to improve natural listening?
status: The identification of persistent cochlear neural injury, as in Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after "temporary" noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`, establishes the repair target; synapse formation alone would not demonstrate restored auditory coding.
