solved_when: Regenerated hair-cell–auditory-nerve synapses demonstrate appropriate tuning, timing, and central integration, plus improved natural listening — synapse formation alone does not suffice.
why: It could restore hearing functions that amplification cannot replace.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`.

title: Individual tinnitus mechanisms
open: Which mechanisms actually sustain tinnitus in a given individual — what combination of peripheral injury, central gain, prediction, and affective learning — and can we use that profile to choose, in advance, an intervention that will work for that person?
status: Peripheral deafferentation and cortical auditory-selection studies constrain the possible mechanisms, but neither supplies a universal tinnitus explanation. Relevant work includes Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`, and Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.
solved_when: A method exists that identifies the sustaining mechanism combination for an individual and prospectively selects an intervention that is demonstrably effective for that person.
why: It would replace a heterogeneous symptom label with actionable mechanisms, turning diagnosis into individually matched treatment.
key_works: Kujawa and Liberman (2009), *Adding insult to injury: cochlear nerve degeneration after “temporary” noise-induced hearing loss*, DOI: `10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2845-09.2009`; Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`.

title: Auditory generalization across speakers and environments
open: How do neural circuits recognize the same word or sound source when the acoustic signal changes — a different accent, an unfamiliar voice, a reverberant room, background noise? More formally, what is the mechanism by which auditory representations preserve linguistic and sound-source identity under these acoustic transformations?
status: Attended-speech representations and language-model alignment provide partial descriptions of auditory processing; Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`, and Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`. These results do not establish a complete causal account of acoustic generalization.
solved_when: A complete causal account of acoustic generalization is established, explaining how linguistic and sound-source identity are preserved across accents, unfamiliar voices, reverberation, and background noise.
why: It would tie robust hearing to learnable transformations of the acoustic signal rather than memorized acoustics, explaining how listeners generalize rather than merely store sound patterns.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Molecule-to-odor prediction through biological mechanisms
open: Can we predict what a molecule smells like from its structure by modeling the actual biological pathway — receptor activation followed by neural processing — rather than from statistical correlations alone? The goal is a mechanism-based predictor that works for unfamiliar molecules and reports explicit uncertainty in its perceptual predictions.
status: The 2023 principal odor map improved diverse perceptual predictions; predictive embeddings do not yet establish the complete receptor-to-percept causal chain. Key work: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`.
solved_when: A model exists that maps molecular structure to odor percepts through explicit receptor-activation and neural-processing stages, generalizes to molecules outside its training distribution, and quantifies uncertainty in each perceptual prediction — including establishing the receptor-to-percept causal chain.
why: It would connect chemistry directly to perception and enable rational sensory design, such as inverse design of molecules for target percepts.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`.

title: Learning-dependent odor identity and valence
open: Which neural circuit changes alter what an odor *is* to the brain, as opposed to what it *means* — its learned pleasantness, threat value, or motivational significance? More precisely, how can experience transform an odor's valence representation while leaving its identity representation intact, and vice versa?
status: Perceptual odor maps provide a baseline organization, but do not explain how experience transforms identity and value separately. Key works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the circuit changes that separately govern odor identity representation versus learned valence, distinguishable from the baseline organization provided by perceptual odor maps.
why: It distinguishes sensory remapping from associative learning, telling us whether learning rewrites perception itself or only the value attached to it.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Taste, postingestive feedback, and nutrient value
open: How do the taste of food on the tongue and the delayed feedback from the gut jointly shape what an animal prefers to eat — including cases where sensed sweetness and actual physiological nutrient value come apart? More formally, the goal is to determine how oral taste signals and postingestive feedback are integrated to establish nutrient preferences, capturing the dissociation between sensory sweetness and nutrient value.
status: A rapid gut-to-brain nutrient-sensing circuit was demonstrated in 2018 (Kaelberer et al., 2018, *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`); integrating that pathway with taste and long-term preference learning remains open.
solved_when: A account — mechanistic or theoretical — is given of how oral taste signals and delayed gut feedback jointly establish nutrient preferences, including how preferences can dissociate from sensory sweetness and track physiological value.
why: It explains food choice beyond immediate taste, grounding preference in physiological value rather than flavor alone.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Individual differences in chemical perception
open: Can we predict how a given chemical will smell and taste to a specific person, rather than to the average person, using that individual's receptor variation, experience, physiological state, and exposure history? Formally, the goal is a model of person-specific percepts that accounts for individual deviations from the shared population-level perceptual map.
status: Population-level odor prediction has been substantially improved — notably by Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401` — but a shared perceptual map does not fully explain individual deviations, which remain uncharacterized.
solved_when: A model exists that predicts odor and taste percepts for individual people from their receptor variation, experience, physiological state, and exposure history, and demonstrably explains individual deviations that a shared perceptual map does not.
why: It would enable personalized sensory diagnostics and make cross-population studies reproducible despite individual variation.
key_works: Lee et al. (2023), *A principal odor map unifies diverse tasks in olfactory perception*, DOI: `10.1126/science.ade4401`.

title: Mechanotransduction-to-touch population code
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Can we predict what a person feels from the mechanics of skin contact — tracing how a touch's force direction, speed, and contact geometry shape receptor activation and population activity all the way to the tactile percept?
status: PIEZO2's major role in touch was established in mice, and its importance in human mechanosensation was demonstrated clinically (Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`), but the full population code remains open.
solved_when: A quantitative model exists that predicts tactile percepts from skin mechanics, receptor activation, and population activity, accounting for changes induced by force direction, speed, and contact geometry.
why: It would bridge mechanical contact with perception and enable principled prosthetic feedback for artificial touch.
key_works: Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`.

title: Construction of a whole-body state estimate
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: How do proprioceptive, vestibular, visual, and motor-command signals combine to produce a coherent estimate of body configuration and its uncertainty? A satisfactory account would specify the algorithm by which the nervous system fuses these heterogeneous signals into a unified whole-body state estimate.
status: Human PIEZO2 deficiency provides a causal probe of proprioceptive contributions, but not a complete algorithm for body-state estimation; see Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account or algorithm is given that explains how these signal modalities are integrated into a coherent body-configuration estimate with an associated uncertainty.
why: Such an account would directly support rehabilitation strategies for proprioceptive deficits and inform embodied control of artificial systems.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`.

title: Individual vestibular compensation
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: Can we predict how, and on what timescale, an individual's nervous system reweights its sensory channels after vestibular injury — and can interventions be designed that accelerate this adaptation without producing maladaptive dependence?
status: Studies of disrupted mechanosensation demonstrate substantial multisensory compensation, but do not provide a patient-specific vestibular recovery model. Key works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.
solved_when: A validated, patient-specific model exists that predicts sensory reweighting and recovery trajectories after vestibular injury, and identifies interventions that improve adaptation without inducing maladaptive dependence.
why: It would address the persistent imbalance and motion intolerance that follow vestibular injury, turning rehabilitation from trial-and-error into guided, individualized treatment.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.

title: Multisensory temporal binding
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: How do neural circuits decide whether signals arriving with different latencies originated from the same external event, and how do the temporal windows that permit such binding adapt with experience and context?
status: Neural models can represent distributed sensory information, but identifying the causal mechanism for common-event assignment remains distinct from decoding each modality. Related work includes Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; and Keller et al. (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`.
solved_when: A theory or mechanistic account is given that (i) identifies the circuit-level mechanism assigning signals to a common cause despite unequal delays, and (ii) explains how the temporal windows for this assignment adapt to experience and context.
why: It would explain how perception remains coherent despite unequal sensory latencies, and it would connect neural representation to causal common-source inference rather than mere decoding of each modality.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; Keller et al. (2012), *Sensorimotor mismatch signals in primary visual cortex of the behaving mouse*, DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.040`.

title: Active touch sampling strategies
subfield: Touch, proprioception, vestibular processing, and multisensory integration
open: How does an animal choose its exploratory hand or whisker movements so as to identify an object's shape, texture, or compliance with minimal time and effort? Formally, what is the control policy that links tactile sensing to purposeful movement selection?
status: Mechanotransduction mechanisms and motor population dynamics provide components, but not an integrated tactile information-acquisition policy. Key works include Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.
solved_when: A unified account exists of how exploratory movements are selected — an integrated tactile information-acquisition policy explaining movement choices that minimize time and effort while identifying shape, texture, or compliance.
why: It would connect perception to purposeful movement, explaining sensing as an active, goal-directed process rather than passive reception.
key_works: Ranade et al. (2014), *Piezo2 is the major transducer of mechanical forces for touch sensation in mice*, DOI: `10.1038/nature13980`; Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`.

title: Generalizable chronic-pain state biomarkers
open: Can we find neural markers that reliably predict clinically meaningful pain states over many days and across many patients, rather than in a single person or session? Formally, the challenge is to decouple pain signals from movement, mood, attention, and treatment effects so the marker tracks pain itself.
status: Intracranial recordings predicted chronic pain states in a small human study in 2023 (Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`); however, this is not a universal or context-free pain meter.
solved_when: A neural biomarker is demonstrated to predict clinically meaningful chronic pain states across days and across patients while remaining robust to (distinguishable from) movement, mood, attention, and treatment effects.
why: Such biomarkers would enable better clinical trials and adaptive, closed-loop treatment, complementing rather than replacing patient self-report.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`.

title: Mechanistic transition from acute to chronic pain
open: Which changes after an initiating injury make pain persist, and can we prospectively predict that transition before chronic pain is established?
status: Chronic-state biomarkers provide observations of established pain; they do not identify the causal transition or a universally preventive intervention. Key work: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`.
solved_when: The causal changes driving persistence are identified, and the transition to chronic pain can be predicted prospectively — before chronic pain is established.
why: A solution shifts treatment toward preventing pain persistence rather than managing established chronic pain.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`.

title: Causal control of pain without broad cognitive suppression
open: Can pathological pain be selectively turned off by a closed-loop device without dulling protective sensation, cognition, or voluntary behavior? Formally, the goal is to build a causal controller that uses a validated individual pain-state model to suppress pathological pain while leaving protective nociception, cognition, and voluntary behavior intact.
status: Neural pain decoding supplies a possible feedback signal for such a controller, but successful decoding does not by itself demonstrate safe causal control. Key works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.
solved_when: A closed-loop system built on a validated individual pain-state model demonstrates suppression of pathological pain while preserving protective sensation, cognition, and voluntary behavior.
why: It sets a stringent engineering target for closed-loop analgesia, where the hard constraint is selectivity — relieving suffering without broadly suppressing the nervous system.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Circuit code separating itch and pain
open: How do patterns of peripheral and spinal neural activity come to be experienced as itch, pain, or mixed sensations? A satisfactory account should explain how stimulus intensity and chronic sensitization shift activity between these perceptual categories.
status: Gastrin-releasing-peptide-receptor circuitry supplies an important mechanistic foothold, but it does not settle all labeled-line versus population-code questions. Key works: Sun and Chen (2007), *A gastrin-releasing peptide receptor mediates the itch sensation in the spinal cord*, DOI: `10.1038/nature06029`; Pagani et al. (2019), *How Gastrin-Releasing Peptide Opens the Spinal Gate for Itch* (verify bibliographic identifier).
solved_when: A mechanistic model is established that specifies how peripheral and spinal activity maps onto itch, pain, and mixed sensations, including the effects of stimulus intensity and chronic sensitization, in a way that resolves the labeled-line versus population-code question.
why: It could yield treatments that suppress pathological itch without impairing protective sensation.
key_works: Sun and Chen (2007), *A gastrin-releasing peptide receptor mediates the itch sensation in the spinal cord*, DOI: `10.1038/nature06029`; Pagani et al. (2019), *How Gastrin-Releasing Peptide Opens the Spinal Gate for Itch* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Nociception-to-experienced-pain mapping
open: Under what conditions does nociceptive activity become conscious pain, and how do expectations, attention, affect, and unconscious states alter that relationship?
status: Current work addresses the problem only in parts: pain-state prediction and consciousness measurements each tackle a different component, and neither identifies a universal mapping from tissue threat to experience. Key works include Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`.
solved_when: A principled account exists that specifies when nociceptive activity gives rise to conscious pain and quantifies how factors such as expectation, attention, affect, and unconscious state modify that mapping.
why: It would clarify pain in noncommunicating patients and separate nociception from suffering.
key_works: Shirvalkar et al. (2023), *First-in-human prediction of chronic pain state using intracranial neural biomarkers*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01338-z`; Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`.

title: Distributed action selection
open: How are competing actions selected through the distributed circuit spanning basal ganglia, cortex, and brainstem, without simply attributing selection to whichever region is found to encode the upcoming choice?
status: Brain-wide recordings reveal widespread behavioral variables, making causal allocation of selection functions more important rather than less. Key work: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account exists that causally assigns action-selection functions across basal ganglia, cortex, and brainstem — distinguishing initiation and inhibition — rather than correlationally localizing choice-encoding activity.
why: It explains how actions are initiated, inhibited, and how action competition goes awry in pathology.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Internal models of changing body mechanics
open: How do neural circuits build and maintain an internal estimate of the body's changing mechanical properties, including those altered by loads, injuries, and external tools? More precisely, can we determine how such estimates are represented and updated, and can predictive models of body physics be distinguished experimentally from learned feedback policies?
status: Findings on motor dynamics and cerebellar learning — including Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`, and Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward`, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726` — support several computational descriptions, but these do not uniquely identify the representation of body physics.
solved_when: A computational account is available that uniquely identifies the neural representation of body physics and cleanly separates predictive internal models from learned feedback policies in explaining adaptation.
why: It would explain how the motor system adapts rapidly to new loads, injuries, and tools — the core phenomenon any theory of motor control must account for.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Fast acquisition of new motor skills
open: Determine how rapid changes in neural activity combine with slower synaptic and myelin changes to produce transferable motor skill. Formally, what is the division of labor across these timescales, and how do their interactions give rise to skill that generalizes beyond the trained movements?
status: Cortical dynamics and causal myelination experiments establish contributions on different timescales; their division of labor remains unresolved. Key works include Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`, and McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account exists that specifies how fast neural-dynamics changes and slower synaptic and myelin changes each contribute to, and jointly produce, transferable motor skill.
why: It would directly guide rehabilitation schedules and the design of skill-training methods.
key_works: Churchland et al. (2012), *Neural population dynamics during reaching*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11129`; McKenzie et al. (2014), *Motor skill learning requires active central myelination*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1254960`.

title: Flexible control through spinal circuitry
open: What is the minimal descending information a brain must send for spinal circuits alone to produce adaptable movement across varying terrains and body states? Formally, characterize the smallest sufficient descending command signal — its dimensionality and structure — such that spinal circuitry can generate flexible locomotion.
status: A brain–spine interface enabled walking after spinal cord injury in a 2023 demonstration (Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`), but the general spinal control code remains open.
solved_when: A characterization of the minimal descending information (e.g., a specified set or dimensionality of command channels) is given, with demonstration that spinal circuits endowed with it generate adaptable movement across terrains and body states.
why: It would simplify restorative neurointerfaces by telling designers exactly what to decode and transmit, and would reveal the natural control hierarchy the nervous system itself uses.
key_works: Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: What climbing-fiber signals teach
open: What do climbing fibers actually teach the cerebellum? Determine when their activity conveys sensory error, reward, prediction, salience, or combinations of these, and derive the plasticity rule that such signals would imply.
status: Reward-related cerebellar signals challenge an exclusively motor-error description; the appropriate task-dependent teaching code remains unsettled. Key works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Larry et al. (2019), *Cerebellar climbing fibers encode expected reward size* (verify bibliographic identifier).
solved_when: A characterization is given of the task conditions under which each signal type (or combination) is carried by climbing fibers, together with a plasticity rule derived from those signals.
why: It defines the learning objective of cerebellar circuits, determining what the circuitry is optimizing and how its plasticity implements it.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Larry et al. (2019), *Cerebellar climbing fibers encode expected reward size* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Granule-cell expansion recoding in natural tasks
open: What do cerebellar granule cells actually compute from their mossy-fiber inputs, and does the expansion from mossy fibers to the much larger granule-cell population serve to increase separability of patterns, support temporal prediction, or achieve some other computational objective?
status: Reward-expectation coding demonstrates that granule-cell signals are richer than a purely static sensory expansion would predict; the general transformation remains unresolved. Key works: Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.
solved_when: A characterization of the granule-cell representation of mossy-fiber input is established that identifies which computational objective (e.g., separability, temporal prediction, or another) the expansion recoding serves, and is validated against the richer-than-sensory signals observed in vivo.
why: It tests central assumptions of cerebellar learning theories, which take expansion recoding as the foundation of how the cerebellum formats its inputs for learning.
key_works: Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Common cerebellar algorithm across motor and cognitive tasks
open: Does the cerebellum's repeated microcircuit architecture implement a single reusable computation across its motor and cognitive domains, or do different regions run distinct, region-specific algorithms?
status: Reward-related activity and cerebellar influence on reward circuitry broaden the functional scope beyond motor coordination, without proving algorithmic uniformity. Key works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581`.
solved_when: A characterization is given that shows either one common algorithm implemented by the repeated microcircuit across motor and cognitive (including reward-related) tasks, or identifies the distinct region-specific algorithms together with what in the circuitry differentiates them.
why: It would connect the cerebellum's anatomical repetition to computational reuse, showing whether a uniform circuit can serve both motor coordination and cognitive/reward functions.
key_works: Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`; Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581`.

title: Biological timing across milliseconds and seconds
open: How do cerebellar and connected circuits learn to produce precise time intervals ranging from milliseconds to seconds, without appealing to an unmeasured universal clock? A satisfactory account should specify a mechanism, grounded in measurable circuit dynamics, that generalizes across these distinct timescales.
status: Classical cerebellar learning theories (Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Albus (1971), *A theory of cerebellar function*, DOI: `10.1016/0025-5564(71)90051-4`) and modern reward-related recordings (Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`) constrain possible timing mechanisms, but no single cross-timescale solution has been established.
solved_when: A single mechanistic theory explains learned interval timing across both millisecond and second scales without positing an unmeasured universal clock, and is consistent with classical cerebellar learning theory and reward-related recordings.
why: It would explain temporal coordination in movement, prediction, and cognition with one unified mechanism rather than timescale-specific patches.
key_works: Marr (1969), *A theory of cerebellar cortex*, DOI: `10.1113/jphysiol.1969.sp008820`; Albus (1971), *A theory of cerebellar function*, DOI: `10.1016/0025-5564(71)90051-4`; Wagner et al. (2017), *Cerebellar granule cells encode the expectation of reward*, DOI: `10.1038/nature21726`.

title: Causal implementation of grid-cell attractors
open: Which circuit connectivity and dynamics actually produce the toroidal population topology seen in grid cells, and can a candidate mechanism correctly predict how that topology deforms under targeted perturbations? In other words, we seek a causal account that maps specific recurrent wiring rules and dynamics onto the observed grid-cell manifold, not merely a description of it.
status: Toroidal population topology was demonstrated in 2022 (Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`); however, observing a torus does not uniquely identify the circuit that generates it.
solved_when: A specified connectivity and dynamics scheme is shown to generate grid-cell population topology, and its predicted deformation under targeted perturbations matches empirical observation.
why: It would connect a striking population geometry to a mechanistic navigation algorithm, turning a topological description into an explanation of how the circuit computes.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Navigation in complex three-dimensional spaces
open: How do spatial codes in the brain represent environments that are volumetric, vertically connected, deformable, or non-Euclidean, and how do these representations support planning within them? More formally, what is the structure of neural population codes for navigation in complex three-dimensional geometry, and what planning computations do they support?
status: Toroidal grid-population results constrain familiar navigation settings but do not settle coding in arbitrary three-dimensional geometry; see Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.
solved_when: An account is given of how spatial codes represent volumetric, vertically connected, deformable, or non-Euclidean environments and how those representations support planning in such settings — going beyond toroidal grid-population findings in familiar navigation settings to arbitrary three-dimensional geometry.
why: It extends navigation theory beyond the simplified flat arenas on which current models rest, connecting to problems in robotics such as 3D simultaneous localization and mapping and geometry's study of navigation on complex manifolds.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`.

title: Shared mechanisms for spatial and abstract maps
open: Do spatial and nonspatial relational representations rely on the same learning and inference mechanisms, or do they merely exhibit similar-looking activity patterns? More precisely, is the mechanistic account forged for spatial population topology computationally identical to what supports abstract relational maps, or only an analogy at the level of observed structure?
status: Spatial population topology offers a strong mechanistic reference point; however, similarity to abstract representations does not establish computational identity. Key works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.
solved_when: A criterion is established that distinguishes genuine mechanistic identity from surface similarity between spatial and abstract relational representations — for example, by showing that the same learning and inference mechanisms do (or do not) generate both.
why: It tests whether navigation circuitry supplies a reusable engine for relational thought, or whether abstract cognition requires distinct computational machinery.
key_works: Gardner et al. (2022), *Toroidal topology of population activity in grid cells*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-021-04268-7`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Anchoring maps despite representational drift
open: How do stable landmarks, self-motion signals, and memory jointly keep spatial behavior accurate even as the neural ensemble representing space changes over time? More formally, what are the anchor and readout mechanisms that map a drifting neural code onto a stable spatial representation?
status: Longitudinal CA1 recordings established substantial dynamics of the place code over time (Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`); however, the anchor and readout mechanisms that keep behavior accurate remain to be identified.
solved_when: A mechanistic account is given that identifies the anchor and readout mechanisms maintaining accurate spatial behavior despite representational drift, consistent with the longitudinal dynamics observed in CA1 place codes.
why: It explains how navigation remains reliable over long periods despite continual turnover in the neural code, and informs analogous problems such as robotic localization under map drift.
key_works: Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Reading the content of an engram
open: Which features of an engram encode the specific content of a memory, rather than just the probability that a learned response will be expressed? Formally, can we identify and decode the representation within an activated memory-bearing ensemble that determines what, as opposed to whether, is recalled?
status: Optogenetic activation of a hippocampal ensemble induced fear-memory recall in Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; this does not reveal a complete content code.
solved_when: A method exists for reading out the particular remembered content from an engram — for example, by decoding or manipulating features of the activated ensemble to predict or alter the specific content of recall, not merely the likelihood of its expression.
why: It moves the field from locating memory-associated cells to understanding the information actually stored in them, connecting neuroscience to information-theoretic accounts of representation content and to interpretable distributed memory in AI.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`.

title: Mechanism of systems consolidation
open: How do the hippocampal and cortical contributions to a single memory change over time — is the information copied, transformed, redistributed, or reconstructed as consolidation proceeds?
status: Engram manipulation and longitudinal hippocampal recordings supply complementary evidence, but neither establishes a complete transfer algorithm. Key works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.
solved_when: A mechanism is specified that accounts for the changing hippocampal and cortical contributions to a specific memory over time, establishing whether the stored information is copied, transformed, redistributed, or reconstructed.
why: It would explain long-term retention and the effects of injury at different memory ages.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Ziv et al. (2013), *Long-term dynamics of CA1 hippocampal place codes*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3329`.

title: Selective memory updating without collateral change
open: Can a single memory association be modified while all related memories, their factual content, and the capacity for adaptive learning remain intact? More formally, the goal is a method for selective memory updating that also characterizes the conditions under which retrieval permits updating and those under which it does not.
status: Engram activation provides selective access to some memory-associated ensembles, but access is not equivalent to precise, durable editing of one association. Key works include Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; and Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.
solved_when: One memory association is edited precisely and durably, with related memories, factual content, and adaptive learning preserved, and a characterization is given of when retrieval permits updating versus when it does not.
why: It sets a stringent engineering target for treating maladaptive memories, where the therapeutic edit must not corrupt the rest of the memory system.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Frey and Morris (1997), *Synaptic tagging and long-term potentiation*, DOI: `10.1038/385533a0`.

title: Which substrate preserves very old memories
open: Which physical substrate actually carries a specific memory once it has been stored for a very long time? The question is to determine the relative necessity of synaptic weights, connectivity, intrinsic excitability, and molecular states for retaining specific memories over long intervals.
status: Synaptic consolidation models, such as Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`, explain possible persistence, while ensemble manipulations, such as Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`, identify relevant cells; neither uniquely identifies the enduring substrate.
solved_when: An experiment (or set of experiments) causally dissociates the candidate substrates — synaptic weights, connectivity, intrinsic excitability, and molecular states — showing which are individually necessary and which are not for retention of a specific memory over a long interval, with a measure that separates storage failure from retrieval failure.
why: It distinguishes storage failure from retrieval failure, telling us whether a memory that seems lost is truly gone or merely inaccessible.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`.

title: Interference-resistant episodic storage
open: How can a memory system keep overlapping experiences distinguishable while still supporting generalization across them? Formally, derive the capacity limits of episodic storage under learning rules that are biologically realistic.
status: Multiscale memory models address retention, but retention alone does not settle interference between structured, overlapping episodes. Key works include Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`, and Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`.
solved_when: A theoretical account explains simultaneous interference resistance and generalization for structured, overlapping episodes, with quantitative capacity limits derived under biologically realistic learning rules.
why: It connects memory capacity, abstraction, and forgetting in a single framework.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Bittner et al. (2017), *Behavioral time scale synaptic plasticity underlies CA1 place fields*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aan3846`.

title: Mechanism of activity-silent working memory
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Do working memories that show no sustained firing persist through synaptic changes, through spiking that current measurements simply fail to observe, through other cellular states, or through some combination of these?
status: TMS reactivated latent working-memory representations in 2016; however, reactivation does not uniquely identify the hidden storage substrate. Key work: Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`.
solved_when: Measurements and perturbations that discriminate among these storage alternatives are carried out, yielding a determination of which substrate (or combination) carries the silent memory.
why: It resolves what actually persists between observable bursts of neural activity, determining whether working memory requires ongoing activity at all.
key_works: Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`.

title: Mechanistic limits on working-memory capacity
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Can the capacity and precision limits of working memory be derived from underlying neural mechanisms rather than posited as fixed parameters? In particular, can a mechanistic account incorporating interference, attention, resource allocation, and representational similarity predict how these task-dependent limits arise?
status: Work on latent-state reactivation, e.g. Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`, has expanded the candidate mechanisms beyond persistent firing, but this does not settle how capacity limits arise. Related theoretical work includes Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.
solved_when: A principled derivation yields quantitative, task-dependent predictions of capacity and precision that follow from specified neural mechanisms, with the derivations accounting for the roles of interference, attention, resource allocation, and representational similarity.
why: It would explain why working-memory capacity changes with the content being stored and the task being performed, grounding those changes in mechanism rather than phenomenology.
key_works: Rose et al. (2016), *Reactivation of latent working memories with transcranial magnetic stimulation*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aah7011`; Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), *Information-limiting correlations*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.3807`.

title: Causal mechanism of attentional competition
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: How does the brain causally enhance or suppress competing representations, and how is that competition controlled across sensory modalities? In formal terms, which mechanism — gain modulation, routing, recurrent competition, or altered readout — is causally responsible for selective processing, and what governs it across modalities?
status: Attended-speaker representations demonstrate selective processing, but do not alone distinguish gain changes, routing, recurrent competition, or altered readout. Key works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.
solved_when: A causal account is identified that distinguishes among gain changes, routing, recurrent competition, and altered readout as the mechanism of selective enhancement and suppression, and is shown to operate across sensory modalities.
why: It explains selective access to working memory and perception without assuming a single attention center, grounding control in the interactions among competing representations themselves.
key_works: Mesgarani and Chang (2012), *Selective cortical representation of attended speaker in multi-talker speech perception*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11020`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Compositional executive control
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: Explain how familiar rules and operations are recombined to solve a novel task without learning every combination separately.
status: Brain-wide task-variable representations and language-model alignment provide relevant observations, but not a verified neural algorithm for compositional control. Key works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.
solved_when: A verified neural algorithm is specified that composes known rules into novel task solutions, with empirical or theoretical evidence that performance does not depend on separately learning each combination.
why: It addresses flexible reasoning rather than repeated task execution, distinguishing genuinely compositional control from memorized task repertoires.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Confidence versus decision evidence
subfield: Working memory, attention, and executive control
open: How does the brain keep track of how confident it is in a decision, separately from the evidence, value, and motor preparation that accompany that decision? Formally, we want to identify whether circuits compute a distinct metacognitive signal of confidence that can be dissociated from these accompanying variables.
status: Brain-wide prior-information representations reveal relevant signals, but shared correlations do not identify a separate metacognitive computation. Key work: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.
solved_when: Confidence can be experimentally or computationally dissociated from decision evidence, value, and motor preparation at the circuit level — that is, a representation or computation is identified that tracks confidence and cannot be explained by shared correlations with the other variables.
why: A solution explains how self-evaluation becomes calibrated, and why that calibration fails in disorders of confidence and metacognition.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`.

title: Dopamine’s task-dependent teaching signals
open: Which dopamine signals actually instruct learning, which instead reflect movement or motivation, and how do postsynaptic circuits interpret these mixed signals?
status: Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation were demonstrated in 2019 (Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`); this argues against treating every dopamine fluctuation as one universal scalar error.
solved_when: A framework exists that identifies which dopamine signals instruct learning versus those reflecting movement or motivation, and explains how postsynaptic circuits interpret the mixed signals.
why: It improves models of reward learning and of dopaminergic dysfunction.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Local control of dopamine release
open: When does dopamine release at axon terminals diverge from the firing of the dopamine neurons themselves, and how does the state of the local circuit alter the behavioral effect of that release? A formal account would specify the circuit conditions under which somatic activity and terminal release decouple, and how that decoupling maps onto behavior.
status: The 2019 dissociation between dopamine dynamics related to learning and motivation highlights the importance of distinguishing somatic activity from local release (Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`).
solved_when: There is a mechanistic, experimentally testable account identifying the conditions under which terminal dopamine release dissociates from source-neuron firing, and showing how local circuit state modifies the behavioral consequences of that release.
why: It makes neuromodulatory measurements interpretable at the site of action, rather than inferring local release from somatic activity.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Arbitration between planning and cached habits
open: How does the brain decide whether to rely on explicit prospective planning or on previously cached action values, taking into account the cost of computation itself? Formally, what algorithm arbitrates between model-based evaluation and habitual control, and how are its signals implemented and identifiable in neural data?
status: Distributed prior and decision signals provide potential neural substrates for arbitration, but observing those signals does not by itself identify an arbitration algorithm. Key works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.
solved_when: A specified arbitration mechanism is articulated that accounts for how the brain selects between planning and cached habits, incorporates the costs of computation, and is identifiable from neural measurements — not merely consistent with observed prior and decision signals.
why: It would explain how behavioral flexibility and habit formation arise, and why deliberation is sometimes overused despite its cost, grounding model-based/model-free arbitration and metareasoning in neural mechanism.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Directed exploration versus behavioral noise
open: What neural mechanisms distinguish purposeful, information-seeking exploration from random behavioral variability, and can they predict how agents explore under novel structures of uncertainty?
status: Large decision datasets expose trial-to-trial variability and prior effects, but these are not sufficient to identify the objective behind exploration. Key works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.
solved_when: Mechanistic neural signatures are identified that dissociate directed exploration from stochastic behavioral noise, and these signatures are shown to predict exploration behavior under previously untested uncertainty structures.
why: It explains how learning proceeds when both rewards and the structure of the world are initially unknown.
key_works: Findling et al. (2025), *Brain-wide representations of prior information in mouse decision-making*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09226-1`; Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`.

title: Neural implementation of compositional meaning
open: How does the brain combine the meanings of individual words and their relations into a meaning for a sentence it has never encountered before, including in counterfactual and structurally ambiguous cases? More formally, what neural mechanism implements the composition algorithm that maps lexical and relational representations into sentence-level meanings?
status: Semantic maps and predictive language models each explain important variance in neural responses, but neither on its own establishes the causal composition algorithm. Key works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account is identified that causally explains how word meanings and relations are combined into novel sentence meanings, covering counterfactual and structurally ambiguous cases — going beyond correlational accounts of response variance.
why: It would explain the human ability to understand sentences never previously encountered, and would clarify whether predictive language models merely correlate with neural responses or actually implement the composition algorithm.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Grounding linguistic concepts in perception and action
open: How do the linguistic, sensory, motor, and relational components of a concept interact, and which of them are actually necessary for grounding meaning in a given context?
status: Natural-language imaging reveals distributed semantic organization in the brain, but a semantic response map is not a complete causal grounding model. Key work: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.
solved_when: We have an account (ideally causal, not merely correlational) specifying which components are necessary in which contexts, supported by experimental evidence rather than descriptive semantic maps alone.
why: It would explain how concepts mean something beyond text-to-text association, connecting language to perception and action.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Cross-language neural representation alignment
open: Which neural representations of language are shared across languages, and which instead depend on a language's learned grammar, writing system, the speaker's proficiency, or age of acquisition?
status: Strong language-encoding models provide a benchmark, but success on particular languages does not establish language-independent mechanisms. Key works: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.
solved_when: A characterization exists that distinguishes cross-linguistically shared representations from language-dependent ones, accounting for grammar, writing system, proficiency, and age of acquisition.
why: Without it, findings from a single language risk being mistaken for universal language neuroscience.
key_works: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`; Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`.

title: Language-specific versus general reasoning computations
open: Can we separate the neural computations that formulate language from those that carry out the underlying reasoning? Concretely, can matched nonverbal tasks combined with causal perturbations isolate which computations are language-specific and which are general to inference?
status: Predictive language models can align with neural responses, but that alignment does not establish that language and thought use identical mechanisms. Key work: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.
solved_when: An experimental design using matched nonverbal comparison tasks and causal perturbation methods demonstrably dissociates neural computations required for linguistic formulation from those required for the underlying inference.
why: It determines what language models can and cannot explain about human cognition — whether alignment with neural responses reflects shared mechanisms or merely superficial correspondence.
key_works: Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Developmental emergence of language circuitry
open: How do genetic constraints, social interaction, perception, and learning jointly give rise to language-selective circuitry over the course of early development?
status: Current work characterizes mature endpoints: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`, describes adult semantic maps, and Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`, aligns models to mature neural architecture. These do not uniquely determine the developmental learning process.
solved_when: A theory or model is given that explains how these factors together produce language-selective circuitry from early development, rather than only describing its mature endpoint.
why: It would bridge developmental biology, learning, and linguistic competence, explaining the origin of language circuitry rather than merely its adult form.
key_works: Huth et al. (2016), *Natural speech reveals the semantic maps that tile human cerebral cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/nature17637`; Schrimpf et al. (2021), *The neural architecture of language: Integrative modeling converges on predictive processing*, DOI: `10.1073/pnas.2105646118`.

title: Neural organization of emotional states
open: Are emotional states organized into discrete circuit categories, continuous dimensions, context-dependent constructions, or some combination of these — and can that account predict interventions?
status: Personalized closed-loop depression work, such as Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`, demonstrates useful state-linked signals, but a clinically useful signal is not a universal taxonomy of emotion.
solved_when: A framework is provided that either discriminates among these organizational accounts or validly combines them, and demonstrates predictive value for interventions.
why: It fixes the mechanistic units that emotion research should compare, grounding future theory and experiments in shared structure.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Inferring another individual’s hidden state
open: How do neural circuits infer another individual's hidden goals, beliefs, or feelings — and can we tell genuine state inference apart from mere learned stimulus-response associations? Formally, the challenge is to identify the circuit mechanisms and computations that support attribution of internal states to others, and to establish criteria distinguishing such inference from associative accounts of social behavior.
status: Studies of social attachment and reward circuits have identified relevant mechanisms — e.g., Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, PMID: `36708707`, and Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581` — but the computational basis of social inference remains unsettled.
solved_when: The neural circuits and computational basis underlying inference of another individual's internal states are identified, with a demonstrated distinction between genuine state inference and learned stimulus-response associations.
why: It explains how social behavior remains flexible in novel situations, where stimulus-response associations alone would fail.
key_works: Berendzen et al. (2023), *Oxytocin receptor is not required for social attachment in prairie voles*, PMID: `36708707`; Carta et al. (2019), *Cerebellar modulation of the reward circuitry and social behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav0581`.

title: Causal interpretation of interacting-brain synchrony
open: Determine which apparent between-brain couplings reflect genuine information exchange between people rather than shared sensory input, synchronized movement, or analysis artifacts.
status: Large-scale recording and reproducibility work sharpen the methodological problem; correlation between brains cannot by itself identify interpersonal causation. International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.
solved_when: A principled account exists that distinguishes true interpersonal causal coupling from common-input confounds and methodological artifacts in interacting-brain (hyperscanning) data, so synchrony findings can be interpreted causally.
why: It makes hyperscanning claims testable and mechanistically interpretable rather than merely correlational.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Generalization of safety learning
open: Why does a learned sense of safety tend to stay locked to the context in which it was acquired, and how can that safety be made to generalize appropriately without erasing the ability to discriminate genuine threat? Put formally, the problem is to identify the mechanisms that keep learned safety context-specific and to find interventions that broaden its expression while preserving useful threat discrimination.
status: Selective memory-ensemble access and reopened social-learning windows offer possible experimental tools, but no complete solution to generalizing safety yet exists. Key works include Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; and Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account explains why learned safety remains context-specific, and an intervention is demonstrated that promotes generalization of safety across contexts while maintaining appropriate threat discrimination.
why: It addresses the relapse of maladaptive fear outside the contexts in which treatment or extinction occurred, a core obstacle to lasting recovery from fear-related disorders.
key_works: Liu et al. (2012), *Optogenetic stimulation of a hippocampal engram activates fear memory recall*, DOI: `10.1038/nature11028`; Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Experiments that discriminate major consciousness theories
open: Can we design experiments whose outcomes genuinely separate the major theories of consciousness, so that at least one framework is constrained rather than merely reinterpreted? That is, can preregistered, adversarially designed measurements yield predictions on which theories like global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory disagree, and that cannot be accommodated after the fact by adjusting the theory?
status: A 2025 adversarial collaboration tested global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories, supporting and challenging different predictions rather than simply declaring one theory solved. Key works: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`; Melloni et al. (2023), *An adversarial collaboration protocol for testing contrasting predictions of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pone.0268577`.
solved_when: A preregistered experiment tests predictions on which competing consciousness theories make opposing claims, and the results are published with an explicit adjudication of which theory's predictions were supported or challenged — such that post-hoc modification of the losing theory to fit the data is ruled out by the design.
why: It turns broad, flexible frameworks about consciousness into cumulative, falsifiable science, where results actually constrain theory rather than being absorbed by it.
key_works: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`; Melloni et al. (2023), *An adversarial collaboration protocol for testing contrasting predictions of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theory*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pone.0268577`.

title: Minimal sufficient neural substrate for a conscious content
open: Can we identify a neural mechanism that is sufficient to produce a particular conscious content — and, in doing so, cleanly separate the constitutive mechanism from enabling conditions, reporting, attention, and downstream consequences?
status: Multimodal theory tests currently constrain candidate locations and dynamics, but correlates and task-related activation do not establish minimal sufficiency. Key work: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`.
solved_when: An experimental intervention demonstrates that a specific neural mechanism is minimally sufficient for a given conscious content, with enabling conditions, report-related processes, attention, and downstream consequences ruled out as constituents.
why: It moves the field beyond merely locating activity associated with awareness, toward causal explanation of what consciousness is made of.
key_works: Cogitate Consortium et al. (2025), *Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08888-1`.

title: Consciousness measurement without report confounds
open: Can we measure the state and content of consciousness without relying on the linguistic, attentional, or motor processes we are trying to distinguish from consciousness itself? Formally, the goal is to validate measures of conscious state and content that do not require the very behavioral capacities under study.
status: Perturbational complexity and dream-related cortical measurements provide partial approaches; neither supplies a universal content-sensitive, report-independent measure. Key works: Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.
solved_when: A validated measure of conscious state and content exists that is report-independent — i.e., universal, content-sensitive, and not confounded by the sensory processing or behavioral channels it is meant to separate from consciousness.
why: Such a measure unlocks rigorous consciousness research in infants, noncommunicating patients, and nonhuman animals, populations where report-based methods fail.
key_works: Casali et al. (2013), *A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior*, DOI: `10.1126/scitranslmed.3006294`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Reliable detection of covert consciousness
open: Can we reliably detect preserved awareness in behaviorally unresponsive patients? The goal is a validated method with calibrated false-negative rates, repeatable bedside applicability, and demonstrated clinical consequences.
status: A 2024 multicenter study by Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`, detected cognitive motor dissociation in a substantial subset of behaviorally unresponsive participants; however, negative tests still cannot be interpreted as simple proof of absent awareness.
solved_when: A detection method exists that (i) has empirically calibrated false-negative rates, (ii) can be repeatably administered at the bedside, and (iii) has been validated against clinically meaningful consequences for patient care.
why: Detection outcomes directly shape communication access, rehabilitation, and major clinical decisions for behaviorally unresponsive patients.
key_works: Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`.

title: Explanatory bridge from mechanism to experience
open: Why should any particular physical process give rise to the particular experience it does, rather than another or none at all? Develop an account that explains why specified physical processes correspond to particular experiences, while making clear which parts are empirical predictions and which are philosophical commitments.
status: The modern "hard problem" formulation dates to Chalmers (1995), *Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness*, Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 200–219. Formal theories and empirical comparisons have advanced since — e.g., Albantakis et al. (2023), *Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011465` — but no generally accepted explanatory bridge follows merely from locating neural correlates.
solved_when: There exists an account that (i) explains the correspondence between specified physical processes and particular experiences, and (ii) explicitly separates its empirical predictions from its philosophical commitments.
why: It clarifies what a complete theory of consciousness is claiming to explain, distinguishing testable content from metaphysical assumption.
key_works: Chalmers (1995), *Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness*, Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3), 200–219; Albantakis et al. (2023), *Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011465`.

title: Functions of dreaming
open: Which effects of dreaming are caused by the dream content itself, as opposed to the sleep physiology that dreaming accompanies? Formally, which consequences of dreaming depend on experienced dream content rather than on the underlying sleep physiology alone?
status: Neural correlates of dreaming were characterized in 2017; identifying when dreams occur does not establish why they occur. Key work: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.
solved_when: A study demonstrates that a given consequence of dreaming is altered by manipulating the experienced dream content while holding the underlying sleep physiology constant — or, conversely, that the consequence persists when dream content is absent despite equivalent sleep physiology.
why: It would distinguish whether dreaming is an adaptive function, a mere by-product of sleep, or a phenomenon whose value lies mainly in subjective interpretation.
key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Selective memory consolidation during sleep
open: Which experiences does the sleeping brain choose to replay or transform, and how do those overnight processes improve later behavior? More formally, can a theory specify the selection policy that determines which individual memories are consolidated, restructured, or weakened during sleep?
status: Memory-consolidation models and sleep-state measurements provide components, but not a complete selection policy for individual memories. Key works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.
solved_when: A theory exists that identifies what selects individual memories for replay or transformation during sleep and explains how those processes improve later behavior — yielding a complete selection policy for individual memories.
why: It would explain why sleep strengthens some information while weakening or restructuring other information, grounding the practical role of sleep in memory.
key_works: Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`; Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`.

title: Distinct computational roles of REM and non-REM sleep
open: Which learning or maintenance operations of the brain require particular sleep states, and does the causal ordering of those states across the night matter for their function?
status: Dreaming is not confined to a single simple state classification, and clearance findings depend on specific sleep dynamics; these observations resist one-function-per-stage accounts. Key works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.
solved_when: A causal account exists that specifies which computational operations depend on which sleep states and demonstrates whether their sequencing is necessary, supported by experimental manipulation of individual states and their order.
why: It would let clinicians target the specific disrupted sleep stage responsible for a cognitive or clearance deficit rather than treating sleep architecture wholesale.
