key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Coordination of local sleep pressure and global timing
open: Explain how local circuit needs interact with global sleep-state transitions and circadian timing to determine when particular regions become unavailable for waking computation.
status: Spatially specific dream correlates and sleep-related vascular dynamics show that whole-brain stage labels omit important local variation, as seen in Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`, and Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.
solved_when: A theoretical account is given that relates local circuit demands, global sleep-state transitions, and circadian timing so as to predict when specific regions become unavailable for waking computation.
why: A solution would connect local dysfunction to global sleep regulation, explaining how region-specific failures disturb whole-brain timing.
key_works: Siclari et al. (2017), *The neural correlates of dreaming*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4545`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Predictive homeostatic control
open: How does the brain predict the physiological consequences of behavior before regulated variables like blood chemistry have actually changed? Formally, what is the predictive-control algorithm by which anticipatory signals — rather than reactive feedback alone — govern homeostatic regulation?
status: Thirst-neuron activity was shown in 2016 to anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking (Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`), but the general predictive-control algorithm remains unresolved.
solved_when: A general predictive-control mechanism is identified that accounts for anticipatory regulation of homeostatic variables, subsuming known cases such as thirst-neuron anticipation of eating and drinking.
why: It explains how the brain achieves anticipatory regulation instead of merely reacting to deviations, grounding interoceptive control in a concrete algorithm.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`.

title: Vagal afferent population code
open: How do populations of vagal afferents jointly encode the combinations of mechanical, chemical, immune, and nutritional conditions within the body, and by what mechanisms does the brain disambiguate signals that overlap across these channels?
status: A defined gut nutrient-transduction circuit was demonstrated in 2018 (Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`), but one pathway does not establish a complete visceral sensory code.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the vagal afferent population code — how mechanical, chemical, immune, and nutritional signals are combined and multiplexed across the population — together with an account of how the brain decodes or disambiguates these overlapping signals.
why: It would enable more selective interpretation and stimulation of visceral pathways, rather than coarse manipulation of vagal signaling.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Bodily signals in affective experience
open: When do signals from the body — thirst, visceral and autonomic state — actually cause changes in emotional experience, and when do emotions instead reshape how bodily signals are interpreted? A satisfying answer would quantify the causal influence in each direction and specify how the two directions interact in a closed loop.
status: Anticipatory homeostatic circuits and individualized mood-linked neural signals provide entry points, but not a complete bidirectional causal model. Key works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.
solved_when: A quantitative bidirectional causal model is demonstrated experimentally: interventions on interoceptive signals are shown to causally alter emotion, emotional manipulations are shown to alter bodily interpretation, and the interaction between the two directions is characterized.
why: It would connect physiological regulation to anxiety, mood, and subjective feeling, grounding affective science in measurable body–brain mechanisms.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Multiobjective autonomic coordination
open: How does the nervous system coordinate cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive, and thermoregulatory demands when improving one variable worsens another? Formally, this asks for a general circuit-level account of how the brain resolves tradeoffs among competing autonomic objectives.
status: Specific anticipatory control pathways are known, such as Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`, and Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`, but a general circuit-level account of tradeoffs across bodily systems remains open.
solved_when: A general circuit-level account of anticipatory tradeoff management across bodily systems is provided — one that goes beyond individual anticipatory control pathways to explain coordinated regulation when improving one variable worsens another.
why: It would explain coordinated physiology under exercise, stress, illness, and recovery.
key_works: Zimmerman et al. (2016), *Thirst neurons anticipate the homeostatic consequences of eating and drinking*, DOI: `10.1038/nature18950`; Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`.

title: Hormonal state-to-circuit reconfiguration
open: How do shifting endocrine states reconfigure neural computations over timescales from hours to months, and how much of that reconfiguration reflects direct hormone-receptor action rather than the altered bodily and social experience that accompanies the transition?
status: Long-lasting pregnancy-associated brain-structure changes were reported in Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`; however, structural change alone does not specify its cellular mechanism or functional meaning.
solved_when: An account distinguishes direct receptor-mediated effects from experience-driven changes in circuit function across endocrine transitions, spanning the hours-to-months timescale, with structural findings linked to a cellular mechanism and functional meaning.
why: It would explain both adaptive and pathological neural changes occurring across major endocrine transitions.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`.

title: Enteric wiring-to-motility prediction
open: Can the motor patterns of the gastrointestinal tract be predicted from the identified cell types of the enteric nervous system, their connectivity, and local sensory inputs — including how these patterns change under perturbation? Formally, this asks for a wiring-to-function map that takes an enteric circuit specification and yields the resulting motility, both at baseline and under intervention.
status: Human and mouse enteric single-cell atlases were published in 2020 (Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`), but a cell census is not a functional motility model.
solved_when: A model exists that, given identified enteric cell types, connectivity, and local sensory inputs, correctly predicts gastrointestinal motor patterns and their responses to perturbation.
why: It would connect the enteric cell-classification program to actual digestive function and dysfunction, turning anatomical atlases into predictive physiology.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Causal microbiome-to-neural pathways
open: Which specific microbial products, acting through which host pathways, causally alter defined neural functions — and can their effects be cleanly attributed to neural, immune, endocrine, or dietary mediation rather than a mixture of these?
status: Direct gut nutrient-transduction mechanisms, as in Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`, provide a tractable route, supported by single-cell resolution maps of the enteric nervous system (Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`), but such mechanisms do not establish the many broader causal claims made about microbiome–brain relationships.
solved_when: A demonstrated causal chain is established: a specific microbial product is identified, its host pathway traced, and its effect on a defined neural function reproduced under experimental separation of neural, immune, endocrine, and dietary mediators.
why: It converts broad microbiome–brain associations into reproducible, mechanistically grounded interventions.
key_works: Kaelberer et al. (2018), *A gut-brain neural circuit for nutrient sensory transduction*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aat5236`; Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Target-accurate peripheral reinnervation
open: Can severed peripheral sensory or motor axons be guided back to their correct original targets, so that function — not just anatomical regrowth — is restored with the appropriate modality and timing? In particular, what are the quantitative limits on successful reinnervation imposed by target distance and chronic denervation?
status: Human mechanosensory deficits and neural-interface demonstrations clarify what functions must be restored; it is recognized that anatomical regrowth by itself would not establish correct reconnection. Key works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.
solved_when: Injured sensory or motor axons reinnervate their appropriate targets with correct modality and timing, and the limits imposed by target distance and chronic denervation are quantified; anatomical regrowth alone does not suffice.
why: It addresses the functional failures that follow nerve injury, where regeneration occurs but useful sensory or motor function does not return.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Longitudinal enteric disease biomarkers
open: Can we build minimally invasive measurements that track specific enteric neuronal or glial dysfunction before irreversible tissue damage occurs, with validation against physiological outcomes?
status: Molecular enteric reference maps, such as Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`, provide candidate markers, but no validated longitudinal disease assay yet exists.
solved_when: A validated longitudinal disease assay exists that minimally invasively measures enteric neuronal or glial dysfunction prior to irreversible tissue damage and tracks physiological outcomes.
why: It would make the enteric nervous system accessible to earlier diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
key_works: Drokhlyansky et al. (2020), *The Human and Mouse Enteric Nervous System at Single-Cell Resolution*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2020.08.003`.

title: Avian–mammalian computational homology
open: Which forebrain computations in birds and mammals are inherited from shared ancestral circuitry, and which instead arose convergently through different implementations?
status: A cortex-like avian canonical circuit was described in 2020 (Stacho et al. (2020), *A cortex-like canonical circuit in the avian forebrain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abc5534`); however, architectural resemblance does not by itself settle evolutionary or computational identity.
solved_when: A comparative account identifies, for bird and mammal forebrain computations, which derive from shared ancestral circuitry and which are convergent solutions implemented differently.
why: It tests whether sophisticated cognition requires a particular cortical architecture.
key_works: Stacho et al. (2020), *A cortex-like canonical circuit in the avian forebrain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abc5534`.

title: Distributed control in cephalopod arms
open: How do the largely autonomous neural circuits within each cephalopod arm coordinate with central brain signals to produce flexible movement, sensory processing, and action selection? A satisfying account would specify the division of labor between local arm circuits and the central brain as a distributed control algorithm.
status: The octopus genome revealed neural and morphological innovations in 2015, but genomic information does not supply the distributed control algorithm. Key work: Albertin et al. (2015), *The octopus genome and the evolution of cephalopod neural and morphological novelties*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14668`.
solved_when: A mechanistic model is identified that explains how local arm circuits and central brain signals together implement flexible movement, sensory processing, and action selection — that is, the distributed control algorithm is characterized, not merely its neural substrate.
why: It would reveal alternatives to centralized control for highly deformable bodies, directly informing soft robotics and decentralized control strategies that operate without detailed central commands.
key_works: Albertin et al. (2015), *The octopus genome and the evolution of cephalopod neural and morphological novelties*, DOI: `10.1038/nature14668`.

title: Computational consequences of neural RNA editing
open: Which RNA-editing events in neural tissue actually change neural computation and adaptive behavior, and which are merely neutral or compensatory? Formally, determine the causal contribution of individual recoding events to neural function and behavior.
status: Extensive recoding in squid neural transcripts was demonstrated in 2015 (Alon et al. (2015), *The majority of transcripts in the squid nervous system are extensively recoded by A-to-I RNA editing*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.05198`); however, a catalog of edits does not establish their individual functional significance.
solved_when: The functional significance of RNA-editing events is determined: for each editing event (or defined class of events), it is established whether it causally alters neural computation or adaptive behavior, or is neutral or compensatory.
why: It tests a form of neural molecular flexibility that goes beyond what genomic sequence alone can encode, and moves the field from cataloging edits to understanding their computational consequences.
key_works: Alon et al. (2015), *The majority of transcripts in the squid nervous system are extensively recoded by A-to-I RNA editing*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.05198`.

title: Minimal circuits for flexible behavior
open: What is the smallest neural system that can still support a given form of learning, planning, or context-sensitive action? More formally, determine minimal neural circuits for specified flexible behaviors, using explicit behavioral criteria and mechanistic models.
status: Worm-wide signal-propagation measurements, reported in Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`, offer an unusually constrained experimental system, but they do not establish general minimality bounds.
solved_when: For a specified behavioral capability, a mechanistic circuit model is shown to achieve it, with a proof that no smaller circuit (under the stated criteria and model class) suffices — establishing general minimality bounds rather than single-system measurements.
why: It identifies which computational capabilities require which circuit resources, linking flexible behavior to concrete neural architecture.
key_works: Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Variant-to-functional-phenotype chains
open: For a defined neurodevelopmental variant, can we establish the full sequence from molecular change through developmental circuit alteration to a specific functional phenotype? That is, can we trace a causal chain from a genetic variant to the mechanism producing a particular impairment?
status: Large autism exome studies, notably Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`, identify developmental and functional gene contributions; however, association alone does not establish the full mechanism.
solved_when: A specific neurodevelopmental variant is traced through its molecular change, the resulting developmental circuit alteration, and a demonstrated link to a specific functional phenotype — a complete mechanistic chain rather than a statistical association.
why: It enables targeted help for particular impairments instead of treating heterogeneous diagnoses as if they had a single mechanism.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Variable penetrance of neurodevelopmental variants
open: Why do individuals carrying similar neurodevelopmental risk variants go on to have such different developmental outcomes? A satisfying account would integrate genetic background, mosaicism, environmental factors, and compensatory mechanisms into a predictive model of penetrance.
status: Large-scale exome sequencing studies establish risk associations across many genes, as in Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`, and single-neuron sequencing documents somatic mutation during brain development, as in Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`; however, these studies do not explain individual penetrance with sufficient mechanistic precision.
solved_when: A framework exists that predicts, with mechanistic precision, an individual's developmental outcome from their risk variant together with genetic background, mosaicism, environment, and compensation — going beyond population-level risk associations.
why: It would improve prognosis for carriers and their families, replacing the notion of genetic risk as destiny with a mechanistic, individualized prediction.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Lodato et al. (2015), *Somatic mutation in single human neurons tracks developmental and transcriptional history*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aab1785`.

title: Reversible versus developmentally fixed consequences
open: Which consequences of an early developmental perturbation can still be reversed later in life, and which are permanently fixed unless the underlying circuit structure itself is rebuilt — and how does the answer change with life stage?
status: Critical-period reopening in mice demonstrates one route to renewed plasticity; it does not establish reversibility of arbitrary developmental conditions. Key works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`; Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.
solved_when: There is an experimental account, for each life stage, of which consequences of a developmental perturbation remain reversible and which require rebuilding circuit structure.
why: It defines which intervention targets are realistic and when they must be applied, separating what pharmacology or plasticity-based approaches can fix from what would require circuit reconstruction.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`; Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`.

title: Mechanistic subgroups within developmental diagnoses
open: Can clinically shared developmental diagnoses be decomposed into reproducible subgroups that are defined by underlying causal mechanisms and support needs, rather than treating everyone with the same label as having the same circuit abnormality?
status: Genetic heterogeneity and the large samples needed for reliable brain-wide associations make simple one-signature accounts inadequate as a research endpoint. Key works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.
solved_when: Subgroups defined by causal mechanism and support needs are identified reproducibly, providing a validated alternative to single-signature accounts as a research endpoint.
why: It enables more relevant trials and individualized support.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Validity of human developmental disease models
open: Which phenotypes observed in organoids or transplanted cells genuinely predict patient-relevant developmental outcomes, and which are artifacts of culture conditions or missing cellular interactions?
status: Organoids have been shown to model aspects of microcephaly (Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`), and transplanted organoids can mature and integrate (Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`), but neither achievement certifies general clinical validity.
solved_when: A validated mapping exists between specific organoid or transplanted-cell phenotypes and patient-relevant developmental outcomes, distinguishing predictive phenotypes from those driven by culture conditions or absent interactions.
why: It would make model selection and drug screening evidence-based rather than heuristic.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Mechanistic psychiatric dimensions
open: Can we identify neural and physiological dimensions that explain psychiatric symptoms, functional impairment, and intervention responses more reliably than diagnostic labels alone? Formally, the goal is a mechanistic characterization of such dimensions that outperforms existing diagnostic categories in predictive and explanatory power.
status: Personalized depression stimulation and large-scale association studies provide complementary evidence, but neither establishes a universal mechanistic taxonomy. Key works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.
solved_when: A set of neural and physiological dimensions is identified and shown to predict symptoms, functional impairment, and intervention responses more reliably than diagnostic labels alone, across patients rather than in isolated cases.
why: It would make treatment development less dependent on heterogeneous diagnostic categories, allowing interventions to target mechanisms rather than labels.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Prospective antidepressant-treatment selection
open: Can we predict, before a patient begins a prolonged trial-and-error process, which antidepressant treatment will actually benefit them — and can such predictions be validated in randomized treatment-selection studies?
status: A 2021 single-patient closed-loop demonstration — Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w` — established an important personalized intervention, but not a broadly validated treatment-selection rule.
solved_when: A treatment-selection rule is developed and its benefit is demonstrated prospectively in randomized treatment-selection studies.
why: It would reduce the time patients spend receiving ineffective treatment.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`.

title: Schizophrenia risk genes to circuit computation
open: How do the risk pathways implicated in schizophrenia actually change specific circuit computations such as inference, working memory, or sensory integration — and which mediating elements of those changes are reversible?
status: The 2022 genomic study by Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia* (DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`), implicates synaptic biology and many loci; it does not collapse schizophrenia into one circuit defect.
solved_when: For an identified risk pathway, its effect on a defined circuit operation (inference, working memory, or sensory integration) is causally characterized, and at least one mediator of that effect is shown to be reversible.
why: It would connect genetic discovery to mechanistically targeted treatment rather than symptom-level intervention.
key_works: Trubetskoy et al. (2022), *Mapping genomic loci implicates genes and synaptic biology in schizophrenia*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04434-5`.

title: Persistent relapse vulnerability in addiction
open: Which learned, motivational, and physiological states preserve relapse risk even after prolonged abstinence, and can they be selectively altered without broadly suppressing reward?
status: Distinct dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation provide a useful mechanistic separation, but do not establish a complete relapse model; relevant groundwork includes Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`, and Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.
solved_when: A characterization of the states maintaining relapse vulnerability is given, together with a demonstrated means of selectively changing them that leaves normal reward processing intact.
why: It targets the persistence of relapse risk itself rather than only acute drug effects, opening the way to interventions that reduce long-term vulnerability.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`; Benna and Fusi (2016), *Computational principles of synaptic memory consolidation*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4401`.

title: Therapeutic plasticity versus nonspecific drug effects
open: Which treatment-induced plasticity changes are actually necessary for durable psychiatric benefit, and how do those changes interact with subsequent experience? More precisely, can candidate plasticity mechanisms be shown to mediate lasting therapeutic outcomes rather than merely accompany drug exposure?
status: Psychedelic reopening of social-reward learning windows in mice (Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`) is a mechanistic result, not proof that the same process explains all human therapeutic effects.
solved_when: A demonstration that specific, identified plasticity changes caused by a treatment are necessary for durable psychiatric benefit, including how those changes depend on or interact with subsequent experience.
why: It would separate genuine candidate mechanisms from broad narratives about "increased plasticity," giving psychiatry mechanistic targets rather than blanket claims.
key_works: Nardou et al. (2023), *Psychedelics reopen the social reward learning critical period*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06204-3`.

title: Rate and function of adult human neurogenesis
open: How many new neurons are produced in the adult human brain, how many survive and integrate, and what do they actually do? A satisfying answer would quantify neuron production, survival, integration, and functional contribution across adult ages and conditions using convergent methods.
status: Proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus were reported in 2025 by Dumitru et al. (2025), *Identification of proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adu9575`; earlier, Eriksson et al. (1998), *Neurogenesis in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/3305`. The remaining target is not a blanket claim that adult progenitors have never been observed.
solved_when: Neuron production, survival, integration, and functional contribution are quantified across adult human ages and conditions, with convergent experimental methods reaching consistent estimates.
why: It determines the relevance of neurogenesis to aging and repair, and thus whether new-neuron biology is a viable target for interventions in aging and neurodegeneration.
key_works: Dumitru et al. (2025), *Identification of proliferating neural progenitors in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1126/science.adu9575`; Eriksson et al. (1998), *Neurogenesis in the adult human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/3305`.

title: Mechanisms of cognitive resilience
open: Why do some individuals maintain cognitive function despite substantial Alzheimer-type pathology? A satisfying account must disentangle the candidate mechanisms — compensatory circuitry, cognitive or neural reserve, cellular resistance to injury, and mere measurement differences — and attribute resilience to them.
status: Amyloid-targeting trials — e.g., van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948` — establish that modifying one pathological process can affect decline, but they do not explain individual resilience to pathology. Single-cell resources such as Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, provide the kind of data that could support distinguishing these mechanisms, though no such account yet exists.
solved_when: A mechanistic explanation is available that separately identifies the contributions of compensatory circuitry, reserve, cell resistance, and measurement differences to preserved function in the presence of substantial pathology.
why: It could reveal protective mechanisms complementary to pathology removal, pointing to interventions distinct from clearing amyloid or other pathological processes.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Amyloid reduction-to-clinical-benefit mechanism
open: What downstream changes actually convert amyloid reduction into clinical benefit in Alzheimer's disease? That is, which mechanisms mediate the effect, why the magnitude of benefit varies across patients, and which combinations of changes would be required for substantially larger functional effects than slowing of decline?
status: Lecanemab reduced decline relative to placebo in its pivotal trial (van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`), and longer follow-up has been reported (van Dyck et al. (2025), *Long-term safety and efficacy of lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s disease: Results from the clarity AD open-label extension study*, DOI: `10.1002/alz.70905`). However, slowing decline is not equivalent to restoring lost function.
solved_when: The mediating downstream changes from amyloid reduction are identified, the sources of variability in benefit are explained, and the combination of changes needed for substantially larger functional effects is specified and validated.
why: It directly guides which treatment combinations to pursue and how to select patients who will benefit.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; van Dyck et al. (2025), *Long-term safety and efficacy of lecanemab in early Alzheimer’s disease: Results from the clarity AD open-label extension study*, DOI: `10.1002/alz.70905`.

title: Restoring function after established dementia-related loss
open: Can lost cognitive function be restored in a patient who already has substantial dementia-related circuit damage? That is, can clinically meaningful memory or daily function be recovered after the damage is established, rather than only slowing further decline?
status: Disease-modifying amyloid trials establish partial slowing of decline, while cell-integration studies provide separate repair tools; neither demonstrates general restoration of lost dementia-related function. Key works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.
solved_when: A demonstration of restored, clinically meaningful memory or daily function in the setting of substantial, established circuit damage — general restoration, not merely partial slowing of progression.
why: It closes the gap between prevention of further damage and actual recovery, turning therapy from damage control into repair.
key_works: van Dyck et al. (2023), *Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer’s Disease*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2212948`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Parkinson’s mechanisms beyond dopamine replacement
open: What mechanisms — beyond loss of dopamine — drive the major nonmotor and treatment-resistant manifestations of Parkinson’s disease, and can they be treated directly? Formally, the goal is to identify and therapeutically target the circuits and cell types responsible for these manifestations, rather than assuming that restoration of dopaminergic signaling resolves the entire disease.
status: Dopaminergic replacement trials target one important component of the disease; their scope does not establish correction of all affected circuits or cell types. Key works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.
solved_when: The mechanisms underlying the major nonmotor and treatment-resistant manifestations are identified and shown to be treatable, with interventions addressing disability that persists despite dopamine-centered therapy.
why: It addresses the substantial disability left outside the scope of dopamine replacement, which is currently the main therapeutic lever.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: TDP-43 loss of function versus toxic gain of function
open: Which mechanism of TDP-43 pathology actually drives disease: is it the loss of nuclear function, the disruption of RNA processing, the toxic gain from cytoplasmic aggregates, or the downstream stress they induce? The question is to quantify the relative causal contributions of each of these processes to ALS and frontotemporal degeneration.
status: Pathological TDP-43 was identified in these diseases in 2006 by Neumann et al. (2006), *Ubiquitinated TDP-43 in frontotemporal lobar degeneration and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1134108`; identifying the protein did not settle which consequences are causally dominant.
solved_when: A quantitative account assigns the relative contributions of nuclear depletion, altered RNA processing, cytoplasmic assemblies, and downstream stress to disease pathogenesis in ALS and frontotemporal degeneration.
why: The answer determines whether therapy should aim to restore lost function, clear cytoplasmic assemblies, or do both.
key_works: Neumann et al. (2006), *Ubiquitinated TDP-43 in frontotemporal lobar degeneration and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1134108`.

title: Biomarker improvement-to-functional benefit in ALS
open: When does a measurable change in a molecular biomarker after an ALS therapy translate into meaningful motor or survival benefit for patients, and at what disease stage should interventions be given for genetically defined ALS? A formal answer would specify the conditions and timing under which biomarker engagement serves as a valid predictor of clinical outcome.
status: The 2022 tofersen trial separated biomarker effects from its primary short-term clinical endpoint; subsequent long-term work underscores the need for timing-sensitive interpretation (Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705`; Miller et al. (2026), *Long-Term Tofersen in SOD1 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis*, bibliographic identifier to be verified).
solved_when: A validated relationship is established between biomarker improvement and functional (motor and survival) benefit, including the optimal intervention timing for genetically defined ALS subtypes.
why: It improves trial design and prevents the field from equating molecular target engagement with clinical recovery, which could otherwise advance therapies that change biomarkers without helping patients.
key_works: Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705`; Miller et al. (2026), *Long-Term Tofersen in SOD1 Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis* (verify bibliographic identifier).

title: Selective neuronal vulnerability
open: Why do specific neuronal populations die in a proteinopathy while neighboring cells exposed to the same pathology survive? A satisfactory account would identify the cell-intrinsic and contextual variables that jointly predict which populations succumb.
status: Molecular cell atlases and disease-protein structures each provide candidate explanatory variables, but neither alone predicts selective death. Key works include Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.
solved_when: A framework — molecular, structural, or combined — that predicts which neuronal populations will selectively degenerate in a given proteinopathy, validated against known patterns of selective vulnerability.
why: It could reveal protection mechanisms shared across degenerative diseases, turning descriptive atlas data into predictive understanding of neuronal death.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Fitzpatrick et al. (2017), *Cryo-EM structures of tau filaments from Alzheimer’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/nature23002`.

title: Reliable individual seizure forecasting
open: Can we forecast an individual patient's seizure risk with calibrated probabilities over horizons long enough to guide daily decisions, remaining reliable as medication, sleep, and disease states change over time?
status: Development and validation studies demonstrate forecasting potential, but reliable long-term individual calibration and actionable warning policies remain separate targets. Key work: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`.
solved_when: A forecasting method is validated to deliver individually calibrated probabilities over clinically useful horizons that persist across changing medication, sleep, and disease states, together with actionable warning policies.
why: It enables risk-aware daily planning and preventive intervention for people with epilepsy.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`.

title: Mechanisms that create an epileptic circuit
open: Which changes after injury or genetic perturbation are necessary for epileptogenesis, and can they be identified and interrupted before recurrent seizures become established? Formally, the goal is to determine which post-insult or genetically driven alterations are causally required for the transition into an epileptic circuit, so that this transition can be prevented.
status: Seizure-risk forecasting describes susceptibility dynamics but does not establish the causal developmental transition into epilepsy, as in Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`; degeneracy of circuit parameters (Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`) complicates attributing the transition to any single parameter change.
solved_when: The necessary causal changes for epileptogenesis are identified and shown to be interruptable before recurrent seizures become established.
why: It distinguishes disease prevention from merely suppressing individual seizures.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`; Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`.

title: Minimal interventions that terminate seizures
open: What is the smallest perturbation — in both space and time — that can terminate a seizure while leaving normal brain function intact? More formally, characterize the minimal spatial extent and temporal duration of an intervention required to abort different seizure types without disrupting healthy dynamics.
status: Current tools improve observation but not control: risk forecasting in adults with focal epilepsy has been developed and validated (Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`), and miniaturized high-density probes enable stable, long-term neural recordings (Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`). A general, patient-specific control law for seizure termination remains open.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the spatially and temporally minimal perturbations that terminate each seizure type while preserving normal function, valid across seizure types rather than a single case.
why: A solution directly reduces the stimulation burden placed on patients and limits unintended effects of intervention, making closed-loop seizure control clinically practical.
key_works: Proix et al. (2021), *Forecasting seizure risk in adults with focal epilepsy: a development and validation study*, DOI: `10.1016/S1474-4422(20)30396-3`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Migraine attack initiation
open: What is the causal sequence that actually initiates a migraine attack in a given individual, and how can the true initiating processes be distinguished from downstream symptoms and amplifying pathways?
status: CGRP-pathway prevention has demonstrated clinical efficacy (Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`); however, efficacy of a downstream intervention does not by itself identify the universal initiating event.
solved_when: The causal sequence of attack initiation is identified for a particular person, with initiating processes demonstrably separated from symptoms and amplifying pathways.
why: A solution would enable prevention that acts earlier in the attack-generating process, before symptoms and amplification take hold.
key_works: Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`.

title: Mechanism-based migraine treatment selection
open: Can validated mechanistic biomarkers predict, for a given individual with migraine, both the response and the adverse effects they will experience across different classes of preventive treatment? Formally, the goal is an experimentally validated individualized treatment-selection rule that generalizes across preventive treatment classes.
status: Controlled trials of erenumab, namely Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`, establish group-level benefit but not a complete individualized treatment-selection rule.
solved_when: A prospective demonstration that mechanistic biomarkers predict individual-level response and adverse effects across preventive treatment classes, yielding a validated individualized treatment-selection rule.
why: It would spare patients the burden of repeated unsuccessful treatment trials by matching them to an effective preventive therapy up front.
key_works: Goadsby et al. (2017), *A Controlled Trial of Erenumab for Episodic Migraine*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1705848`.

title: Long-distance CNS axon regeneration with correct targets
open: Can severed axons in the adult central nervous system be induced to regrow over clinically relevant distances, reconnect with their appropriate targets, and restore useful, stable function? In formal terms, the goal is regeneration that achieves correct target selection and functional integration without maladaptive sprouting.
status: Manipulating PTEN/mTOR promoted adult CNS axon regeneration in 2008 (Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`), but growth promotion alone does not solve target selection and integration.
solved_when: Injured central axons are regenerated over clinically relevant distances, reconnect to appropriate targets, and useful, stable function is demonstrated without maladaptive sprouting.
why: It addresses a core barrier to repairing severed central pathways, since growth promotion alone is insufficient without correct target selection and integration.
key_works: Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`.

title: Large, durable recovery in chronic stroke
open: Can a therapy produce substantial functional recovery in the chronic phase of stroke, working across heterogeneous lesion locations rather than a single deficit type, with gains that transfer to daily activities and persist over time?
status: Paired vagus-nerve stimulation and rehabilitation improved upper-limb outcomes in a 2021 controlled trial — Dawson et al. (2021), *Vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation for upper limb motor function after ischaemic stroke (VNS-REHAB): a randomised, blinded, pivotal, device trial*, DOI: `10.1016/S0140-6736(21)00475-X` — but that does not establish broad restoration across stroke deficits.
solved_when: A demonstrated intervention achieves substantial functional recovery in chronic stroke patients across heterogeneous lesion locations, with verified transfer to daily activities and sustained, durable benefit.
why: It addresses the disability that remains after spontaneous recovery has slowed, which is when most patients are left with permanent deficits and few effective options.
key_works: Dawson et al. (2021), *Vagus nerve stimulation paired with rehabilitation for upper limb motor function after ischaemic stroke (VNS-REHAB): a randomised, blinded, pivotal, device trial*, DOI: `10.1016/S0140-6736(21)00475-X`.

title: Mechanistic prognosis after diffuse brain injury
open: Can we predict recovery after diffuse brain injury from measurements that separate what is truly damaged, what is reversibly dysfunctional, what retains preserved awareness, and what can be compensated by remaining pathways?
status: Multicenter detection of cognitive motor dissociation shows that behavioral unresponsiveness can conceal preserved processing, complicating simple prognostic labels; see Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`.
solved_when: A prognostic method exists that distinguishes damaged pathways, reversible dysfunction, preserved awareness, and compensatory capacity in distributed injury, and uses these separable components to predict recovery better than behavioral unresponsiveness labels alone.
why: It improves allocation of rehabilitation resources and reduces premature prognostic certainty, which currently risks writing off patients whose behavioral unresponsiveness conceals preserved processing.
key_works: Bodien et al. (2024), *Cognitive Motor Dissociation in Disorders of Consciousness*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2400645`.

title: Repair without losing protective injury responses
open: Can we design interventions that let damaged neural tissue regenerate without dismantling the protective responses — wound containment, immune defense, and tissue stability — that injury normally triggers? In formal terms, the goal is an intervention that simultaneously achieves functional regeneration and preserves the necessary components of the injury response.
status: Growth-promoting manipulations and protective microglial effects illustrate the field's different, competing requirements; maximizing growth alone is not a complete repair strategy. Key works: Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`; Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.
solved_when: An intervention is identified that demonstrably permits regeneration while preserving necessary wound containment, immune defense, and tissue stability.
why: It avoids exchanging one form of damage for another — a therapy that promotes growth at the cost of protective injury responses would leave tissue vulnerable in new ways.
key_works: Park et al. (2008), *Promoting axon regeneration in the adult CNS by modulation of the PTEN/mTOR pathway*, DOI: `10.1126/science.1161566`; Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.

title: Selective disruption of neuron–glioma communication
open: Can we interrupt the neural interactions that support glioma growth without broadly impairing normal synaptic transmission, and thereby improve clinical outcomes?
status: Glioma integration into neural circuits was demonstrated in 2019, notably by Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`, and Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`; however, identifying tumor-associated synapses is not yet equivalent to a selective effective therapy.
solved_when: A selective intervention that disrupts tumor-supporting neuron–glioma communication while sparing normal synaptic transmission is demonstrated, with improved clinical outcomes.
why: It targets a tumor-support mechanism distinct from autonomous cancer-cell growth, opening a therapeutic axis that standard oncology approaches do not address.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`; Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`.

title: Tumor-induced circuit remodeling
open: How do brain tumors reshape the computation performed by the neural circuits around them, and which of those changes drive seizures, cognitive deficits, or further tumor growth? A satisfactory answer would identify the causal circuit alterations linking tumor presence to each clinical consequence.
status: Neuron–glioma electrical integration supplies a mechanism for bidirectional interaction, but not a complete model of surrounding circuit dysfunction; see Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`.
solved_when: A mechanistic account exists that identifies which tumor-induced circuit changes cause seizures, cognitive deficits, and tumor growth, supported by experimental evidence distinguishing causal from correlational changes.
why: It connects tumor biology to neurological symptoms, and would let treatment priorities be set by which circuit changes actually drive harm rather than by symptoms alone.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`.

title: Clearing neural infection without immune-mediated injury
open: Can we design treatment schedules for brain infections that clear the pathogen without triggering destructive inflammation or disabling the immune responses the brain needs? Formally, which dosing or intervention schedules jointly control pathogen load while preserving necessary immune function?
status: Microglial protection in experimental coronavirus encephalitis shows that indiscriminately suppressing brain immunity can remove a beneficial mechanism: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.
solved_when: A treatment schedule is identified that controls the pathogen while preventing destructive inflammation and preserving necessary immune functions.
why: It balances infection control against preservation of neural tissue, so patients can clear infection without the immune response itself injuring the brain.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`.

title: Persistent dysfunction after pathogen clearance
open: Do patients who remain unwell after an infection has cleared carry residual pathogen, altered immune memory, vascular damage, synaptic loss, or some other lasting change? Identifying which mechanism dominates in defined patient groups would turn a descriptive syndrome into an explainable disease process.
status: Acute neuroinfection studies establish protective immune responses — e.g., Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229` — while EBV–MS evidence establishes a long-latency disease connection (Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`); neither supplies a universal postinfectious mechanism.
solved_when: A mechanistic account of persistent postinfectious dysfunction is demonstrated in defined patient groups, distinguishing among residual pathogen, immune memory, vascular damage, and synaptic loss (or establishing another mechanism).
why: It prevents heterogeneous postinfectious states from being treated as one process, which currently blocks both diagnosis and targeted therapy.
key_works: Wheeler et al. (2018), *Microglia are required for protection against lethal coronavirus encephalitis in mice*, DOI: `10.1172/JCI97229`; Bjornevik et al. (2022), *Longitudinal analysis reveals high prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus associated with multiple sclerosis*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abj8222`.

title: Longitudinal tumor–neuron interaction atlas
open: Can we build a longitudinal atlas that tracks, in the same patients over time, how tumor genotype, cell state, neural connectivity, and electrical activity evolve alongside treatment and clinical outcomes?
status: The 2019 neuron–glioma studies established the relevant tumor–neuron interactions: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`; Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`. A standardized longitudinal intervention-linked atlas remains a further data target.
solved_when: A standardized longitudinal atlas exists that matches tumor genotype, cell state, neural connectivity, electrical activity, treatment, and clinical outcome measurements within subjects over time.
why: Such an atlas would enable prediction of tumor–circuit evolution and treatment escape.
key_works: Venkatesh et al. (2019), *Electrical and synaptic integration of glioma into neural circuits*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1563-y`; Venkataramani et al. (2019), *Glutamatergic synaptic input to glioma cells drives brain tumour progression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1564-x`.

title: Perfused neural tissue with realistic support cells
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Can we engineer neural tissue that is reproducibly perfused and supported by realistic auxiliary systems — barriers, immune components, and glia — at a scale sufficient to sustain complex physiology over time? Formally, this is the challenge of integrating all supporting compartments into a single construct that functions reliably rather than partially.
status: Cerebral organoids and transplanted organoids provide partial systems, as in Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`, and Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`; however, combining all supporting compartments reproducibly remains a distinct engineering problem. Related efforts span biofabrication of vascularized tissue and microfluidic approaches to physiological perfusion.
solved_when: A reproducibly built neural tissue construct combines functional perfusion, barrier properties, immune components, and glial support at scales sufficient for sustained complex physiology.
why: It removes the artifacts caused by missing supply and support systems, making engineered neural tissue a faithful substrate for physiology and, ultimately, for cell-replacement applications.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Reproducible organoid assembly across laboratories
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Can we specify how an organoid must be manufactured and tested so that any batch, from any donor, in any laboratory, meets predictable standards of cellular composition, connectivity, and function?
status: Foundational organoid work, including Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`, establishes useful models, but model availability is not equivalent to interchangeability or standardized functional quality. Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`, documents how analyst variability undermines cross-team reproducibility.
solved_when: A set of manufacturing and acceptance criteria exists that demonstrably predicts organoid composition, connectivity, and function across batches, donors, and laboratories.
why: Without such criteria, organoid experiments cannot be meaningfully compared or replicated; with them, drug screening and replication studies become interpretable.
key_works: Lancaster et al. (2013), *Cerebral organoids model human brain development and microcephaly*, DOI: `10.1038/nature12517`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Target-specific integration of grafted neurons
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: Can grafted neurons be made to integrate into a host brain in a target-specific way — receiving appropriate inputs, projecting to their intended targets, and improving the desired function — without producing pathological activity? Formally, the goal is to direct the connectivity of transplanted cells so that integration is not merely structural but functionally appropriate and safe.
status: Transplanted human cortical organoids can integrate with host circuits, but integration itself does not guarantee task-appropriate connectivity or clinical benefit. Key works: Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`; Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson's disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.
solved_when: A transplantation approach is demonstrated in which grafted neurons receive appropriate inputs, project to intended targets, improve the desired function, and show no pathological activity.
why: It would turn cell replacement from a cell-survival strategy into a genuine circuit-repair strategy.
key_works: Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`; Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`.

title: Long-term safety assurance for neural grafts
subfield: Organoids, engineered tissue, and cell replacement
open: How can we assure, over the long term, that a neural graft contains no dangerous residual cell states and remains safe after implantation? Formally, this asks for sensitive and scalable methods to exclude residual hazardous cell populations and to detect later overgrowth, migration, immune incompatibility, or dysfunctional integration.
status: Early clinical cell-replacement trials — Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y` — establish a path to testing, but long-term safety requires evidence beyond initial tolerability. Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.
solved_when: Scalable, sensitive assays exist that both exclude dangerous residual cell states prior to transplantation and detect overgrowth, migration, immune incompatibility, or dysfunctional integration over the long term after implantation.
why: It is what lets neural grafts move from small trials to dependable treatment; without it, early tolerability cannot be assumed to predict long-term safety.
key_works: Tabar et al. (2025), *Phase I trial of hES cell-derived dopaminergic neurons for Parkinson’s disease*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08845-y`; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.

title: Years-long identity of individual recorded neurons
open: Can we track the same individual neurons across years of recording with explicit, quantified confidence that each tracked unit is truly the same cell? A full solution must further disentangle genuine biological change in a neuron's properties from apparent change caused by probe motion and recording instability.
status: Neuropixels 2.0 demonstrated substantially improved stable long-term recordings (Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`), but that milestone is not equivalent to years-long verified identity in arbitrary conditions.
solved_when: A recording system can maintain verified identity of individual neurons over multi-year timescales, with identity confidence stated explicitly, while separating true biological change from probe motion and recording instability — and this holds in arbitrary recording conditions, not just favorable ones.
why: It unlocks rigorous longitudinal studies of learning, aging, and disease progression at the level of single identified neurons.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Tenfold lower photon burden for voltage imaging
open: Can we cut the light needed for accurate voltage imaging by an order of magnitude? Formally: reduce the required illumination per accurately detected voltage event by at least tenfold against a specified baseline while maintaining temporal resolution, coverage, and biological safety.
status: This is a proposed moonshot. Chemigenetic voltage indicators such as Voltron improved brightness and photostability (Abdelfattah et al. (2019), *Bright and photostable chemigenetic indicators for extended in vivo voltage imaging*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav6416`), but the tenfold target must be assessed with end-to-end detection and toxicity measurements.
solved_when: An approach achieves at least a tenfold reduction in illumination per accurately detected voltage event relative to the specified baseline, with temporal resolution, coverage, and biological safety preserved, verified through end-to-end detection and toxicity measurements.
why: A solution extends the duration of voltage recordings and opens access to fragile tissue that current illumination levels would damage.
key_works: Abdelfattah et al. (2019), *Bright and photostable chemigenetic indicators for extended in vivo voltage imaging*, DOI: `10.1126/science.aav6416`.

title: Multiplexed fast chemical signaling measurements
open: Can we build a measurement device that reads out many chemical signals of the brain at once — transmitters, peptides, ions, and metabolic variables — with enough spatial and temporal resolution to be scientifically useful? The core difficulty is doing this without substantial cross-talk between channels or buffering artifacts that distort the very signals being measured.
status: Local dopamine measurements illustrate why electrical activity alone is insufficient — Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y` — and Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`, points to metabolic variables as behaviorally consequential. A comprehensive multiplexed chemical readout remains a broader open instrumentation target.
solved_when: A single instrumentation approach simultaneously measures multiple transmitters, peptides, ions, and metabolic variables at useful spatial and temporal resolution, without substantial cross-talk or buffering artifacts.
why: It would make neuromodulatory and metabolic circuit states directly observable, which electrical recordings alone cannot capture.
key_works: Mohebi et al. (2019), *Dissociable dopamine dynamics for learning and motivation*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-019-1235-y`; Suzuki et al. (2011), *Astrocyte-neuron lactate transport is required for long-term memory formation*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2011.02.018`.

title: Reversible cell-type-specific perturbation in humans
open: Can we build methods to safely and reversibly manipulate defined populations of human neural cells, with enough cell-type specificity to support causal experiments and therapy?
status: Human neuromodulation and cell atlases are each advancing — the former improving intervention, the latter improving targeting — but their combination does not yet yield arbitrary cell-type-specific control in humans. Relevant advances include Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`, and Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.
solved_when: A method exists that achieves safe, reversible control of arbitrary, defined human neural cell types with sufficient specificity to test causal hypotheses and treat dysfunction.
why: It bridges the current gap between causal circuit experiments in animals and actual treatment of human neurological dysfunction.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Cellular interpretation of human hemodynamic imaging
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Which cellular activities gave rise to a measured hemodynamic signal, and can the answer carry uncertainty that accounts for vascular and metabolic variation across physiological states?
status: Existing work exposes important non-neuronal determinants of the signal — neural energy budgets (Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`) and sleep-related vascular mechanisms, specifically norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion driving glymphatic clearance during sleep (Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`) — but the inverse mapping from hemodynamic signal to cellular activity remains unsolved.
solved_when: A cellular-level interpretation of a hemodynamic measurement is available under different physiological states, with uncertainty quantification that includes vascular and metabolic variation.
why: Without it, indirect hemodynamic measurements invite overprecise claims about neural activity; with it, such imaging becomes a trustworthy window onto cellular processes.
key_works: Attwell and Laughlin (2001), *An energy budget for signaling in the grey matter of the brain*, DOI: `10.1097/00004647-200110000-00001`; Hauglund et al. (2025), *Norepinephrine-mediated slow vasomotion drives glymphatic clearance during sleep*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2024.11.027`.

title: Identifiability limits of EEG and MEG sources
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Which configurations of neural sources can actually be told apart from EEG and MEG recordings, given realistic sensors, anatomical uncertainty, and noise — and which additional measurements would resolve the remaining ambiguities? Formally, the task is to characterize the identifiability limits of the electromagnetic inverse problem and to determine what added data break its inherent degeneracies.
status: Wearable MEG has improved measurement access (Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`), but sensor innovation does not eliminate the underlying inverse problem.
solved_when: A characterization is given of which source configurations are distinguishable (and which are provably ambiguous) under practical sensor layouts, anatomy, and noise, together with an account of which added measurements remove the ambiguities.
why: It determines what spatial and mechanistic claims about brain sources can be made defensibly from noninvasive recordings, rather than over-reading an ill-posed inverse.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`.

title: Tenfold cheaper practical MEG
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Can magnetoencephalography be made an order of magnitude cheaper in fully loaded cost while remaining genuinely useful in practice — that is, preserving sensitivity, localization performance, movement tolerance, and operational reliability measured against preregistered benchmarks?
status: Proposed moonshot with no solution yet. Wearable optically pumped magnetometer systems established an alternative measurement architecture in 2018 (Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`); the total-cost and deployment targets still require separate verification.
solved_when: A practical MEG system achieves at least a tenfold reduction in fully loaded acquisition cost while maintaining preregistered sensitivity, localization performance, movement tolerance, and operational reliability.
why: MEG access is currently confined to a small number of specialized facilities; cutting total ownership cost tenfold would bring the modality to far broader clinical and research use.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`.

title: Same-subject multiscale brain measurements
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Can we acquire molecular, cellular, circuit, whole-brain, and behavioral measurements from the very same individuals, aligned across scales with registration uncertainty made explicit? Formally, this asks for a data resource in which cross-scale correspondences are established within single subjects and each alignment carries a quantified uncertainty.
status: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`, combines important functional and structural scales, while human atlases such as Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, provide molecular breadth; comprehensive same-subject integration remains a larger target.
solved_when: A dataset exists that combines molecular, cellular, circuit, whole-brain, and behavioral measurements from the same individuals, with explicit registration uncertainty propagated across the cross-scale alignments.
why: Without same-subject data, cross-scale explanations of brain function rest entirely on comparisons across unmatched populations; solving this makes those explanations testable within individuals.
key_works: MICrONS Consortium (2025), *Functional connectomics spanning multiple areas of mouse visual cortex*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-08790-w`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Physical limits of noninvasive cellular-resolution recording
subfield: MRI, MEG, EEG, and multiscale imaging
open: Can deep human neural activity be recorded at cellular resolution through fully noninvasive means, or do physics-imposed constraints rule it out? The goal is to establish modality-specific lower bounds — on resolution, depth, bandwidth, heating, and signal-to-noise — for any candidate noninvasive recording technology.
status: Wearable magnetic sensing (Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`) and invasive high-density probes (Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`) represent different tradeoffs; neither establishes the ultimate feasible noninvasive frontier.
solved_when: Rigorous lower bounds are derived for each modality (e.g., MRI, MEG, EEG) that quantify the best achievable resolution, depth, bandwidth, heating, and signal-to-noise tradeoffs, together showing which cellular-resolution targets are physically attainable and which are not.
why: It separates plausible moonshots from targets blocked by specified physical constraints, telling the field where noninvasive recording investment can pay off.
key_works: Boto et al. (2018), *Moving magnetoencephalography towards real-world applications with a wearable system*, DOI: `10.1038/nature26147`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Decade-scale stable neural interfaces
