open: Can an implanted neural interface keep delivering useful bidirectional performance over a full decade of service? Formally, the goal is a system that sustains such performance with manageable maintenance, no unacceptable tissue damage, and graceful recovery from component failure.
status: Long-term recording advances and successful speech interfaces establish important components — e.g., Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`, and Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132` — but decade-scale dependable service remains a separate systems target.
solved_when: A bidirectional neural interface demonstrates a decade of useful performance with manageable maintenance, no unacceptable tissue damage, and graceful recovery from component failure.
why: A solution turns implants from short research demonstrations into practical lifelong tools.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Cross-user and cross-language neural decoding
open: Can a speech neuroprosthesis decoder be built that transfers across users, languages, and recording configurations, and adapts to changing impairments, with minimal safe calibration for each new person? Formally, the goal is general decoders whose per-user adaptation requires only a short calibration burden while remaining robust to shifts in language, recording setup, and the user's condition over time.
status: High-performance and rapidly calibrating speech interfaces demonstrate major progress toward this goal, but general transfer with validated failure detection remains a broader open requirement. Key works include Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`, and Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.
solved_when: A decoder demonstrates transfer across users, languages, recording configurations, and changing impairments while achieving minimal safe calibration, with validated failure detection for cases where transfer does not hold.
why: It reduces the setup burden that currently limits clinical deployment and expands access to users beyond those willing or able to undergo lengthy calibration.
key_works: Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Naturalistic continuous speech restoration
open: Can a speech neuroprosthesis support real, unrestricted conversation — with low latency, natural turn-taking, prosody, self-initiated corrections, and reliable silence detection — under user control rather than a laboratory script? Formally, the goal is a continuous, closed-loop system whose decoded output behaves like natural dialogue in everyday settings.
status: Speech neuroprostheses and 2025 streaming brain-to-voice work establish substantial components of the problem; dependable unrestricted everyday conversation remains a systems-level target. Key works include Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`, and Littlejohn et al. (2025), *A streaming brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis to restore naturalistic communication*, PMID: `40164740`.
solved_when: The system restores low-latency conversational speech outside laboratory scripts, with reliable turn-taking, prosody, corrections, silence detection, and user control, as evaluated in actual communication rather than isolated decoding scores.
why: It measures success in actual communication rather than isolated decoding scores, which is what ultimately matters for people with speech impairment.
key_works: Willett et al. (2023), *A high-performance speech neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06377-x`; Littlejohn et al. (2025), *A streaming brain-to-voice neuroprosthesis to restore naturalistic communication*, PMID: `40164740`.

title: Biomimetic sensory feedback for prostheses
open: Can a prosthetic limb deliver touch, position, and force feedback that a user experiences as natural and interpretable, enabling dexterous control without excessive training or interference?
status: Work on PIEZO2 has clarified the requirements of natural mechanosensation, and brain–spine interfaces have demonstrated restorative motor control; however, replacing the corresponding rich sensory feedback remains a distinct, unsolved problem. Key works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.
solved_when: A prosthesis provides useful touch, position, and force feedback that demonstrably supports dexterous control and feels interpretable to the user, without requiring excessive training or causing interference.
why: It closes the loop between intended action and sensed outcome, which is what makes dexterous control possible.
key_works: Chesler et al. (2016), *The Role of PIEZO2 in Human Mechanosensation*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa1602812`; Lorach et al. (2023), *Walking naturally after spinal cord injury using a brain–spine interface*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06094-5`.

title: Distinguishing intended communication from private thought
open: How can a communication brain–computer interface be made to emit only what the user genuinely intends to say, while reliably suppressing accidental activations and letting the user transparently inspect and correct its output?
status: Speech-decoding successes, such as Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`, have made intention gating an important independent acceptance criterion, since accuracy on instructed attempts does not establish privacy during unrestricted use; the issue is also flagged by UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.
solved_when: A communication BCI demonstrates robust intention gating — accidental activations are suppressed during unrestricted use, and users can transparently confirm and correct intended output — rather than merely showing accuracy on instructed attempts.
why: It preserves agency and trust in assistive communication: users must be able to rely on the device never voicing thoughts they did not authorize.
key_works: Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Focal noninvasive stimulation of deep targets
open: Can a prescribed deep neural target be stimulated noninvasively while sparing the intervening and neighboring tissue, with target engagement verified independently of the stimulation itself?
status: Temporal interference was introduced experimentally in Grossman et al. (2017), *Noninvasive Deep Brain Stimulation via Temporally Interfering Electric Fields*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.05.024`, and investigated in the human hippocampus in Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`; general focality and the underlying mechanism remain active questions.
solved_when: A specified deep target is stimulated noninvasively with independently verified engagement, and off-target effects on intervening and neighboring tissue are minimized below a stated focality criterion.
why: It could reduce the need for invasive access, enabling deep-brain-therapy-grade interventions without implanted electrodes.
key_works: Grossman et al. (2017), *Noninvasive Deep Brain Stimulation via Temporally Interfering Electric Fields*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2017.05.024`; Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`.

title: Patient-specific stimulation response models
open: Can we predict, for an individual patient, how stimulation parameters will reshape their circuit dynamics and symptoms over time — including adaptation, side effects, and a changing disease state? More formally, this asks for a predictive model of a patient's stimulation-response mapping that remains valid as the brain and the disorder evolve.
status: Personalized closed-loop depression treatment has demonstrated that a useful individual approach is possible — Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w` — but generalizable identification of patient-specific response models remains unresolved. Related work includes Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`; the problem connects to system identification of individual response models and adaptive control.
solved_when: A model exists that predicts a given patient's circuit and symptomatic response to stimulation parameters, including adaptation, side effects, and disease-state changes, well enough to replace empirical parameter search with predictive control.
why: It would replace the repeated trial-and-error parameter search that dominates therapeutic neuromodulation with genuinely predictive control of an individual's symptoms.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Violante et al. (2023), *Non-invasive temporal interference electrical stimulation of the human hippocampus*, DOI: `10.1038/s41593-023-01456-8`.

title: Selective delivery to distributed neural cell populations
open: Deliver molecular therapies to the intended neural cell populations across clinically relevant tissue volumes while minimizing off-target expression and immune toxicity.
status: Human cell atlases improve target definition and antisense trials establish molecular intervention potential — see Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, and Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705` — but precise broad delivery remains a separate bottleneck.
solved_when: A delivery method reliably reaches the intended neural cell populations across clinically relevant tissue volumes with off-target expression and immune toxicity held to a minimum.
why: It determines whether molecularly precise therapies can actually reach their targets; without broad, selective delivery, the precision offered by molecular therapeutics cannot translate into clinical effect.
key_works: Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`; Miller et al. (2022), *Trial of Antisense Oligonucleotide Tofersen for SOD1 ALS*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2204705`.

title: Artifact-free simultaneous neural reading and writing
open: Can we measure neural responses during active stimulation with error bounds tight enough to tell genuine biological signals apart from electrical, optical, and computational artifacts? Formally, this asks for a recording-and-analysis pipeline that quantifies, rather than merely acknowledges, the artifact contribution to simultaneously acquired neural measurements.
status: Closed-loop treatment (Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`) and high-density recording (Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`) demonstrate the key components separately, but the fidelity of simultaneous measurement remains an independent validation requirement that has not been met.
solved_when: Neural responses relevant to the targeted application can be measured during stimulation with explicit error bounds that separate biological effects from electrical, optical, and computational artifacts, validated independently of the components being demonstrated.
why: Without such bounds, closed-loop control systems risk reacting to their own stimulation artifacts rather than the brain's actual response, corrupting therapy; with them, simultaneous reading and writing becomes trustworthy for closed-loop treatment.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`.

title: Safe autonomous home neuromodulation
open: Can a therapeutic closed-loop neuromodulation system be operated safely and effectively by a patient at home, without continuous clinical supervision? Formally, the system must maintain bounded stimulation, detect and correct sensor or model drift over time, recover from failures, and preserve patient override, all while demonstrating clinical benefit.
status: Individual closed-loop demonstrations, such as Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`, establish feasibility, but universal unattended reliability and long-term serviceability remain undemonstrated; ethical framing is provided by UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.
solved_when: An autonomous closed-loop neuromodulation system has been operated in patients' homes with bounded stimulation, drift detection, recoverable failures, patient override, and demonstrated clinical benefit.
why: It would convert laboratory neurotechnology into accessible ongoing care rather than clinic-bound demonstrations.
key_works: Scangos et al. (2021), *Closed-loop neuromodulation in an individual with treatment-resistant depression*, DOI: `10.1038/s41591-021-01480-w`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Minimum interventions for circuit identification
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: How few interventions — and how diverse must they be — to uniquely pin down a circuit's causal dynamics when some inputs are hidden, observation is partial, and measurements are noisy? Formally, what is the minimum number and diversity of interventions required for identification of the circuit's causal structure under these constraints?
status: Nonuniqueness is a demonstrated obstacle: circuit degeneracy shows that vastly different circuit parameters can produce indistinguishable activity, so activity alone cannot identify a circuit (Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`). On the positive side, worm-wide perturbation maps illustrate what richer interventions can reveal about circuit dynamics (Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`).
solved_when: A characterization exists of the minimum number and diversity of interventions that suffice to identify a circuit's causal dynamics in the presence of hidden inputs, partial observation, and measurement noise, together with matching lower bounds showing no smaller or less diverse intervention set can succeed.
why: It would let experimenters plan causal perturbation experiments that are maximally efficient, and make the conclusions drawn from such experiments defensible rather than confounded by nonuniqueness.
key_works: Prinz, Bucher, and Marder (2004), *Similar network activity from disparate circuit parameters*, DOI: `10.1038/nn1352`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Interpreting perturbations that change many variables
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: When does perturbing a neural network reveal the natural role of the perturbed component, rather than merely pushing the network into an unnatural state, triggering a compensatory response, or producing off-target effects? More formally, under what conditions does an intervention identify the causal role a unit plays in normal computation?
status: Analysis on a fully known system (Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`) showed that standard neuroscience-style tools can yield incomplete explanations even when the entire system is available, so the gap is demonstrated but unresolved.
solved_when: A criterion (theoretical or operational) exists that determines, for a given perturbation, whether its observed effects reflect the target's natural role or an artifact of unnatural state, compensation, or off-target impact — validated at least on a fully known system.
why: It upgrades the inference from "perturbation changes behavior" to an actual claim about mechanism, which is what perturbation experiments in neuroscience and mechanistic interpretability are ultimately meant to deliver.
key_works: Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`.

title: Benchmarks for mechanistic understanding
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Can we construct benchmarks on which a model's claim to "understand" a neural or mechanistic system is tested by genuine prediction rather than correlation? Formally, the tests should require predicting the outcomes of unseen interventions, system failures, and recovery dynamics, not merely matching recorded activity.
status: The microprocessor study supplies a cautionary known-ground-truth example; latent-variable benchmarks assess another useful but narrower capability. Key works: Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`; Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark '21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`.
solved_when: A benchmark suite exists whose tasks demand prediction of unseen interventions, failures, and recovery, and models are evaluated on those extrapolative predictions rather than on correlation with recorded activity.
why: It gives "understanding" an operational criterion, replacing vague appeals to insight with a measurable, falsifiable standard.
key_works: Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`; Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark ’21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`.

title: Transporting causal findings across individuals and species
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: When should a causal effect measured in one organism or context be expected to hold in another, and what measurements suffice to justify transporting it?
status: Comparative atlases and multicenter standardized experiments improve comparability, but similarity of labels or average responses is not a transportability proof. Key works: Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.
solved_when: A formal criterion exists that specifies the conditions under which a causal finding transfers across individuals or species, together with an identification of the minimal measurements needed to certify that transfer.
why: It would put translation from model systems to human interventions on rigorous footing rather than relying on assumed similarity.
key_works: Krienen et al. (2023), *A marmoset brain cell census reveals regional specialization of cellular identities*, DOI: `10.1126/sciadv.adk3986`; International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`.

title: Behavioral completeness for interpreting neural activity
subfield: Causal inference and mechanistic theory evaluation
open: Which aspects of behavior — unmeasured movements, strategies, internal states, and environmental variables — must be captured before a neural explanation can be trusted? The goal is to identify the variables that materially confound interpretations of neural activity and to establish sufficient standards for behavioral measurement.
status: Brain-wide task maps reveal widespread behavioral signals, and increasingly comprehensive neural recording does not automatically compensate for incomplete behavioral observation. Key works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the behavioral variables that materially confound neural explanations, together with sufficient behavioral measurement standards that account for them.
why: Without it, neural activity gets assigned to the wrong psychological process, corrupting the interpretation of every downstream explanation.
key_works: International Brain Laboratory (2025), *A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-025-09235-0`; Jonas and Kording (2017), *Could a neuroscientist understand a microprocessor?*, DOI: `10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005268`.

title: Interoperable whole-experiment records
open: Can the full life of a neuroscience experiment — acquisition, behavioral events, interventions, calibration, anatomy, processing, and uncertainty — be captured in machine-readable records whose meaning survives transfer across laboratories?
status: Neurodata Without Borders provides a substantial ecosystem (Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`), but existing standards do not mean every experimental modality or semantic relationship is covered consistently.
solved_when: A record standard exists that interoperably represents all of the listed components (acquisition, behavioral events, interventions, calibration, anatomy, processing, uncertainty) such that meaning is preserved consistently across laboratories.
why: It makes pooled analysis across labs feasible and allows independent reconstruction of an experiment from its record.
key_works: Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`.

title: Persistent identity across neural datasets
open: How can long-term neural datasets keep a trustworthy link between the same subject, sample, cell, or recording as data are reprocessed across sessions and pipeline revisions? The goal is a practical infrastructure that maintains auditable identity links over time rather than merely assigning stable identifiers.
status: Existing long-term recording hardware and community data standards supply the components — stable, long-term brain recordings (Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`) and the Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science (Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`) — but assigning a stable identifier does not by itself eliminate identity uncertainty, and the problem remains open.
solved_when: A working system demonstrably maintains auditable identity links across subjects, samples, cells, recordings, anatomical reconstructions, and derived models through multiple sessions and processing revisions, with identity uncertainty explicitly tracked rather than assumed eliminated by the identifier.
why: Without it, longitudinal analyses can report spurious changes and multimodal analyses can join the wrong entities; with it, cross-session and cross-modal neuroscience results become reproducible and trustworthy.
key_works: Steinmetz et al. (2021), *Neuropixels 2.0: A miniaturized high-density probe for stable, long-term brain recordings*, DOI: `10.1126/science.abf4588`; Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`.

title: Intervention-generalization benchmark suite
open: Can we build benchmark suites that test whether models of neural circuits generalize to conditions they were never trained on? Concretely, this means held-out perturbations, laboratories, animals, and behavioral conditions, with calibrated predictions required of both neural and behavioral outcomes.
status: The Neural Latents Benchmark ’21 (Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark ’21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`) provides standardized evaluation of latent variable models; extending evaluation to causal intervention generalization is a distinct, unmet target, and recent work such as Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`, offers relevant causal-intervention data.
solved_when: A benchmark suite exists whose evaluations are held out across perturbations, laboratories, animals, and behavioral conditions, and on which models must deliver calibrated predictions of both neural and behavioral outcomes.
why: Such benchmarks reward models that predict mechanisms outside their training distribution, rather than models that merely interpolate within it.
key_works: Pei et al. (2021), *Neural Latents Benchmark ’21: Evaluating latent variable models of neural population activity*, arXiv: `2109.04463`; Randi et al. (2023), *Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-023-06683-4`.

title: Quantifying analysis-pipeline uncertainty
open: How can defensible variation in preprocessing, modeling, and statistical choices be propagated into the final uncertainty attached to a neuroscience claim? Formally, the task is to construct a framework that treats the space of reasonable analysis pipelines as a source of uncertainty and quantifies its effect on the reported result.
status: A 2020 many-team analysis of one imaging dataset demonstrated substantial analytical variability, showing that selecting one pipeline does not remove that source of uncertainty. Key work: Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.
solved_when: A method exists that takes a dataset and an ensemble of defensible analysis choices and yields a final uncertainty estimate for the scientific claim that incorporates pipeline-level variability, so that selecting a single pipeline no longer silently omits this uncertainty.
why: It prevents precision estimates from ignoring researcher choices, so that reported confidence in a neuroscience finding reflects not only sampling noise but also the analytic decisions behind it.
key_works: Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Usable negative-result and failed-replication datasets
open: Can we build a standardized, searchable repository of well-powered null findings, failed perturbations, and unsuccessful replications, rich enough in metadata that an informed failure can be told apart from a technical breakdown?
status: Large-sample and many-analyst studies have documented significant reliability problems in the field — notably Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`, and Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9` — but a reusable infrastructure for failure data remains only a proposed target.
solved_when: A reusable failure-data infrastructure exists that standardizes records of null findings, failed perturbations, and failed replications with sufficient metadata to distinguish informative failures from technical breakdowns, and is searchable at scale.
why: Such a resource would spare researchers from repeatedly pursuing dead ends and would counteract publication-driven distortions of the evidence base.
key_works: Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`; Botvinik-Nezer et al. (2020), *Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-020-2314-9`.

title: Sex-related mechanisms rather than average-group labels
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Can the distinct contributions of chromosomes, hormones, development, body physiology, and social environment to a specified neural mechanism be separately identified, rather than collapsed into average male–female group comparisons?
status: Hormone-associated structural changes — e.g., Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458` — demonstrate that physiological state matters, and average male–female comparisons cannot independently identify the responsible causes; reproducibility constraints on brain-wide association studies (Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`) underscore the challenge.
solved_when: An experimental design or causal-inference approach is demonstrated that independently isolates the effects of chromosomes, hormones, development, body physiology, and social environment on the named neural mechanism.
why: It produces more precise biology without treating within-group variation as negligible.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Cellular basis of pregnancy-associated brain changes
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Which cellular, vascular, extracellular, and circuit changes give rise to the imaging differences observed during pregnancy, and how do these changes relate to brain function?
status: Long-lasting structural brain changes were reported in 2017 (Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`), but MRI volume changes do not directly establish neuron loss, improved function, or impairment.
solved_when: The imaging differences associated with pregnancy are traced to specific cellular, vascular, extracellular, and circuit mechanisms whose relationship to function is characterized.
why: It prevents unsupported interpretations — such as assumed neuron loss, improvement, or impairment — of a major human physiological transition.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`.

title: Menopause-related neural change versus chronological aging
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Can we tell apart the neural changes driven by the menopausal hormonal transition from those that simply come with chronological aging? More precisely, can longitudinal causal designs isolate the specific effect of the ovarian hormonal transition from the intertwined contributions of vascular change, sleep, treatment, and prior health?
status: Work on pregnancy has shown that endocrine transitions can be accompanied by persistent neural changes — Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458` — but this does not address the distinct causal question of menopause specifically. Reference atlases of cell-type diversity across the adult human brain, Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`, provide supporting context, but no study answers the menopause-specific causal problem.
solved_when: A longitudinal causal study design is specified that successfully separates menopause-related neural change from chronological aging, vascular change, sleep, treatment, and prior health history.
why: It enables mechanism-based evaluation of menopausal symptoms and of interventions targeting them.
key_works: Hoekzema et al. (2017), *Pregnancy leads to long-lasting changes in human brain structure*, DOI: `10.1038/nn.4458`; Siletti et al. (2023), *Transcriptomic diversity of cell types across the adult human brain*, DOI: `10.1126/science.add7046`.

title: Gene–environment mechanisms across the life course
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: How do specific environmental exposures interact with an individual's genetic and developmental state to alter neural trajectories across the life course? A satisfactory answer requires measurements of the exposures themselves, rather than broad proxies, together with models of their interaction with genetic variation and developmental stage.
status: Genetic discovery and reliable population-level brain associations have each advanced substantially, but as largely separate literatures; their mechanistic interaction remains far harder to establish than either marginal association. Key works include Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`, and Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.
solved_when: A framework exists that identifies how specific measured exposures modify neural trajectories as a function of genetic and developmental state — going beyond marginal genetic associations and marginal brain-wide associations to a validated mechanistic interaction.
why: It would connect environmental prevention strategies to biological susceptibility, allowing interventions to be targeted to those whose genetic and developmental context makes them most vulnerable.
key_works: Satterstrom et al. (2020), *Large-Scale Exome Sequencing Study Implicates Both Developmental and Functional Changes in the Neurobiology of Autism*, DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2019.12.036`; Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`.

title: Population-inclusive neural reference models
subfield: Sex, hormonal transitions, diversity, and environment
open: Can we build normative (reference) models of the brain and behavior that stay calibrated for every population they are applied to — across ancestry, language, disability, age, socioeconomic conditions, and acquisition sites — rather than only for well-represented groups? Formally, the goal is normative models whose predictive distributions remain valid (with explicit, honest uncertainty) for poorly represented groups.
status: Large-sample reproducibility studies establish that sufficient data is necessary for reproducible brain-wide association, yet large sample size alone does not guarantee representative coverage or fairness — leaving population-inclusive calibration open. Key works: Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.
solved_when: Normative models are constructed that remain calibrated across ancestry, language, disability, age, socioeconomic conditions, and acquisition sites, and that carry explicit uncertainty quantification for poorly represented groups.
why: Without such models, reference datasets systematically misclassify people from underrepresented groups, embedding bias into clinical and scientific inference.
key_works: Marek et al. (2022), *Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Verifiable privacy for neural data
open: How can we build combined technical and governance controls that prevent unauthorized inference from neural recordings — including inferences that become possible only after the data were collected? In formal terms, the goal is a system whose privacy guarantees remain verifiable and enforceable against decoding capabilities that were not anticipated at collection time.
status: UNESCO adopted its Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in 2025, but a normative framework alone does not provide enforceable, technically verified privacy guarantees. The need is sharpened by rapid progress in neural decoding, e.g. Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`; related tools may come from privacy-preserving computation in cryptography and the study of future inference attacks in security.
solved_when: A deployed control scheme exists that both limits unauthorized inference from neural recordings as currently possible and demonstrably covers future, unanticipated inference uses, with the guarantees technically verified and enforceable rather than merely normative.
why: As decoding methods improve and recorded data are reused, people's private mental information becomes vulnerable in ways they never consented to; such controls protect them across that evolving landscape.
key_works: UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*; Card et al. (2024), *An Accurate and Rapidly Calibrating Speech Neuroprosthesis*, DOI: `10.1056/NEJMoa2314132`.

title: Funded lifetime obligations for neural implants
open: Who pays for — and actually provides — the long-term care of a neural implant after a study ends? The goal is to establish enforceable, financed arrangements covering maintenance, software support, explantation, replacement, data access, and continuity of care when a trial concludes or a developer disappears.
status: Post-trial neural-implant obligations have been explicitly examined in neuroethics, but identifying responsibilities is not the same as funding and operationalizing them; no enforceable financed framework currently exists. Key works: Dasgupta et al. (2024), *What Happens After a Neural Implant Study? Neuroethics Expert Workshop on Post-Trial Obligations*, DOI: `10.1007/s12152-024-09549-2`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.
solved_when: Binding, funded arrangements exist that specify who is responsible and with what resources for maintenance, software support, explantation, replacement, data access, and continuity in the events of trial end or developer disappearance, and these arrangements are operational rather than merely articulated.
why: Without such arrangements, trial participants can be left with unsupported hardware implanted in their brains — a harm that identified-but-unfunded responsibilities do nothing to prevent.
key_works: Dasgupta et al. (2024), *What Happens After a Neural Implant Study? Neuroethics Expert Workshop on Post-Trial Obligations*, DOI: `10.1007/s12152-024-09549-2`; UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*.

title: Sustainable funding for shared neuroscience infrastructure
open: How can the field establish durable funding and maintenance models for shared neuroscience infrastructure — standards, archives, reference datasets, and essential software? Concretely, what governance and financing arrangements can sustain such infrastructure with measurable service quality and succession plans?
status: Neurodata Without Borders demonstrates the value of shared infrastructure, but a functioning ecosystem does not eliminate its continuing maintenance and financing requirements (Rübel et al. (2022), *The Neurodata Without Borders ecosystem for neurophysiological data science*, DOI: `10.7554/eLife.78362`).
solved_when: A funding and maintenance model exists that is durable across grant cycles, includes measurable service quality and succession plans, and covers standards, archives, reference datasets, and essential software.
why: It prevents foundational scientific assets from decaying between grants.

title: Closing neurological-care access gaps
open: How can neurological care — diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and essential services — be delivered sustainably to underserved populations, and what delivery models, once identified and financed, actually close those access gaps?
status: The WHO intersectoral action plan supplies agreed objectives, but implementation, workforce capacity, procurement, and financing remain separate, locally testable problems. Reference: World Health Organization (2022), *Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders 2022–2031*, ISBN: `9789240076624`.
solved_when: Delivery models are identified and financed that sustainably improve access to diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and essential neurological services in underserved settings.
why: Converts scientific capability into actual population benefit; without workable delivery and financing, clinical advances do not reach the people they are meant to serve.
key_works: World Health Organization (2022), *Intersectoral global action plan on epilepsy and other neurological disorders 2022–2031*, ISBN: `9789240076624`.

title: Adaptive consent and oversight for evolving neural capabilities
open: How can consent and review systems for neural technologies be designed so that they stay meaningful as the technologies themselves change? Formally, the goal is to develop governance mechanisms that adapt as neural datasets gain new uses, implanted devices change function, and engineered neural tissues acquire more complex capabilities.
status: UNESCO's 2025 recommendation, *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*, establishes an international normative reference, while organoid integration and decoding advances — e.g., Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w` — change the capabilities that oversight must address.
solved_when: A consent and review framework exists that adapts to evolving neural capabilities — new uses of neural data, changing implant function, and increasingly complex engineered neural tissues — while remaining meaningful for the parties whose consent it governs.
why: It makes governance track actual capability rather than fixed historical assumptions, so oversight does not become obsolete as neurotechnology advances.
key_works: UNESCO (2025), *Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology*; Revah et al. (2022), *Maturation and circuit integration of transplanted human cortical organoids*, DOI: `10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w`.
